title: Bills' Bye Week Injury Update: Will DJ Moore, Dalton Kincaid Return Next Game?
full_text:
It sounds, and looks, as if the Buffalo Bills expect to come out of their Week 7 bye nearing full health throughout the roster.
The Bills scratched only two injured players prior to their October 18 road win over the Las Vegas Raiders. It was the second game in a row that wide receiver DJ Moore and defensive lineman Ed Oliver were inactive.
"I'd like to think that they're close [to being healthy enough to play]," said Brady as Buffalo hits its bye week.
Additionally, both tight end Dalton Kincaid and edge rusher Bradley Chubb left the Week 6 game due to rib issues, but both subsequently returned at some point.
Other than what appear to be minor issues with those four players, the Bills have no other injury concerns on the 53-man roster at the moment.
"I think we're going into it fairly healthy," said franchise quarterback Josh Allen after a 33-30 win in Las Vegas. "Bye weeks are always great for that, getting guys back, but we got to continue to grow."
Furthermore, defensive back Jordan Hancock, who has been on the shelf due to a calf strain, is eligible to come off Injured Reserve in time for the November 1 home game against the Baltimore Ravens.
Moore's issue extends back to late in the second quarter during the Week 2 game against the Detroit Lions. He came down hard on his shoulder while diving for a pass in the end zone in the September 17 primetime affair.
Having not missed a game since December 2020, when his was with the Carolina Panthers, Moore fought through the AC joint sprain to make himself available in Weeks 3 and 4. Against the New England Patriots on October 4, however, Moore reaggravated the injury while falling to the ground trying to make a catch.
For the past two weeks, Moore missed back-to-back practices before participating on a limited basis on the third day. He was questionable to appear in the last two games, but the Bills chose not to dress their WR1, presumably with the idea that giving him three uninterrupted weeks of rest and recovery will yield 100 percent health coming out of the bye.
Buffalo was likely playing the long game, out of precaution, with Oliver, too.
Oliver was also banged up during the Week 4 home loss to New England. He took a hit to the knee area on his left leg at the end of a okay near the sideline.
The Bills held Oliver out of five consecutive practices before he finally returned in a limited fashion last Friday.
Chubb was the first to leave the October 18 road game, suffering a ribs injury that sidelined the edge rusher early in the second quarter.
The Bills labeled Chubb as questionable to return. Although he did subsequently re-enter the game, he saw limited action with second-round rookie TJ Parker taking the large majority of snaps the rest of the way. Chubb was on the field for 21 of 66 defensive snaps.
Kincaid left midway through the third quarter as he was seen grabbing at his torso, in apparent discomfort, after running a route in the red zone. The Bills took him into the locker room, ruling his return questionable.
The tight end was back on the field when Buffalo took possession with 8:01 remaining in the fourth quarter. He gained 14 yards on a catch three snaps after returning.
The fact that both Chubb and Kincaid returned to action to some extent bodes well for their availability immediately following the bye.

title: What to Expect from Bills Safety Room After CJ Gardner-Johnson's Suspension
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills will already be down at least one starter for their next matchup, when they play the Baltimore Ravens in two weeks.
With safety CJ Gardner-Johnson suspended for one game , the rotation in the secondary will look different for at least one week.
We already saw how Jim Leonhard handled the loss of a starting safety mid-game against the Raiders, but the defensive coordinator now has two weeks to gameplan for it.
Here's what options Leonhard has at his disposal to deploy against an offensive in Baltimore with plenty of talnet.
When Gardner-Johnson left the game, the main beneficiary in terms of snaps was Damar Hamlin. While he doesn't provide an intruging ceiling, he does raise the flloor of the DB room and help calm the storm on the back end.
Leonhard specifically complimented his calming precense, effective communication and positional flexibility in his press conference on Monday, citing the 45 defensive snaps he played as evidence.
"He does not get the credit for the amount of things he's asked to do within a gameplan," Leonhard said.
Per PFF, Hamlin wasn't even targeted while in coverage, despite Kirk Cousins attempting 41 passes. The DB played 31 snaps at free safety, 10 in the box, three in the slot and one on the line of scrimmage, showcasing his versatility.
Fifth round rookie Jalon Kilgore finally got meaningful defensive snaps, and it was a mixed bag for the DB out of South Carolina.
Kilgore played 11 defensive snaps, one of which was a key pass break up on third down to force a punt. Later in the game, he got burned by Tre Tucker in an obvious prevent situation, where he allowed the receiver to get behind him for a touchdown to keep the Raiders alive.
The rookie is no where close to the reliable player Hamlin is, but his off the charts athleticism should intriuge the Bills enough to get him on the field more.
The safety had a 9.60 relative athletic score going into the draft, highlighted by his 4.40 40-yard dash and "elite" speed and explosion grades. For comparison, Hamlin's relative athletic score was a 7.00, with a "good" speed grade and "okay" explosion grade.
Calls have only grown for the Bills to move on from Gardner-Johnson, so Leonhard and the Bills might need to prepare for a longer-term solution that lasts them the rest of the season.
For now, with the starting safety slated to miss just one game, expect to see a majority of snaps go to the veteran in Hamlin. If Jordan Hancock is able to return from IR to back up Dee Alford in the slot, Hamlin won't need to sub into the nickel at all, meaning he'd likely see the lion's share of snaps.
However, if the team decided to move on from Gardner-Johnson, it would be beneficial to give the rookie with the higher ceiling more playing time, and implement more of a rotation between Kilgore and Hamlin before the rookie is (ideally) able to take over full-time.

title: Bills' Snap Counts in Las Vegas: Keon Coleman, Four Rookies Win Big Entering Bye Week
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills head into their Week 7 bye with a 5-1 record, but they're still not clicking on all cylinders.
"I'm not happy with how the team's playing right now," said first-year head coach Joe Brady one day after the 33-30 win over the Las Vegas Raiders.
The Bills' snap counts from that October 18 road victory are proof that the coaching staff is still trying to figure out who fits best at certain spots, especially on the defense.
Safety Cole Bishop only defensive player to see 100 percent of snaps in Week 6.
Buffalo totaled 68 offensive snaps and 66 on defense.
Here are five clear winners based upon Week 6 playtime percentages.
Official Bills' Week 6 Snap Counts [ @NFL345 ] pic.twitter.com/Fc6ZdROP55
With DJ Moore inactive , Keon Coleman was the Bills' most frequently deployed wide receiver against the Raiders.
Coleman, who is experiencing a renaissance of sorts thus far this season, recorded 58 snaps. He caught a touchdown pass for the third game in a row.
“He's where he needs to be. He's handling everything like a pro," said Brady. "There's so much trust we have for him as the player, the development. He continues to just make plays.”
In addition to his improvement as a professional , Coleman's willingness and ability to block in the run game explain why he was on the field 85 percent of the time.
Outside linebacker TJ Parker had been relatively quiet outside of a couple plays over the first five weeks of his career.
On Sunday, the Bills needed their highest drafted rookie to step up, and the No. 35 overall pick delivered. With starter Bradley Chubb temporarily unavailable due to a rib issue, Parker totaled 41 defensive snaps, which amount to 62 percent.
"I thought some guys stepped up. TJ's one. He played a great game for us. We needed him to. [Bradley] Chubb battled through some injuries," said defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard.
Second-round rookie cornerback Davison Igbinosun earned his second consecutive start over Maxwell Hairston on Sunday in Las Vegas.
The aggressive Igbinosun totaled 42 snaps on defense compared to 26 for Hairston, a 2025 first-round pick who has struggled. Igbinosun brings size and a contagious energy to the outside CB spot.
"I think what he's done the last couple weeks, he's definitely earned a high majority of the snaps at the corner position," said Leonhard. "I know what I'm getting, play in and play out. I think he's stepped in and done a great job handling more volume in this defense."
With starting safety Chauncey Gardner-Johnson's ejection as a result of repulsive behavior , veteran Damar Hamlin was called into full-time action.
Meanwhile, fifth-round rookie Jalon Kilgore picked up important reps as a dime safety. Kilgore logged a key pass breakup before surrendering a late touchdown.
It was a defensive debut for Kilgore, who saw 11 snaps with the unit in Sunday. He was active for the first time ever in the Monday Night Football win over the Los Angeles Rams, appearing exclusively on special teams.
With Brady saying he hoped to see more of fourth-round rookie linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr last week, the raw talent was part of the defensive formation 33 percent t of the game against the Raiders.
Playing a season-high 22 snaps, Elarms-Orr appeared to miss assignments in a couple of instances. He was on the field spelling Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams at different points in the game.

title: Panthers’ Experienced Linebacker Duo Has Emerged as a Force
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers will host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday looking for their third straight win. The team returned from its off week this past Sunday and shut down the Jalen Hurts-less Philadelphia Eagles. Dave Canales’s club outgained the Birds, 399-222, in total yards in what proved to be a 25-14 victory.
Six weeks into the season, the Panthers own a 3-2 record and are all alone in first place in the NFC South. The team has won two three straight and three of their last four games following a 59-37 home loss to the Chicago Bears . Quarterback Bryce Young has played exceptional football all season, and Ejiro Evero’s defensive unit has settled in since that forgettable start.
General manager Dan Morgan added several new faces to this side of the ball via free agency in March, and another notable performer after the conclusion of the preseason. Edge rusher Jaelan Phillips (Eagles) inked a four-year, $120 million deal, while 2025 Pro Bowler Devin Lloyd (Jaguars) signed a three-year, $42 million contract.
Finally, Bobby Okereke—late of the New York Giants— joined the club in late August via a one-year, $ 1.5 million deal. It’s the latter two linebackers that have combined to make a huge impact.
DEVIN LLOYD JUST HAD ONE OF THE GREATEST LINEBACKER PERFORMANCES IN NFL HISTORY 9 TKL, 2 TFL, 2 INT, 1 SACK, 1 TD, 1 QBH, 3 PD Carolina may have landed one of the best defensive pickups of the offseason. pic.twitter.com/4BGRbQ7jxq
Lloyd leads Carolina with 35 tackles, despite the fact that he missed the Week 3 game at Cleveland. There’s also a pair of sacks, two interceptions (1 returned for a touchdown), four quarterback hits, and three passes defensed.
Okereke is right behind Lloyd with 34 stops. He’s totaled one sack, a pair of QB hits, one pick, a forced fumble, and four passes defensed. In Sunday’s victory at Philadelphia, he led Carolina with eight stops, three of those for losses, and knocked down two passes.
1st and 10 · Philadelphia Eagles Tanner McKee ( @McKeeTmckee ) is sacked at PHI 15 for an 11-yard loss by Bobby Okereke ( @BobbyOkereke ) https://t.co/p3gaDF1CnO pic.twitter.com/NWlRQomQPK
On the Eagles’ first play from scrimmage, he dropped quarterback Tanner McKee for an 11-yard loss and set the tone for a game in which Nick Sirianni’s team was limited to just 3.6 yards per play.
Best LB duos in the NFL through Week 6: 1. Lloyd/Okereke (CAR) 2. Jones/Thomas (SEA) 3. Edmunds/Reese (NYG) 4. Smith/Simpson (BAL) 5. Oluokun/Miller (JAX) Carolina's LB duo ranked 22nd in these same categories in 2025. Now it's first. Incredible upgrade by Dan Morgan this… pic.twitter.com/mjD8ccCW4W
After six weeks of play, Lloyd is Pro Football Focus’ 14th-ranked linebacker with a 71.8 grade, while Okereke is just two spots below him (70.5).
Again, this has been a much-improved defense still that Week 1 home debacle against Caleb Williams and company. In their last four outings, the Panthers have given up a total of 64 points and surrendered only six offensive touchdowns. That’s a far cry from allowing 552 yards and eight offensive TDs in 60 minutes of play vs. the Bears..
Thanks to these two key offseason additions, as well as contributions from other newcomers, Carolina’s defense appears to finally be making some significant strides.

title: 3 Panthers Who Came Out of Nowhere in Sunday's Win Over the Eagles
full_text:
There are some pretty easy choices if we're talking about the biggest names from the Panthers' 25-14 win over Philadelphia. Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards, Bryce Young threw for 281, and Jalen Coker had 97 yards in his first game back.
But I wanted to go a little deeper than that. There were a few guys who probably weren't getting much attention before the game and ended up having a lot to do with Carolina winning it. One caught two touchdowns, another came up with a huge play on special teams, and the third seemed to be around the ball all afternoon.
Here are three guys I didn't expect to be talking this much about after the game.
Be honest. Who had Tommy Tremble catching two touchdowns Sunday?
Tremble only caught four passes, but he made them count. His first touchdown went for 12 yards and gave Carolina a 10-0 lead in the second quarter. The second one was even bigger because Philadelphia had just cut the lead to 19-14 when Young found him for a 19-yard touchdown.
I liked what Tremble did in the running game, too. Carolina lined him up at fullback on fourth-and-1, and he helped clear the way for Hubbard to break a 19-yard run. The Panthers showed a similar look on another fourth-and-1 later in the drive, and Young got Philadelphia to jump with a hard count.
That's really the thing with Tremble. He can go through a game doing a bunch of little things that most people probably aren't paying attention to, and then you look at the box score, and he has one catch for eight yards. Sunday, he finally got some numbers to go along with all that other stuff.
Four catches, 46 yards and two touchdowns will get your attention.
Tyus is probably my favorite one on this list because you aren't going to understand what he did by just looking at the box score. Philadelphia had cut Carolina's lead to 19-14 in the fourth quarter, and the Eagles were about to get the ball back with a chance to take the lead.
That's when Tyus nearly got to the punt. He deflected it, though it went forward, so it wasn't an official block. The kick went only nine yards, and instead of Philadelphia flipping the field, Carolina got the ball back in Eagles territory. A few plays later, Young hit Tremble for the touchdown that made it 25-14.
Think about how different that looks with a normal punt. Carolina probably starts deep in its own territory, and Philadelphia's defense has a chance to get the ball right back to its offense. Instead, the Panthers were already on the Eagles' side of the field and turned it into seven points.
That's a pretty big moment from a guy most of us probably weren't thinking about when the fourth quarter started.
It didn't take long for Okereke to show up Sunday. On Philadelphia's first offensive play, he came through for an 11-yard sack of Tanner McKee, and he kept popping up from there.
Okereke finished with a team-high 11 tackles, a sack, three tackles for loss, and two passes defended. The Eagles finished with only 222 total yards and 35 on the ground, and Okereke was right in the middle of a lot of what Carolina was doing defensively.
With Devin Lloyd getting so much attention early this season, and deservedly so, I thought Okereke deserved some love after this one. You don't hear his name talked about nearly as much, but Sunday was probably his best game of the season.
From the sack on the first snap to everything he did against the run, this was one of those games where you kept noticing No. 58. Okereke was everywhere, and on a day when Carolina's defense allowed only 222 yards, he was a big reason why.

title: Panthers' Super Bowl Odds Continue to Climb After Impressive Road Win
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers did what they were supposed to do: control the game and find a win on the road against a depleted Philadelphia Eagles team. The 25-14 win moves Carolina to 3-2 on the season and gives them a steady cushion atop the NFC South.
With both the Falcons and Buccaneers losing on Sunday, Carolina's odds of winning the division rose. Winning the division, of course, means making the playoffs, and that means the Super Bowl is in sight.
Does that make Carolina a Super Bowl favorite? Of course not, but the Panthers' Super Bowl odds are rising, and rightfully so.
With wins over the Eagles, Lions, and Falcons, the Panthers are starting to change the national narrative. Theres a consistency, at least on offense, that Carolina hasn't had in the Canales-Young era, but now theres real growth.
As the narrative shifts, so have the current Super Bowl odds. In terms of value, the Panthers could be at a better price than teams that have shorter odds.
Sports Illustrated's Peter Dewey dropped his Week 7 NFL power rankings based on Super Bowl 61 odds . This list isn't based solely on who has the shortest odds, but on which teams offer the best value at their current odds.
With that said, Dewey slotted the Panthers at No. 15. Per DraftKings Sportsbook, the Panthers currently have +5500 odds to win Super Bowl 61, that's the 17th shortest odds in the league.
Meanwhile, the Los Angeles Rams are sitting at +1200 to win the Super Bowl, the sixth-shortest odds, despite being 2-4 on the season and possibly being the NFL's most-injured team.
The Panthers ranked one spot ahead of the Rams in Dewey's power rankings, which is completely justified based soley on value at the current odds.
The Rams are tied for last place in their division. The roster is riddled with injuries to key contributors such as Davante Adams, Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, Kobie Turner, and many more.
LA even lost its second kicker of the season after Blake Grupe tore his ACL before his first game with the team concluded.
Meanwhile, the Panthers play in the second-worst division in football, Carolina already has a comfortable lead at the top, and has a division win against the second-best team in the NFC South, the Falcons.
This can easily change if the Rams find a groove and get healthier towards the end of the season, but for right now, it's perfectly fair to like Carolina's Super Bowl odds more than the Rams'.

title: The Panthers Won in Philadelphia — Here's What I'm Buying and What I'm Not
full_text:
The Panthers went into Philadelphia and came away with a 25-14 win, and there was plenty to like about what they did.
Carolina moved the ball, Bryce Young made some big throws, and the defense never let the Eagles get much going. Jalen Coker also looked pretty comfortable in his first game back, giving Young another weapon alongside Tetairoa McMillan. Still, I'm not ready to get carried away with this one.
Philadelphia was missing some important players and became even more shorthanded as the game went along, so you have to keep that in mind when looking at this win. Carolina deserves credit for taking care of business, but Sunday also gave us a little more to think about with this team.
Let's start here because I don't want it to sound like I'm taking anything away from the Panthers. They went on the road, controlled most of the game, and beat Philadelphia by 11 points. That's a good Sunday, no matter who was on the other side.
But the Eagles weren't close to full strength. Jalen Hurts and Saquon Barkley were already out, and Philadelphia lost more help as the game went along. Carolina wasn't exactly getting the best version of the Eagles.
The Panthers still had to beat the guys who were out there. We've seen Carolina lose enough games over the years that it probably should've won, so I'm not going to hold it against them for taking care of business. The Panthers were the healthier team and played like it.
That's what they were supposed to do.
We've been waiting a few weeks to see what Young would look like with McMillan and Coker on the field together, and Sunday gave us another good look at it. Coker finished with six catches for 97 yards, while McMillan had six for 86. For me, this was probably the most encouraging thing to come out of the game.
That's 183 receiving yards between the two of them, but it's not just about the number. Young had another receiver making plays opposite McMillan, and everything didn't have to go through one guy. Teams are still going to worry about McMillan, but Coker gives them somebody else to deal with.
I'm not expecting those two to combine for nearly 200 yards every week. But Carolina finally got both of them on the field together, and we saw what it could do for Young and the passing game.
Now let's see what it looks like when defenses have a few weeks to adjust to it.
I still don't know how the Panthers managed to have 149 penalty yards and win by 11 points. Carolina was flagged 13 times, and some of them came at the worst possible times. There were several moments where the Panthers would make a play, only to give some of it right back because of a flag.
They got away with it Sunday, but against a healthier team, I'm not so sure they do. That's what's frustrating because Carolina actually did a lot of things well. Young didn't turn the ball over, Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards, and the defense held Philadelphia to 222 total yards.
Clean up even some of those penalties, and this game probably isn't as close for as long as it was. Carolina can fix that, but it needs to happen because 149 penalty yards isn't something you're going to keep overcoming.
I don't think Sunday proved the Panthers are suddenly one of the best teams in the NFC, as Philadelphia was too beat up for me to go that far. But I do think we're learning a little more about Carolina. The Panthers are starting to win games they're supposed to win, which hasn't always been a given around here.
Young has more help around him, the defense is doing its part, and Carolina is finding ways to win even when it makes things harder on itself. There's still plenty to fix, and 149 penalty yards is a pretty obvious place to start. But the Panthers went into Philadelphia as the healthier team, handled a game they should've won, and came home 3-2.

title: Early Panthers-Buccaneers Odds Revealed, But There's a Big Catch
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers are coming off two straight wins (sandwiching a needed bye week) to surge into first place in the NFC South. They were favored last time out on the road against the Philadelphia Eagles, but only after some late injury updates for Philly.
This week, they're headed back home to take on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in an early-season rivalry bout. While the Buccaneers are struggling at the bottom of the division, these matchups are always tough and important.
So, what do the odds tell us this week?
The Panthers open as 3.5-point favorites at home ( FanDuel ) over the Buccaneers. One could argue that the spread is a little too small given the trajectory of the two franchises and the most recent outings for both.
Regardless, the Panthers are favored at home. They're -105 to cover the spread, while the Buccaneers are -115 to cover. That's also a little bit interesting. The Panthers have won three contests by an average of 16 points.
The Panthers are -180 on the moneyline, so they are expected to win outright. The Buccaneers are +152 to win. The over/under is set at 44.5, and the over and under are both currently set at -110.
So, based on that, the oddsmakers expect the Panthers to win a tight contest, 24-21. In other words, the Panthers are not expected to blow out a 1-5 team at home.
Now, there is a huge caveat to these odds and what they're telling us. Right now, it is totally up in the air as to which QB the Panthers will see. Jalon Daniels has been filling in for Baker Mayfield, who has been nursing a thumb injury on his throwing hand.
He's supposed to return to practice this week, and the Buccaneers may be able to start him. His moronic, stubborn need for a revenge narrative against the Panthers will probably push him to try to play at all costs.
That would change thing. Mayfield struggled before getting hurt and will be coming back from a difficult injury on his throwing hand, which will limit him. Still, he is better than Daniels at this point, and that would shift the odds.
What's telling about the current odds is that the Panthers aren't favored by more. They are clearly the best team in the NFC South. They're at home. The Buccaneers are 1-5, and right now, Daniels is in line to start again. The Panthers are getting healthier, and they're coming off two pretty substantial wins.
It's the NFL, and any team can win any game, but the odds aren't meant to reflect that. It seems Carolina is still being wildly underestimated and perhaps a little disrespected.

title: The Panthers Finally Won the Kind of Game They Usually Find a Way to Lose
full_text:
Not every win is going to look good, and Sunday's 25-14 win over Philadelphia definitely didn't. The Panthers committed 13 penalties for a franchise-record 149 yards, couldn't run the ball early, and let an Eagles team missing several key players hang around way longer than it should have.
There will be plenty for Dave Canales to complain about when they go back and watch this one, and I'm sure the penalties will be pretty high on that list.
But I'll take an ugly win like that all day.
We've watched enough Panthers football over the last few years to know what usually happens when Carolina starts piling up mistakes. One bad penalty turns into another, the other team hangs around, and eventually you're sitting there wondering how the Panthers managed to blow another one. Sunday had a few moments where I thought we might be headed there again.
The penalties were ridiculous. Carolina had eight for 105 yards in the first half alone, something I wrote about at halftime when it was hard to believe the Panthers were still winning .
They finished with 13 for 149, and Panthers.com noted that Carolina also had three good returns wiped out by penalties , including a 50-yard kickoff return from David Moore. Somehow, the Panthers still went into halftime leading 10-7.
The offense wasn't exactly lighting it up early, either. Chuba Hubbard had only 24 yards on eight carries in the first half, and while Carolina was moving the ball, it wasn't doing enough with those drives. Against an Eagles team this beat up, I thought the Panthers should've had a much bigger lead.
Carolina didn't get away from the running game in the second half, and eventually Hubbard started finding some room. He finished with 120 yards and a touchdown on 28 carries after averaging only 3.0 yards per carry in the first half. That jumped to 4.8 yards per carry after halftime , which says a lot about why Carolina kept giving him the ball.
Bryce Young missed some throws, but he still threw for 281 yards and two touchdowns without turning the ball over. Having Jalen Coker back certainly didn't hurt. He finished with 97 yards, Tetairoa McMillan had 86, and suddenly Young had two guys on the outside making plays instead of everything falling on McMillan.
I've been high on Coker for a while. I had him No. 1 in my Panthers young player power rankings , and Sunday was a pretty good reminder of why. That's something we really haven't gotten to see much of yet with Coker and McMillan healthy together.
The defense deserves some credit here, too. Philadelphia finished with only 222 total yards, which looks even better when you consider how many yards Carolina was giving away with penalties. The Eagles didn't do much offensively for most of the afternoon, but they stayed close enough to finally make things uncomfortable in the fourth quarter.
Tanner McKee found DeVonta Smith for a 19-yard touchdown to cut Carolina's lead to 19-14. After everything the Panthers had done to keep Philadelphia in the game, the Eagles were suddenly one stop away from getting the ball back with a chance to take the lead. We've watched enough Panthers games over the years to know how that can go.
This time, Carolina answered.
Tre Tyus got pressure on Philadelphia's next punt, which went only nine yards and gave the Panthers the ball in Eagles territory. Young and the offense took advantage of it, with his 19-yard touchdown pass to Tommy Tremble pushing the lead back to 25-14. Instead of giving Philadelphia another chance to make things interesting, Carolina finally put the game away.
That's probably what I liked most about Sunday. The Panthers had spent a good part of the afternoon shooting themselves in the foot, and when Philadelphia finally got close enough to make them pay for it, Carolina didn't give the game away. They made the plays they needed to make and got out of there with a win.
I'm not going to make too much out of beating this version of the Eagles. Philadelphia was without Jalen Hurts, Saquon Barkley, and several other players, while Carolina was the healthier team. This was a game the Panthers should've won, even if they made it a lot harder than it needed to be.
But that's also why I came away liking this win a little more than I thought I would. Carolina wasn't sharp, the penalties were awful, and there were a few decisions from Canales that I still don't understand. In other years, that has been more than enough for the Panthers to find a way to lose.
That doesn't mean Carolina can keep playing this way. Give away 149 yards in penalties against Tampa Bay next Sunday, and there's a pretty good chance we're having a completely different conversation afterward. The Panthers have plenty to clean up this week, and nobody should look at Sunday and think they played particularly well.
But you're not going to play well every week. Sometimes the running game takes a while to get going, the quarterback misses some throws, or you spend half the afternoon getting in your own way. There are going to be games where you just have to get out of there with a win and worry about fixing everything else later.
That's what Carolina did in Philadelphia.
It was ugly, but 3-2 looks pretty good to me.

title: Panthers’ Week 1 Defensive Disaster Becoming a Distant Memory
full_text:
In 2024, the Carolina Panthers fielded one of the worst defensive units in the league in recent memory. The team was dead last in total defense and rushing defense in terms of yards allowed. The team gave up 534 points, the most in a single season in NFL history. Coordinator Ejiro Evero’s unit gave up 59 offensive touchdowns, including a league-high 35 through the air.
The following offseason, general manager Dan Morgan used free agency to add defensive linemen Tershawn Wharton and Bobby Brown III, pass rusher Patrick Jones II, and physical safety Tre’von Moehrig. The draft brought edge rushers Nic Scourton (2-Texas A&M) and Princely Umanmielen (3-Mississippi). The Panthers improved to 16th in the NFL in fewest total yards allowed, and 20th vs. the run.
Now comes the 2026 offseason. Morgan opened up the checkbook in a big way. He inked edge rusher Jaelan Phillips to a four-year, $120 million deal and 2025 Pro Bowler Devin Lloyd to a three-year, $42 million contract. In August, he added New York Giants’ castoff Bobby Okereke.
Dave Canales’s team welcomed the Chicago Bears to Bank of America Stadium on the opening Sunday of the season in a clash of defending division champions. The contest produced a combined 96 points, but the Bears had 59 of those in a 22-point road victory. It was the most points allowed by the Panthers in a game in the franchise’s 32-year history.
Posting #Bears top 3 plays of every game, in the 2026 season. Week 1: Chicago Bears @ Carolina Panthers 🏈 #1: Caleb Williams with the handoff to Kyle Monangai. Monangai runs up the middle, breaks the tackle for a 61 yard rushing touchdown. THIS WAS AN AWESOME RUN!!! 🤩 🐻⬇️ pic.twitter.com/u7FmZHA5Kn
Chicago’s offense gained a whopping 552 yards —291 yards on the ground—and averaged an imposing 7.9 yards per play. Ben Johnson’s club scored at least 14 points in each quarter. All told, not a good start for Canales’ club.
1st and 10 · Philadelphia Eagles Tanner McKee ( @McKeeTmckee ) is sacked at PHI 15 for an 11-yard loss by Bobby Okereke ( @BobbyOkereke ) https://t.co/p3gaDF1CnO pic.twitter.com/NWlRQomQPK
Talk about a turnaround? Carolina apparently learned a lot after facing Chicago’s potent attack. And this has been a much different defense ever since. In their last four contests, the Panthers have allowed a combined 64 points and six offensive TDs while permitting just 304.8 yards per game. In fact, Evero’s defense has limited three of its last four opponents to fewer than 300 yards of total offense.
The run defense has gotten better on a weekly basis. In their last four contests, Canales’s team has given up 157, 132, 46, and 35 yards on the ground, respectively. And while the club hasn’t come up with a takeaway in their last two games, the Panthers have played turnover-free in those contests.
It will be interesting to see if the recent progress continues this Sunday when the NFC South leaders host the rival Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

That includes television, as he spent more than two decades at ESPN, and was part of shows that garnered five Emmy Awards. He also spent the 2015 NFL season with Thursday Night Football on CBS/NFLN.

title: 3 Panthers Who Made a Statement in Philadelphia & 1 Thing Carolina Can't Ignore
full_text:
The Panthers came out of the bye and took care of business Sunday, beating the Eagles 25-14 in Philadelphia to improve to 3-2.
It wasn't always pretty, especially with all the penalties, but Carolina was the better team for most of the afternoon. The Panthers finished with 399 yards, didn't turn the ball over, and held Philadelphia to just 222 yards on the other side. That gives us quite a few choices for Stock Up and one pretty obvious choice for Stock Down.
I was interested to see what Coker would look like in his first game back, and it didn't take long to see how much Young missed having him out there.
Coker led Carolina with six catches for 97 yards on 13 targets, including a 32-yard catch on third-and-8 in the third quarter when the Panthers were backed up at their own 10. That drive eventually went 92 yards and ended with a Chuba Hubbard touchdown, and Coker's catch was the play that really got it started.
Before Coker went down, I had him sitting at No. 1 in my Panthers young player power rankings , and Sunday was a pretty good reminder of why. McMillan finished with six catches for 86 yards, so the two combined for 183. Young doesn't have to spend the entire game looking for McMillan when Coker is on the other side, and Sunday gave us a pretty good look at what that can mean for this offense.
Coker isn't going to have 13 targets every week, but that's not really the point. Carolina got one of Young's favorite targets back, and he immediately led the team in receiving.
I'd say Young is pretty happy to have him back.
Hubbard is another one who didn't look like an obvious Stock Up at halftime. He had eight carries for only 24 yards, and Philadelphia was doing a pretty good job of keeping Carolina from getting much going on the ground.
The Panthers didn't get away from it, though, and that ended up being a big part of the second half. Hubbard finished with 28 carries for 120 yards and a touchdown, and his 19-yard run on fourth-and-1 was one of my favorite plays of the game. Carolina needed one yard, gave the ball to Hubbard, and got 19 instead.
I've written before about how Hubbard has quietly become another weapon for Young , and Sunday was another example of how much he means to this offense. We've seen him have games where he gets stronger as they go along, and that's pretty much what happened Sunday. He averaged 3.0 yards per carry in the first half and 4.8 after halftime.
Sometimes you just keep feeding Chuba.
By the fourth quarter, Carolina was able to lean on him and make Philadelphia keep tackling him. That's the kind of game Hubbard can give this offense, and it came at a good time with the Panthers trying to protect a lead on the road.
There are going to be games where Tremble does a lot for this offense, and his receiving numbers don't really show it. Sunday wasn't one of them.
He only caught four passes, but two of them went for touchdowns. The second one was the bigger of the two for me because Philadelphia had just cut Carolina's lead to 19-14 and finally had a little momentum. Young came right back and found Tremble for a 19-yard touchdown that put Carolina up 25-14.
I also liked the way Carolina used him in the running game. On Hubbard's 19-yard fourth-down run, Tremble lined up at fullback and helped lead the way. A few plays later, Carolina showed the same look on another fourth-and-1, and Young's hard count got Philadelphia to jump.
That's probably the best way to explain Tremble's value. He can catch two touchdowns, line up at fullback and block for Hubbard, and spend the rest of the afternoon doing things that aren't always going to show up in the box score. Sunday, he finally got some numbers to go along with all of it.
There really wasn't a Panthers player I wanted to force into Stock Down after this game. The penalties, on the other hand, made this one pretty easy.
I wrote at halftime about the almost unbelievable number of Carolina penalties piling up , and somehow it got worse. The Panthers finished with 13 penalties for a franchise-record 149 yards after already having eight for 105 in the first half.
That's way too much to overcome on a regular basis. Carolina got away with it because it didn't turn the ball over, held Philadelphia to 222 yards and was facing an Eagles offense already missing starting quarterback Jalen Hurts and its first three running backs, including Saquon Barkley.
I'm not going to complain too much about an 11-point road win, but Dave Canales has plenty to point to when they watch the film. The Panthers did enough good things Sunday to win despite giving away 149 yards in penalties.
Against a better or healthier offense, they might not be so lucky.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Dave Canales Had Two Weeks to Prepare. Did Panthers Coach Pass the Test?
full_text:
Coming out of a bye week, I expect a team to look better. It doesn't have to be perfect, but with an extra week to look at what's working and what isn't, I want to see some evidence that the time off actually helped.
I think we saw some of that from the Panthers in Sunday's 25-14 win over Philadelphia. Carolina finished with 399 yards, didn't turn the ball over, and held the Eagles to 222 yards. More importantly, the Panthers went on the road and won a game they were supposed to win.
But if we're grading Dave Canales specifically, I can't just look at the final score and give him an A. There were things I liked, especially as the game went along, but there were also a couple of decisions that I didn't understand.
The Panthers didn't have much of a running game in the first half. Chuba Hubbard had eight carries for 24 yards, and Philadelphia was doing a pretty good job of keeping him from getting anything going.
Carolina stayed with it, and eventually Hubbard started finding room. He finished with 28 carries for 120 yards and a touchdown, including a 19-yard run on fourth-and-1 in the second half. I liked that the Panthers didn't decide after a bad first half that the running game wasn't going to work.
We also finally got to see what the passing game could look like with Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan out there together. Coker finished with six catches for 97 yards, McMillan had six for 86, so the two combined for 183 yards. That's something Carolina can build on because Young doesn't have to spend the entire game depending on McMillan to make every big play.
Tommy Tremble was another part of the offense I liked. He caught four passes for 46 yards and two touchdowns, but Carolina also found other ways to use him. Tremble lined up at fullback and helped lead Hubbard on that 19-yard fourth-down run, then the Panthers showed a similar look later, and Young got Philadelphia to jump with a hard count.
The fourth quarter was probably what I liked most. Philadelphia cut the lead to 19-14 and suddenly had some life, but Carolina didn't let the game get away from them. Young and the offense answered, with Tremble's 19-yard touchdown giving the Panthers some breathing room again.
That's something this team hasn't always done very well.
The penalties are the obvious place to start. Carolina finished with 13 of them for a franchise-record 149 yards, and eight of those penalties for 105 yards came in the first half.
Canales called the number "outrageous" afterward, and that's a pretty good way to describe it. He's obviously not the one committing the penalties, and some of them were more costly than others. But when your team is coming out of a bye and gives away 149 yards, I think the head coach has to own part of that.
The decision at the end of the first half bothered me even more.
Carolina faced fourth-and-1 at its own 45 with more than 30 seconds remaining and still had all three timeouts. Canales didn't want to go for it on fourth down, which I can understand, with the Panthers already leading 10-7 and getting the ball to start the second half.
What I didn't understand was letting the clock completely run out. Why not run it down, call a timeout with a few seconds left, and at least give Young a chance to throw one toward the end zone? Maybe nothing comes from it, but there wasn't much to lose by trying.
There was another decision earlier in the half that I didn't love. Canales chose not to challenge what appeared to be an incomplete pass on Philadelphia's only touchdown drive of the first half. The play stood, the drive continued and the Eagles eventually scored.
Neither decision cost Carolina the game. That's important, but it also doesn't mean I forget about them when I'm grading the head coach.
I thought there was more good than bad from Canales and the Panthers coming out of the bye. The offense stuck with the running game, found some different ways to use Tremble, got Coker and McMillan going together, and answered when Philadelphia made it a five-point game in the fourth quarter.
But I can't get to an A with 149 penalty yards and a couple of game-management decisions that could've mattered a lot more if this game had gone differently. Carolina won on the road, improved to 3-2, and did what it was supposed to do.
I'll take the B and the win.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Overreaction? Panthers Winning Ugly Cements Them as Playoff Contender
full_text:
Admittedly, it’s a division that has had its issues as of late as a whole. Dating back to 2022, there has been only one example, the 2024 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, of an NFC South team finishing the season with a winning record. The Bucs were a 10-7 division champion, but were one-and-done come playoff time via a home loss to the Washington Commanders.
Of course, the Buccaneers were also an 8-9 NFC South champion in 2022, just as were the Carolina Panthers this past season. These days, Dave Canales’s club is all alone in first place in the division. On Sunday, the well-rested Panthers came away with a 25-14 over the depleted Philadelphia Eagles in the City of Brotherly Love.
How did Tommy Tremble get wide open Eagles down 11 with 6:33 to go pic.twitter.com/GeJ63YyOEd
Carolina owned a 19-7 fourth-quarter lead and the Birds would make it interesting, but Bryce Young’s second TD pass of the day to tight end Tommy Tremble with 6:33 to play gave Canales’s club a comfortable cushion.
The Panthers outgained the Eagles, 399-222, in total yards, the Birds hung around in part due to some sloppy play by the defending NFC South champions. They finished the game with 13 accepted penalties for 149 yards—six of those for 72 yards in the second quarter alone.
Canales: The penalties were outrageous. Adds afterward that he didn’t have a problem with any of the calls. pic.twitter.com/0wkq5N9BVO
Yet, Carolina still managed a double-digit victory and own a two-game winning streak for the first time since posting three consecutive victories from Weeks 5-7 in 2025.
The adage of not playing your best game and still coming up with a win certainly applies here. And the fact that no other team in the NFC South has taken the proverbial bull by the horns this season to date certainly is a factor. Both the Atlanta Falcons and New Orleans Saints own 2-4 records, and the Buccaneers are all alone in the divisional basement with a 1-5 mark. Carolina hosts Todd Bowles’s club on Sunday.
Panthers RB Chubba Hubbard Week 6 🏈 28 CAR 🏈 120 YDS 🏈 1 TD Panthers defeat the Eagles 25-14 pic.twitter.com/laajx6putG
Let’s not get it twisted. There are 12 weeks remaining in the regular season. A year ago, Carolina dropped its first two games, opened 1-3 and made the playoffs. The Houston Texans were 0-3 in 2025 and reached the postseason. Every team in the NFC South has at least four divisional games remaining. The matter here is not whether the Panthers will repeat as division champions, but are they on course to reach the playoffs for a second straight season.
Young is playing the best football of his career. Running back Chuba Hubbard has once again emerged as a reliable performer and leads the team in scrimmage yards and total touchdowns. Ejiro Evero’s defense has rebounded well after the Week 1 debacle vs. the Bears. This looks like a different Panthers’ team even compared to last season, and it adds up to a lot of optimism in Carolina.
Russell S. Baxter has been writing and researching the game of football for more than 40 years, and on numerous platforms. That includes television, as he spent more than two decades at ESPN, and was part of shows that garnered five Emmy Awards. He also spent the 2015 NFL season with Thursday Night Football on CBS/NFLN.

title: Kevin Byard Commands Attention of Caleb Williams and Bears Offense
full_text:
Oh yes, Caleb Williams went there.
The Bears quarterback brought up the age of 33-year-old Patriots safety Kevin Byard , his former Bears teammate .
“Being able to go versus him in practice for two years; I mean he's a super savvy vet," Williams said Tuesday after practice. "I know he's getting up there in age, but he's still fast."
Williams did say it with a smile while everyone laughed, a sure sign he was kidding his former teammate.
There is not animosity there and Williams even pointed out when the Bears and Patriots play Thursday his former teammate does have a bit of an advantage.
What a great play Sunday from #Patriots Kevin Byard to start the game and not allow the Jets 6 👏 pic.twitter.com/oNftKhObCJ
"I've seen him work, he studies film, he still moves extremely well and he knows the route concepts really well," Williams said. "Excited to go versus him. It's going to be a great challenge for us, a great challenge for me and the wide receivers to be able to go out there and execute and complete passes and keep being the offense and identity that we want to be.”
This will be a reunion game for the second straight week. The Bears fared well last week against former Bears defensive tackle Gervon Dexter and former Bears receiver Olamide Zaccheaus. Byard commands a little more respect as a top 100 player in the NFL.
Byard remains a player all the Bears talk of with reverence, whether player or even head coach Ben Johnson —  even if GM Ryan Poles and the coaching staff chose not to cough up $9 million in cap space the Patriots did to sign him in free agency, while spending it instead on younger free agent Coby Bryant.
No. 61 on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2026… @Patriots S Kevin Byard! @NFLFilms pic.twitter.com/o8L2Lf6tGF
"KB, it’ll be great," wide receiver Rome Odunze said. "We’re on opposing teams so it’ll be a little bit of action there but I’m excited about it. He’s a tremendous player. I’m looking forward to going up against him and hopefully after the game, after the win, I’ll say my hellos."
Byard is already warning his teammates in the secondary not to get too comfortable at Soldier Field because they'll be facing an offense known for trickery.
"I know Ben," Byard told New England reporters. "Being Thursday night, he’s gonna have some stuff up his sleeve. It’s a primetime game. He’s gonna want to show off his expertise on Thursday night.”
Side-by-side of Kevin Byard and @terrellowens , 18 years apart, celebrating on the star at midfield in Dallas. 👀 @KB31_Era pic.twitter.com/d5FgFjVDUG
The signing of Bryant hasn't worked yet for the Bears, as he suffered a knee/leg injury in training camp and hasn't played this year. Sure, they could have used Byard for another year instead. Byard still has never missed a game in what is now an 11-year career.
"I love Kevin Byard and what he brings to the table," Johnson said. "You can tell he really fits their defense well in terms of the communication and what they're asking them to do."
How Patriots coach Mike Vrabel is using Byard is much like in their stint together with the Titans for 5 1/2 seasons. His passer rating against is an outstanding 76.8, better even than last year's 96.5 when he made All-Pro and the Pro Bowl for the Bears.
Former Bears S Kevin Byard says he already knows Ben Johnson is going to have tricks up his sleeve on Thursday Night Football: “I know Ben. Being Thursday night, he’s gonna have some stuff up his sleeve. It’s a primetime game. He’s gonna want to show off his expertise on…
What Byard isn't doing is getting beat for touchdowns this year. He hasn't allowed one yet, per Pro Football Reference. He gave up 10 in two seasons with the Bears and two the previous half season with Philadelphia after he left Tennessee.
Pro Football Focus' grading for Byard hasn't been so generous. They have him 78th of 98 NFL safeties overall, 80th of 98 in pass coverage and 68th stopping the run. They're blaming him for a lot more plays against the Patriots' secondary than PFR's Stathead does, giving him a 110.6 passer rating against.
If it's not Byard doing it, then someone is for the New England defense because they're 11th against the pass,. ninth against the run and sixth overall, and have allowed the fifth fewest points.
Why did the Bears let Kevin Byard walk to the Patriots in free agency in the offseason? Byard "was everything they could've asked him to be" in Chicago, @BradBiggs says before offering his best read on Byard leaving for New England. pic.twitter.com/kwvx9XOKy1
"(Cornerback) Christian Gonzalez on the outside just trying to figure out where he'll be and where he'll line up," Johnson said. "But all of those guys, they're fundamentally sound. They tackle really well. They shed blocks really well.
"And then schematically, they try to take away what you do best. And that's the challenge.”
It can't hurt having a wise old veteran in back directing it, one who always seems to answer the bell.
The Bears definitely have missed that this year as defensive coordinator Dennis Allen may be juggling his lineup again this week just as he has virtually every week since the season began without Bryant and also without Kyler Gordon, who is now back. Cam Lewis is at safety now after they cut Xavier Woods last week.
Rookie Dllon Thieneman continues to learn lessons each week in back.  There's a lot to be said for experience.
. @nyjets @Patriots @KevinByard one of the great FS to play this game...He isn't saving lives; but he is saving Touchdowns. #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/DqiLhyh7HH
Gene Chamberlain has covered the Chicago Bears full time as a beat writer since 1994 and prior to this on a part-time basis for 10 years. He covered the Bears as a beat writer for Suburban Chicago Newspapers, the Daily Southtown, Copley News Service and has been a contributor for the Daily Herald, the Associated Press, Bear Report, CBS Sports.com and The Sporting News. He also has worked a prep sports writer for Tribune Newspapers and Sun-Times newspapers.

title: Caleb Williams Can't Call It His Favorite Game But Did Love the Accuracy
full_text:
Sunday's effort in a win over Atlanta vaulted Caleb Williams to the top of the NFL completion percentage rankings one year after his accuracy was considered a joke by some.
He's not too impressed by it all. In fact, he doesn't even consider the effort coming back from hiatus due to a hamstring injury his favorite or among his favorite games.
"Naw, I mean, I've had some pretty cool games in my career," Williams said. "It was cool getting back but I think it was just kind of another game for me."
Now who's exaggerating? Williams' 83% was the best for a game by a Bears quarterback with at least 30 attempts and set up the early 31-7 lead they had before Atlanta made a late charge.
The 30-for-36 looked even more impressive when NFL Next Gen Stats posted how he had been 24-for-24 from a clean pocket.
What the Bears offense looks like with Caleb Williams vs without him, 2026: Week 1 at Carolina, with Caleb: 59 points. +0.41 EPA per play, 54% success rate. Caleb went 21/31 for 269 yards, 2 TD, 0 INT and ran for 65 more. Weeks 3–5 with backups: 19 points per game, and the… pic.twitter.com/j3oBe9WUEw
"Shout out to the O-line," Williams said. "That tells me shout out to the O-line. That tells me shout out to the running backs for when they had to pick up they picked up and picked up well.
"Then shout out to the wide receivers for running great routes and being decisive in their routes and allowing me to see that and give them a good ball."
Don't forget the coach. Ben Johnson and Williams had a bit of a rocky relationship to start because of Johnson's demanding style and the natural presnap mistakes that resulted when the offense first was introduced in 2025. Their relationship has become tight now, and Williams sees this as a factor in getting game plans he likes.
Caleb Williams has done more than Jordan Love this season in HALF THE GAMES PLAYED. The difference between a contender and a pretender. pic.twitter.com/W5SDeDx0uK
"It’s been fun," he said. "We’ve gotten better with some of the things that really bother him. There’s a little bit less hyper-communication, let’s say, in those situations. But it’s been awesome being able to have him, being able to have him as a teacher, as a coach and just keep growing our relationship between each other."
So the first play last week after three weeks away with an injury almost made Williams chuckle. Johnson was testing him with a bootleg pass.
"It was a keeper," Williams said, smiling. "Yeah, that's him. That's him. Like I said, if I'm out there I feel good with my legs and the injury itself. That's who he is and that's what we love about him.
Highest completion percentage this season (*air yards/attempt, QB rank): 1. Caleb Williams – 72.5% (5.8, 32nd) 2. Joe Burrow – 71.4% (7.4, 24th) 3. Lamar Jackson – 70.8% (10.2, 2nd) *Per @NextGenStats
"He put me on a keeper on the first play. It was a big play for us and Colston (Loveland) made a great catch."
Of course, Williams did have to take some credit after a 58.1% completions performance in all of 2025. He found things about his game he could carry over into Thursday night against New England.
"Something that I've been just preaching over and over again throughout my years with Ben so far — or year and a half with Ben — giving the guys a shot, runners ball, good footwork, and getting the ball out my hands," Williams said.
Anyone who says this is on Caleb Williams is trippin. It's on Colston Loveland to be on Caleb's timing on a designed play-action rollout like this. Not vice versa. Caleb threw the ball as soon as he cleared the chasing defender and started climbing from his half circle rollout.…
Nothing much has changed as far as his goals weekly since training camp began. The only thing different is he added more experience, went through an injury and is back.
"Just trying to stay focused on those things, and then when the shots are there, it's almost every pass play we almost have at least a shot or an alert shot in each of them," Williams said. "So when they give us the shots, let's take it. But if not, let's get the ball to our guys, get the ball in their hands and let them go."
It's worked to a league-high 72.5% completions and he'll try to keep it going Thursday against a Patriots pass defense a solid 11th in yards allowed.
What does Caleb Williams do better than Drake Maye? https://t.co/1wGPAYxPn9
Not even the injury is a problem moving into the short week.
"I didn't get hit much," Williams added. "Those couple of sacks that I probably could have just dirted the ball or probably could have just threw it out of bound or something, you know, some of them were in third-and-long situations. And so just trying to protect the ball in those situations.
"But I felt great, my body feels good. I didn't take many hits. I didn't take any devastating hits at least. And so I'm feeling good, leg feels good, everything else is kind of normal."
Except his accuracy. That's above normal by quite a bit.
Caleb Williams had an ADOT of just 3.3 yards in Week 6 Of the 187 individual QB performances with at least 10 pass attempts in a game this season, Williams' outing ranks 186th in ADOT Only Atlanta's Jack Strand in Week 2 had a lower mark But yay completion percentage! https://t.co/PrhZ9uxwAF

title: Kyle Monangai Injury Update and Everything Else From Bears' Tuesday Practice Report
full_text:
Tuesday was the second day of practice for the Chicago Bears before their Week 7 game against the New England Patriots and Chicago's latest injury report has dropped.
The Monday injury report had more bad news than good, as guys like T.J. Edwards, Jonah Jackson, Kyle Monangai and Jack Sanborn were all estimated non-participants.
The good news was Keyshaun Elliott and Tyrique Stevenson were both estimated to be full participants, which puts them on track for a return on Thursday night.
Did the second-to-last injury report of the week on Tuesday give us any positive news on the four players who were projected as non-participants on Monday?
The injury report was once again an estimation, as the Bears only conducted a walkthrough once again.
Some good news on Tuesday, as Jackson saw an upgrade in his estimated participation.
We did get an update on Jackson on Monday night, with ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reporting that Jackson is considered week-to-week with a hip flexor .
Fowler also noted that Jackson's Week 7 status is in question, but the good news is his injury is not considered a long-term issue.
"Bears OG Jonah Jackson has a hip flexor injury and is considered week-to-week, per source. Status for TNF in doubt but shouldn’t be long term," Fowler wrote .
With the estimated limited practice for Jackson, he now has a chance to suit up, although a short week hurts his odds of ultimately suiting up.
Edwards, Monangai and Sanborn were all estimated non-participants once again.
With that, Monangai, Edwards, and Sanborn are all on track to sit out this week. The deck was stacked against all of them to begin with because it's a short week.
We still don't have anything concrete on Edwards, who sat out last week with his hamstring injury. Monangai has now missed two games in a row with turf toe.
Head coach Ben Johnson did say last week that Monangai is on the right track, so we believe he'll be back in Week 8. To add to the optimism of a Week 8 return, the Bears didn't place Monangai on injured reserve, so they don't expect him to miss four games.
The Bears have deployed Roschon Johnson behind D'Andre Swift with Monangai out the last two games and we don't expect that to change, even after Johnson's late-game fumble in Week 6.
Luke Newman replaced Jackson on Sunday and we would expect him to do so again in Week 7. Newman didn't allow a pressure in relief of the Bears' starting guard.
At linebacker, D'Marco Jackson will start if Edwards is ruled out, and Noah Sewell should pick up most of what's left over behind Jackson and Devin Bush. We may also see Elliott get his first career snaps on defense.

title: Chicago Bears Named Perfect Landing Spot For Pro Bowl Cornerback
full_text:
Kyler Gordon's triumphant return provided a beacon of light for the Chicago Bears defense.
The nickelback finished the contest with 3 sacks and 2 forced fumbles despite playing only 17 snaps , reinvigorating a defense that desperately needed a spark after a blowout loss against Green Bay. His presence should shore up the nickelback position and allow Malik Muhammad II to play his more natural position on the perimeter.
However, with Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson both struggling mightily this season, some believe the Bears could still use some reinforcements in the secondary. ESPN's Benjamin Solak thinks Chicago can capitalize on the Eagles' misfortune and swing a trade for cornerback Riq Woolen.
"If a team comes calling with a strong enough offer, the Eagles can dodge the comp pick calculations and get value for Woolen now," Solak wrote. "That team might be the Bears, who should be desperate for cornerback help after what they saw the Packers do to Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson Sr. in Week 5.
"For as much man coverage as defensive coordinator Dennis Allen wants to play (34%, the fourth-highest rate in football, per NFL Next Gen Stats), the cornerback play in Chicago needs to be stronger."
If there's one thing about Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen, it's that he's going to be aggressive. He's going to send the house. That puts pressure on players to hold up in man-to-man situations on the back end.
To Allen's credit, the blitzes have gotten home more often than not this season. However, that has much more to do with the defensive line than it does the secondary.
Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson have arguably been their two worst starters on defense this season. They're routinely a few steps behind in coverage and haven't held up well against fast receivers.
Jaylon Johnson… pic.twitter.com/Cl3yH7J9lN
Meanwhile, Woolen is still one of the league's most physically gifted cover men. Despite standing 6'4", he can still keep up with any receiver in the league.
Woolen might not be as flashy as he was early in his career (he led the league with six interceptions during his Pro Bowl rookie campaign), but he's still more than capable of holding his own on the perimeter. He's played 425/430 of the defensive snaps for Philadelphia and has allowed only 51.7% of the passes thrown his way to be completed.
The 27-year-old signed a one-year, $12 million deal with Philadelphia this offseason. It seemed like a win-win for both sides. He expected to raise his stock and have a chance at a Super Bowl with a perennial contender, and they expected a rock-solid starter for a potential playoff push. The fact that they would also get a compensation pick for him if he were to ball out and leave in free agency wouldn't hurt, either.
However, with the Eagles currently sitting at 2-4 and losing their starting QB for the rest of the season, the sky is officially falling in Philadelphia. The Bears could cash in on their misfortune and shore up their most glaring weakness for a potential playoff push of their own.

He has survived the 2010 NFC Championship Game, a career-ending injury to his favorite player (Johnny Knox), the Bears' 2013 season finale, a Double Doink, Mitchell Trubisky, Justin Fields, and Weeks 8-17 of the 2024 NFL season. Nevertheless, he still Bears Down!

title: Bears' Reason for D'Andre Swift's Uneven Workload Further Proves Kyle Monangai's Importance
full_text:
One thing that has been apparent since Week 4 is the Chicago Bears have not utilized D'Andre Swift on the ground much in the second half of games.
We know why that was the case in Week 4, as Swift was benched because of what head coach Ben Johnson said was an "egregious" fumble .
But in Week 5 against the Green Bay Packers, Swift saw just one carry in the second half, and then he had just four in the final two quarters of the win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 6.
Even in a crucial drive to close out the game on Sunday, it was Roschon Johnson, not Swift, handling the work.
When asked about this on Monday, Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor said the reason is Chicago is trying to keep Swift fresh for the entire season.
"I think a little bit is I think there's a mindfulness to preserve him a little bit. It's a long season," Taylor explained , per ESPN's Courtney Cronin. "Just aware of D'Andre and how he's been throughout the course and how invaluable he is for us throughout the course of the season."
"And there's an opportunity... obviously Roschon unfortunately had a fumble in the fourth quarter there, but we felt like Roschon was really contributing pretty well for us in a number of aspects," Taylor added. "He showed up in the pass game quite a bit, had some good carries, some good runs. Obviously, we've got to eliminate the turnover itself, but Roschon was rolling pretty good there too, so we felt comfortable rolling with him in there as well. And Swifty was ready to go if we needed it. So no, there's nothing really too much beyond that."
Johnson, who is filling in for the injured Kyle Monangai , played a lot better on Sunday than he did the week before, but he had a costly fumble in the fourth quarter that gave the Falcons a chance to even the score. Thankfully, Chicago's defense made a stop.
But if that didn't happen, there would have been plenty of second-guessing about the Bears not deploying their better running back, and rightly so.
As good as Johnson looked, the fumble notwithstanding, he is a clear downgrade from Monangai, who has been the Bears' best running back this season overall.
With the Bears taking this approach with Swift, it only further shows just how important Monangai is.
Not only are the Bears a better team with their duo of Swift and Monangai intact, but there is also zero drop-off when Swift is sitting for a large swath of a game.
Monangai continues to recover from his turf toe injury as we turn the page to Week 7.
He was a non-participant on the estimated practice report on Monday and he appears to be trending toward sitting again, which isn't much of a surprise because of the short week the Bears are operating on and his lack of progress at practice last week.
But the hope is Monangai will be ready to go by Week 8 after he wasn't placed on injured reserve, which means the Bears believe he won't miss more than the third game he's on track to miss this week.

title: Why Caleb Williams is Still an MVP Candidate Despite Missing Three Games
full_text:
Coming into the 2026 NFL season, enormous expectations awaited the Chicago Bears after their 2025 awakening on offense . Suddenly, the Bears looked very much like Super Bowl contenders, or at the very least a strong candidate to reach the NFC Championship game. But that's not all. Caleb Williams' breakout season heaped sky-high expectations on his shoulders, and any regression would be brutally punished in the media.
Well, we're one-third of the way through the season and neither the Bears nor Williams are showing any signs of slowing down. The Bears look every bit a legit Super Bowl contender, and Williams has been playing like an NFL MVP, especially after securing a bounce back Week 6 win over the Atlanta Falcons , his first game back from a hamstring injury that sidelined him for three weeks.
Unfortunately, that very injury may prevent Williams from earning MVP honors no matter how well he plays. Voters tend to punish even the best quarterbacks for missing more than one game, and Williams missed three. ESPN's Benjamin Solak noted in his seven things to think about for Week 7 how Jalen Hurts had led the MVP race in 2022 by Week 14, but he missed Week 16 and 17 with an injury and MVP honors were awarded to Patrick Mahomes, instead.
That doesn't mean that Williams' MVP chances are D.O.A., however. There's still a very compelling case for the voters to make him Chicago's first NFL MVP since Walter Payton, and here's why.
It took longer than Bears fans may have liked, but Caleb Williams is finally living up to his pre-draft projections. Through three games, he's earned a 77.5 QBR from ESPN, which is the third-best mark in the league. His 82.8 impact grade from Pro Football Network is sixth best. He's leading the league with a 72.5% completion rating, a massive improvement from last year's 58.1% mark.
The numbers paint a portrait of a strong MVP candidate, but the voters don't go on stats alone. There's a human element to the voting, and that's where things may work in Williams' favor. Let's say Williams continues to play as a Top 5 quarterback and leads the Bears to another division title. Becoming an elite quarterback for a franchise that hasn't seen one since arguably the 1940's would likely be a powerful motivator for voters.
Most importantly, the timing of Williams' injury may also benefit him in the long run. As Solak noted, Hurts' injury likely cost him an MVP award. But his injury occurred near the end of the season. Williams still has 11 games ahead of him. As aforementioned, there's a human element to the NFL Honors voting and the voters tend to lean towards more December games than what transpires in September and October.
At the end of the day, there's no getting around the fact that Williams missed three games this season due to injury. As Solak mentioned in his article for ESPN, the last time any player won the MVP award while missing more than one game in a season was Steve McNair in 2003, and he had to be the co-MVP with Peyton Manning. Even if Williams catches fire for the rest of the season, his final stats still may not compare favorably to other MVP candidates.
Another thing working against Williams, and this is fairly obvious, is the rest of the field. Brock Purdy is on pace for over 4,100 yards and 40 touchdowns, and his 83.0 QBR leads the NFL. Lamar Jackson has only missed two games, and he also is having a terrific season. Even if Williams concludes the greatest season in franchise history, he could still fall behind these other terrific quarterbacks.
An MVP award for Williams would be an incredible development for a player who, just two years ago, appeared to be the next tombstone in Chicago's graveyard of quarterbacks. But team success is first and foremost, and I don't think it would bother Bears fans if Williams is snubbed for an NFL award so long as he leads the Bears on another postseason run.
A former Marine and Purdue Boilermaker, Pete has been covering the Chicago Bears since 2022 as a senior contributor on BearsTalk. He lives with his wife, two kids and loyal dog.

title: How Drake Maye Forces Bears to Drastically Alter Successful Approach
full_text:
The Bears defense is about to get a real understanding of what everyone else in the league experiences when they run up against Caleb Williams.
Facing quarterback Drake Maye and New England's offense Thursday night is going to provide their first real experience this season of playing against a quarterback who extends plays and runs extensively. They did play against Jalen Hurts and the Eagles, but Hurts simply didn't run it or scramble to throw. Either this was the result of the Bears defensive approach or Hurts' own reluctance or maybe related to the physical problems no plaguing him. Either way, the Bears defense hasn't seen anything like Maye's mobility and combination of deep throwing and mobility.
"I think Drake Maye's one of those guys that does an outstanding job with his feet," Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said. "There's been times where you watch it and there's pressure on the quarterback and he makes people miss and creates some plays down the field. I see him doing a lot of good things.
"I see especially his athleticism showing up and his ability to throw the ball down the field has been exceptional.”
DRAKE MAYE IS ACTUALLY NOT FROM THIS PLANET… THIS IS ONE OF THE MOST UNDERRATED PLAYS YOU WILL SEE ALL SEASON. Maye escaped a sack, stiff-armed a defender to avoid being brought down & somehow threw an absolute DIME down the sideline while falling away. pic.twitter.com/0ChYJzqxCL
Maye is seventh in yards per attempt at 8.0 and fifth in average intended air yards, according to NextGen Stats. He's not messing around with dinking and dunking. He's attacking downfield when he gets out of the pocket. The Bears have suffered greatly on defense when trying to cover downfield against deeper throws.
The loss to Green Bay was only evidence of  this Bears problem, and it probably stems from their inexperience at several position in the secondary along with the fact so many players have been lining up at different places. Communication wasn't great, especially in the loss to the Packers.
Drake Maye Touchdown: 62nd Regular Season TD; 42 Yard Passing TD to Romeo Doubs pic.twitter.com/QiSmwvVqFi
A telltale problem for the Bears defense is who they tend to get burned by on passes. The Bears went into last week allowing more yards to wide receivers per target than any defense in the NFL. It wasn't that close. They were giving up 10.4 yards per target to wide receivers while Tennessee was next worse at 10.1. Their explosive play rate allowed of 7.6%, according to Sharp Football Analysis, was fifth worst in the league.
The effort against Atlanta probably did nothing to improve their standing as they gave up nine catches for 158 yards to wide receivers. They're blitzing a great deal and that's done to compensate for 1) lack of pass rush; 2) problems with coverage; 3) a defensive line struggling to stop the run; 4) to create pressure and force turnovers. They are No. 5 in blitz percentage (38.7%).
Drake Maye having himself a ball game 11/15 160 Pass Yards 2 Pass TD 147.2 Pass Rating pic.twitter.com/zV0eYhu5z5
The tradeoff is they leave their DBs explose in man-to-man coverage too much and they are in man coverage at the second highest rate at 31.5%. It's about the worst coverage you can be in against a running quarterback and they should know this from seeing what Caleb Williams does each week to opponents with his off-platform passes or runs for first downs.
"They do an excellent job of throwing the ball down the field," Allen said. "They’ve got some speed at the receiver position. They take their shots."
Best safety in the NFC huh? That’s cute pic.twitter.com/ddLtbjQksp https://t.co/8Ktq0J57YN
The images of Dillon Thieneman, Jaylon Johnson, and former Bears safety Xavier Woods being beaten deep against Green Bay are still fresh in memories. It's something Maye and Patriots receivers like Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams, A.J. Brown and former Packer Romeo Doubs have been able to accomplish against opposing secondaries.
It's likely the Bears will need to stand and cover more than attack with the blitzes like they did last week. And it's worth wondering whether they have the capacity to do it after they've been beaten for big gains so often.
