title: Jaguars' Biggest Need Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline Is Painfully Obvious
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are sitting in a perfectly good spot at 4-2 entering their Week 7 bye week, but things could always be better, and they could always improve.
The trade deadline is the most obvious avenue for a team to find in-season improvement, as we saw last year with the Jaguars' trade for Jakobi Meyers. And just like the Jaguars needed receiver help a year ago, it has become clear that there is one position they must target this year.
The Jaguars have all that they need at a few positions: they should be very happy with their linebacker play, and they clearly have the depth required, and then some, at wide receiver, tight end, running back, and quarterback. That does beg the question of a few other positions, though, and namely on the defensive side of the ball.
Jacksonville was one of the NFL's top-ranked defenses entering Sunday, but they got absolutely lit up against the Texans and their passing game in Week 6. Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud had several high-level throws and found plenty of deep and red-zone success against Jacksonville, burning them for explosive plays, efficient gains, and everything in between.
The defensive line is one position that will draw a lot of attention ahead of the deadline, especially after a day in which the Jaguars hardly pressured Stroud without sending the house on blitzes ... that Stroud then picked apart. The Jaguars' biggest issue with the defensive line appears to be the ceiling when it comes to their backups, with most of the Jaguars' backup spots consisting of cheap journeyman or young former undrafted free agents.
With that said, I think the loss to the Texans exposed the cornerback position more than the defensive line. As Coen noted after the game, and as you could see as players slipped all day, the surface was not one that exactly helped a pass-rush unit.
"The surface, obviously, I didn't feel like we were under a ton of duress, either. I think that venue benefits the offense in a lot of ways in terms of the pass rush. If we weren't feeling them, they probably didn't feel us," Coen said.
The cornerback group can't say the same thing, however. Jarrian Jones and Jourdan Lewis each struggled and allowed big plays at times against the Texans, with Lewis allowing a red-zone touchdown and Jones allowing an explosive play to set the Texans up in the red-zone before the end of the half. Travis Hunter was beat by Nico Collins twice, too, but he also managed to intercept Stroud and proved to be a more effective coverman than anyone else in the cornerback room on Sunday.
But then you have to consider the Hunter experience. Hunter also starred on offense in limited snaps on Sunday, and with Brian Thomas Jr.'s recent struggles it would make sense for Hunter to start getting more and more snaps on offense eventually. It is hard to afford to do that when dealing with injuries and up-and-down play at the cornerback position, though.
I mean, the Jaguars added two cornerbacks to the active roster two weeks ago for a reason in Jaylon Jones and 
Alijah Huzzie, but those are special teams and depth options. The Jaguars need someone who can step in and play, and they can't just hope Montaric Brown's hamstring suddenly heals and he reverts back to his 2025 form.
The Jaguars need at least one more solid cornerback to be the complete team they want to be. This was clear in Week 2 when they gave up too many explosives. It was clear in Week 5 when the same thing happened. Then more explosives have hit over the last two weeks, and the need has started to become a screaming red flag.

title: Shipley's Dozen: What the Jaguars' Loss to Texans Means and Travis Hunter's Next Step
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- That was a tough one.
The Jaguars left London with a Week 6 loss to the Houston Texans, and we break it all down in this week's Shipley's Dozen column, with 12 takes on where the Jaguars must go next.
Travis Hunter is starting to prove himself. Had the Jaguars won on Sunday, the entire story from the game would have been all about Travis Hunter and his two-way impact. Hunter's fourth-quarter touchdown drive and his red-zone interception were two of the biggest moments of the game, and the fact that they came from the same player is mind-boggling. Now that the Jaguars have seen a taste of what Hunter can do in one game, the question is where do they go from here. Hunter, naturally, should see more and more snaps and chances on offense in the weeks ahead, but that also could mean changes for a defensive role that he is clearly key in.
The Jaguars are certainly in a good spot entering the bye week. They are 4-2, hold a two-game lead in the AFC South, and have an easy second-half schedule. With that said, the Jaguars are still not in a great spot. They would have been with a win since they would have held a three-game lead over Houston, but the Texans have the ability to make up a two-game gap, and the Jaguars know that. The Jaguars' playoff chances are still very, very healthy. They are still a very good team. But a win would have gone a much longer way than the loss.
Yes, the Jaguars have gotten jobbed out of several touchdowns by bad calls -- four over the last three games, somehow. But I still do not think one can pin this game on the refs. The Jaguars are still the team that gets in their own way too often, whether it be drops, red-zone turnovers, false starts, whatever you want to call it. Same on defense with missed tackles and penalties. The Jaguars have gotten a really bad hand with officials in recent weeks, but it isn't why the Jaguars lost Sunday. The Jaguars lost because of their own self-inflicted mistakes, which is why they have lost in Week 2, and to Buffalo last year, and so on and so forth.
After the Jaguars benched Brian Thomas Jr. against the Texans in the second-half, they more or less closed the door on him ever becoming a factor in the offense. It seems like the Jaguars' only real option is to shop him on the trade market over the next few weeks, but which teams would make sense as potential trade partners?
Las Vegas Raiders: Tre Tucker has turned it on and Brock Bowers is a beast, but those are the only NFL pass-catchers on that roster. The Raiders have a ton of picks and a young franchise quarterback they need to surround with talent. They seem like a team that would swing big on Thomas.
Atlanta Falcons: The Atlanta Falcons already have a few explosive play-makers, but their offense could use another pass-catcher opposite of Drake London. Thomas would bring a different element that could fit within their scheme and with their quarterback room, too.
Seattle Seahawks: The Seahawks' offense looks like a mess, and they can not just keep spamming the JSN button without giving him support. They do not have real wide receiver depth behind him, and they need to make a big move to ensure they can make the playoffs in a tight NFC.
The trade deadline is still a month away , but the Jaguars should spend the bye week thinking about how they can add to the roster and improve it. The Jaguars have the draft picks and the ammo to make moves happen, but what are the needs they would have to hit? After the Texans game, I think a few are clear.
Cornerback: The Jaguars clearly need to play Travis Hunter both ways, so more cornerback depth is needed ... especially with Montaric Brown injured. I do not think the cornerbacks are as bad as some of the yardage numbers say, but they could use some reinforcements.
Defensive Tackle: The Jaguars might have the least amount of resources allocated to their backups on the defensive line in the entire NFL, and defensive tackle is a big part of that. Taking a swing for a starting-level player would make a big difference.
EDGE: The Jaguars are getting very, very little from their backup defensive ends such as Danny Striggow and Bryan Thomas Jr. Dennis Gardeck is a nice change of pace situational pass-rusher, but the Jaguars need to start winning by rushing four, and they can't rely on Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen every snap.
Sunday was a classic quarterback duel between Trevor Lawrence and C.J. Stroud. Stroud was throwing dots drive after drive against the Jaguars' defense, while Lawrence led the Jaguars to a 10-point comeback in the fourth-quarter after some terrific throws to all levels of the field. Lawrence and Stroud have had some great battles over the years, and I think this game rivaled the 2023 duel they had in Houston. This is the best quarterback rivalry in the AFC South, and one of the very best in the entire NFL. It isn't Mahomes/Allen, but there are not many better than it in the NFL today.
The Jaguars had just four drops on the season entering Week 6, but they collected five in Week 6: two from Brian Thomas Jr., two from Parker Washington, and one from Jakobi Meyers. The Jaguars had not had many, if any, drops during the first few weeks of the season but they have seven over the last three games. The Jaguars have gotten into their own way far too many times during the 2026 season, and this was one of the biggest reasons they lost on Sunday. If the drops linger on post-bye week, then the Jaguars should consider it a serious issue.
How well the Texans ran the ball. The Jaguars allowed their longest rush of the season, their most rushing yards allowed all season, their highest average yards allowed per carry, and their highest yards after contact allowed per rush. The Texans running game has genuinely stunk against every other defense in the NFL the last two seasons but the Jaguars'. This is the second meeting in a row in which they have ripped off big plays on the ground against the Jaguars, so it seems like a real-deal concern for the next matchup.
C.J. Stroud's success. I figured this would be a shootout, but I didn't factor in the turf making it a 7-on-7 game. Still, Stroud has been a top-10 quarterback this season who has been able to hunt explosives while still being efficient as a quick-passer, which was always bound to be a bad matchup for the Jaguars' defense. This wasn't a great matchup on paper to begin with, and Stroud proved why this was the case.
This one is obvious, no? Hunter became the third player since at least the 1970 merger to have an interception and a receiving touchdown in a regular season game, joining HOF S Brian Dawkins (Week 4 of 2002) and Cardinals WR Roy Green (Week 3 of 1981). He also became the first player since 2014 to record 50-plus receiving yards, two tackles and a touchdown in a game. He is truly a unicorn.
The Jaguars now hold a two-game lead in the AFC South leaving Week 6, which saw two different AFC South divisional battles take place. The Texans improved to 2-4, while the Indianapolis Colts had a woeful performance at home in a loss to the winless Tennessee Titans to also fall to 2-4. The Colts seem like they are teetering on implosion, while the Titans won a sloppy game that saw their quarterback fail to hit 110 passing yards.
As usual, that leaves the Jaguars and the Texans. The Jaguars' post-bye schedule has them playing the Colts, New York Giants, and Tennessee Titans twice in their first five games. The Texans' next four games are winnable as well, though, with four expected wins against the Giants, Los Angeles Chargers, Cleveland Browns, and then the Colts.
With both teams facing soft schedules over the next few months, the race is officially on in the AFC South. Neither team can allow the other the keep pace, and the margin for error for each squad is nearly nothing. If this feels a lot like last year's race, well, it is.
The Jaguars have a bye week in Week 7, so their focus will clearly be on mending their wounds from the…

title: 3 Overreactions to the Jaguars' Last-Second Loss to Texans: AFC South Shakeup
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It is far from time for the Jacksonville Jaguars to panic, but that doesn't mean Week 6 can't be a wakeup call.
The Jaguars stormed back in the fourth quarter to give themselves a chance to win, but they failed to find a way to win the AFC South clash with the Houston Texans in London.
So, what are some overreactions to the Jaguars' 34-31 loss that are rooted in reality at 4-2? We break it down below.
Can anyone say comfortably that Brian Thomas Jr. will be ahead of Josh Cameron on the wide receiver depth chart when the Jaguars return from the bye week? Thomas had already become the forgotten man in the Jaguars' offense for the most part with just a handful of catches in the first few games, but he has caught zero passes on five targets in the last two weeks and has arguably cost the Jaguars four scoring opportunities in that span with drops. The Jaguars' staff trusts Cameron, and Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence has not appeared to have any issues doing the same.
Then there is the fact that Travis Hunter got more run on offense. He didn't appear to play a heavy snap count on offense, but he did see four targets and caught them all for 59 yards and a touchdown. Had the Jaguars won, the story of the game would be Hunter's impact on offense. He will likely continue to see more touches, which really makes it seem like Thomas is receiver No. 5, and better off getting traded within the next month.
The Jaguars will be entering the bye week with a two-game lead in the AFC South since the Texans and the Indianapolis Colts are both 2-4. It is far from an awful spot to be in after the first six games, especially considering how difficult this early stretch appeared before the season began. 4-2 has long been seen as a successful outcome, and that is what the Jaguars got.
With that said, the AFC South race is now on. A two-game lead is an OK one in terms of security, but there are still 11 games to go. Things can get completely turned upside down by January if the Jaguars do not clean up their issues, because the Texans are still very much in this. Beating the Texans would have given the Jaguars a three-game cushion, a better place to be in than the one the Jaguars now occupy. The Jaguars should still feel good about the AFC South, but they could have felt great.
The Jaguars' defense had one of its worst games of the Anthony Campanile era on Sunday, allowing the Texans to score on 6-of-10 drives and allowing 34 points after allowing 40 points in the previous three games combined. C.J. Stroud picked the Jaguars apart no matter the blitz or the coverage, and the Texans also had far much more rushing success than anyone could have predicted entering the game.
"Yeah, wasn’t good enough for sure. Got to go back and look at it. Thought they made too many plays in the pass game, and they ran it better than anybody has on us so far. Got to evaluate it, get it cleaned up, but definitely disappointing," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game on Sunday.
It doesn't feel fair to really throw blame at the pass-rush considering the disadvantage they were at by the field -- as evidenced by the Texans' lack of pass-rush production, which Coen noted after the game. Still, the Jaguars looked like a unit that could surely use another difference-maker on defense. They like their cornerback room, but could that be addressed with a trade before the deadline? It is worth considering after all of the big plays through the air.

title: Game Balls From Jaguars' Disheartening Loss to Texans: One Standout Emerges
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. --  The Jacksonville Jaguars will be limping into the bye week.
The Jaguars failed to get it done against the Houston Texans in Week 6, falling 34-31 on a walkoff field goal a week after their own last-second win. But even with the loss, there are still a few Jaguars who were able to move forward with strong performances and efforts. So, which of those Jaguars have earned a game ball as a result?
This one feels easy. Trevor Lawrence was one of the best players on the field on Sunday, throwing for over 300 yards and four touchdowns against a defense and a head coach that has given him fits in the past. The Texans' defense isn't what it has been in past years, but it is still a good unit with some blue-chip players on it, and Lawrence had one of the best performances of his entire career against the Texans with his latest outing.
If this is the version of Lawrence we see for the rest of the season, the Jaguars are in very good hands. He did have an end-zone interception that the Jaguars can't afford, but it did come after the Jaguars got jobbed on a bad holding call, so perhaps he never should have even been in that situation. Regardless, Lawrence had another impressive showing for the Jaguars, and once again proved to be their most important piece.
Travis Hunter was undeniably special on Sunday afternoon. Hunter gave up a few big plays, such as a long gain to Nico Collins on a stop-and-go and a few penalties, but he also made the most important play of the day for the defense. On a day where the Jaguars allowed the Texans to score on 6-of-10 drives, there were not many Jaguars defenders to consider. The Jaguars' defense got shredded, but Hunter still made an impact play with his fourth-quarter red-zone interception of C.J. Stroud.
Hunter became the first defender to intercept Stroud in 2026 with his stellar play, which ensured the Jaguars continued their run of red-zone takeaways. It was one of the only times the Jaguars slowed Houston down on Sunday, and it proved that Hunter is, at the end of the day, a play-maker who is going to get the ball. With a pass defensed against Houston, Hunter also extended his streak to five consecutive games with at least one pass defensed, tied for the longest active streak in the NFL.
"Made some critical plays for us on both sides of the football, obviously. Had the interception late, that gave us a chance to win the game. Proud of the way he completed, made some plays for us on offense and got to keep building off it," Liam Coen said after the game.
While the decision to kick the field goal by Liam Coen was certainly one that is going to be debated until the next time the Jaguars kick off, that doesn't change the fact that Cam Little was fantastic when his number was called. Little nailed the 60-yard field goal seemingly with relative ease, and it feels safe to say he could have saved the day for the Jaguars at some point if given the chance to do so.
With the kick, Little recorded the third 60-plus-yard field goal of his career, the most in franchise history. Since entering the league in 2024, his three field goals of 60-plus yards are the second most in the NFL. He is well on his way to becoming one of the highest-paid kickers in the entire NFL, because the Jaguars are tough to imagine without him and his booming field goals.

title: Chiefs Rookie and Sophomore Power Rankings: Who's in for a Big Post-Bye Stretch?
full_text:
Another week, another Kansas City Chiefs victory. Fresh off a bye to rest up but still nursing some injuries, KC hosted the Los Angeles Chargers and didn't have much trouble en route to a 22-6 victory in front of a raucous crowd at Arrowhead Stadium.
With the win came plenty of positive contributions from young players. Others, however, are raising questions of whether they've plateaued for the time being. Week 7's showdown with the Seattle Seahawks on the road should help us learn plenty about the true colors of Kansas City's youngsters.
Following Week 6, let's break down the Chiefs' rookies and sophomores by ranking each qualifying 53-man roster member in tiers. Be sure to return to this series each week to see who's moving and shaking.
Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott isn't included due to him currently being on the physically unable to perform list .
This list contains plenty of usual suspects, headlined by the cornerback duo of Nohl Williams and Mansoor Delane. The former had a brilliant Sunday, making multiple pass breakups and also flashing his ability as a tackler. The latter did have one terrible rep on a deep pass, although it served as one of the few low points in his debut campaign to date.
Along the defensive line, second-round edge rusher R Mason Thomas continues to win quickly. The sack numbers may not be there yet, but there's no denying his raw talent that simply must always be accounted for. First-round tackle Peter Woods is quiet in the box score for the most part but did earn the first half-sack of his career in Week 6.
Moving up a tier this week are a rookie and a sophomore. At the left tackle spot, Kansas City continues to game plan around having undrafted man Kahlil Benson in the lineup, but he shored up his play a bit coming out of the bye. He still has the occasional lapse — head coach Andy Reid alluded to one on Monday — but he's faring better than expected. Even if he isn't a clear-cut starter, he deserves props.
On the other side of the ball, defensive end Ashton Gillotte appears to be putting his plantar fascia injury behind him at least a little bit. He got a sack on Los Angeles quarterback Justin Herbert on Sunday and, per Pro Football Focus , has three pressures in consecutive games.
It brings me no joy bumping fifth-round rookie halfback Emmett Johnson down here, but his last few games haven't been very productive at all. In Weeks 4-6, he's toted the ball nine times and managed just 23 yards. That's despite combining to play 48 offensive snaps. Johnson's time should still be coming — this feels like a temporary demotion.
2025 fourth-round receiver Jalen Royals got targeted four times in the passing game with Rashee Rice ( hamstring ) out, recording a pair of receptions for 24 yards. He also played 45 snaps, marking the second game in a row his share has increased. Elsewhere as far as pass catchers are concerned, Jake Briningstool's elevation stems solely from workload (his snaps have increased by two in Weeks 4 and 6) and rookie wideout Cyrus Allen recorded his first two NFL catches over the weekend.
UDFA defensive tackle Bryson Eason isn't a primary special-teamer (he hasn't played there at all) but he also isn't seeing the field much on defense. He's somewhere in the middle, albeit not in his own tier.
There still isn't anything to see here. Simmons is making progress as he works his way back from a bulging disc , and Reid was noncommittal about his playing status on Monday. If the 2025 first-round pick isn't back this Sunday, look for Week 8 as a potential season debut spot.
Safety Nwankpa feels like he might be on the verge of increased playing time, although it might require an injury before he's unleashed on the defensive end. Running back Brashard Smith makes sense as a candidate to take special teams opportunities from wideout Nikko Remigio, who struggled once again against Los Angeles.
Jeffrey Bassa is turning himself into a trusted core player for coordinator Dave Toub on teams. Similar to Nwankpa, though, he's buried on the depth chart on defense.
Since playing 47 special teams snaps in the first three weeks of the season, fourth-round rookie cornerback Jadon Canady hasn't been active for a game. He's got to come down a tier.
Elsewhere, the trio of quarterback Garrett Nussmeier, tackle Diego Pounds and defensive end Jack Pyburn can be classified as organizational depth for now.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: Is the Chiefs' Offensive Line Set for a Disappointment in Seattle?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are 5-0 and alone atop the AFC as the only undefeated team in the conference, but they still have plenty of questions to answer ahead of their primetime Sunday night showdown against the Seattle Seahawks this weekend.
Every week here in the Chiefs On SI mailbag , we take your questions from @chiefs_kcsn on Twitter/X and @jbbrisco.com on Bluesky , navigating the biggest unknowns the Chiefs have as the season rolls on. Let's get to it!
Does the dam eventually break on the O-line without Josh Simmons? - @oscarbobo.bsky.social
It's sure looking like Sunday night's game in Seattle will be the O-line's most difficult test yet. With left tackle Josh Simmons still appearing to be in "ramp-up" territory this week, I'm assuming that undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson will get his sixth start at left tackle, while right tackle Jaylon Moore's status is questionable after leaving the Chiefs' win over the Los Angeles Chargers due to a concussion. With the inherent unknowns of concussions and the NFL's concussion protocol, Joshua Ezeudu could be getting the start at right tackle.
According to ESPN , the Seahawks have the No. 1 pass rush win rate in the league through Week 6. That has resulted in 16 sacks and the league's highest quarterback knockdown percentage and second-highest pressure percentage , so this isn't a great time to have a banged-up line.
Still, the Chiefs' interior of Kingsley Suamataia, Creed Humphrey and Trey Smith can still be trusted, and they've managed without Simmons so far. I'd be surprised if the KC O-line was entirely overwhelmed in a game-altering way in Seattle, but I'd also be surprised if they pitched a shutout against the Seahawks.
Do all roads lead to another Chiefs vs. 49ers Super Bowl? - @toptrevor.bsky.social
It sure feels that way, doesn't it? I've been enormously impressed by how the 49ers have managed yet another injury-ravaged season, and I think their ability to stay afloat (and undefeated) despite health woes has earned them a reasonable claim to the No. 1 spot in some power rankings . However, those losses can stack up and cause more significant damage later in the year, so I fear for the Niners' long-term health.
While the Chiefs still have flaws, just like every other team in the NFL, I'm hugely excited by the possibility of them regaining Simmons and potentially ending the year healthier than they started it.
KCSN’s NFL Power Rankings heading into Week 6 📊 These rankings reflect the average of our hosts’ votes — who’s too high and who’s too low? 🤔 pic.twitter.com/dGx1EC3wdL
Good, bad, or both, what has surprised you the most about the Chiefs so far this season? - @MrEd315
The biggest positive surprise has to be the absolute dominance from Kenneth Walker III . I'm not surprised that he's been good—that was to be expected—but I'm amazed by how good, how consistent, and how diversely superb he's been, while totally transforming the KC offense.
The bad surprises come from the Chiefs' special teams. Many assumed that Harrison Butker's recent issues had been largely due to lingering injury issues, giving him a chance to return to his previous level after another offseason to settle back in, but he's still missing enough kicks to cause some fair concern .
Adding in issues with special teams penalties , Nikko Remigio's fumbled punt against the Chargers and the lack of a role for Brashard Smith amidst a generally underwhelming return game, the Chiefs' third phase still has a lot of work to do.
Considering the Broncos' upcoming schedule, is the AFC West still a live fight? - @oscarbobo.bsky.social
It absolutely is! The Broncos are coming off of a gross, uninspiring win over the Seahawks, but they're still 4-2 ahead of a relatively soft stretch in their upcoming schedule. If the Broncos beat the Chiefs in Denver on November 1, the divisional race will immediately be back on after KC's early lead. If the Chiefs win at Mile High Stadium in two weeks, it would make it extremely difficult for Denver to come roaring back.

title: Chiefs Stock Watch: Who Helped and Hurt Their Case in Week 6 Win vs. Chargers?
full_text:
Five games into the 2026-27 season, the Kansas City Chiefs have helped themselves in a major way by already picking up three wins against divisional opponents. Sunday's Week 6 triumph over the Los Angeles Chargers wasn't the prettiest of victories, but Andy Reid's team thoroughly outplayed its rival by a multitude of measurements nonetheless.
In the 22-6 outcome in favor of the hosts, several critical players managed to make an impact on their respective side of the ball. Others struggled to execute what was asked of them, although there's still plenty of time to turn things around.
Let's dive into the good and bad from Week 6's Chiefs victory against Los Angeles and single out three players whose stock is trending up, as well as three who could use a better showing in Week 7 and beyond.
These players stood out for positive reasons over the weekend, potentially changing the trajectory of their seasons in the process.
The Chiefs' defense is performing at a very respectable level this season, and its new-look secondary is a significant reason why. A returning player from a year ago, 2025 third-round pick Nohl Williams, has starred to this point in the campaign and may have turned in his best outing yet on Sunday.
After making a big-time downhill tackle on the Chargers' opening drive, the Cal product was banged up but stayed in the game and continued to get noticed. A pair of pass breakups — one on a second-and-9 on the next possession and a third-and-goal stop in the second half — showcased his instincts and timing. Finally, Williams prevented wideout KeAndre Lambert-Smith from converting on a fourth down in the final frame.
The sophomore stopper is disruptive, tough and thorough in the defensive backfield, which is precisely what Kansas City needs.
What a turnaround it's been over the last month for one Xavier Worthy. Through three outings, he'd averaged five targets a game but managed only 6.3 yards per reception and looked more and more like an afterthought in the offense. In his last two weeks of play, he's gone for seven targets each time and racked up 143 yards in the process, good for 13 yards per catch. Sunday was his most complete showing to date.
Worthy had a 33-yarder wiped out by an illegal block by tight end Travis Kelce right out of the gate, then followed it up with a gain of 15 on the very next play. He notched 70 yards on five receptions in the first half alone and made a nice diving snag in the second half. With the KC wideout room severely banged up at the moment , Worthy's ability to step up and rise to the occasion is a pleasant surprise for the Chiefs as the season approaches its midpoint.
Speaking of players who made the most of their opportunities in Week 6, Noah Gray matched the receiving output of Kelce by mustering 53 yards in the home win. Gray hauled in each of the three targets thrown his way and displayed some rare post-catch chops on a 31-yard rumble to boot. Kelce's ankle injury limited his effectiveness and availability a bit, so Gray being the one to help insulate the pass catchers was a nice development.
There's only room for three here, but defensive end George Karlaftis deserves considerable praise for his recent play. He's undoubtedly turning into quite the productive player for Kansas City and has been a driving force in multiple victories.
This group of three didn't live up to the hype in Week 6. It isn't necessarily time to panic, but it's certainly time to be on watch.
Back to the aforementioned receiver injuries. Given that Tyquan Thornton is on injured reserve due to a dislocated ankle and Rashee Rice needed (at least) another week to rehab a hamstring issue , this was a massive chance for a lesser-discussed wideout like Nikko Remigio to take a role and run with it on Sunday. He did nothing of the sort on the offensive end, receiving all of two offensive snaps. He also had a special teams fumble.
Coordinator Dave Toub has preached patience with his group getting out to a slow start, but mistakes persist in multiple areas of special teams. Remigio, whose role seems defined, isn't doing anything to justify being a long-term solution as a returner.
It's now been several years in a row of Harrison Butker not matching the leaguewide perception of him being one of the best in the business. It's this writer's take that those days are clearly over now , even if the team won't admit it, especially given another missed extra point and some waning effectiveness on long-range boots.
Butker's trump card is his ability to make pressure-packed kicks, which is one heck of a positive to bring to the table, but everything else is questionable right now. Week 6 only underscored that.
Had he not gotten ejected for throwing a punch, defensive back Chris Roland-Wallace wouldn't have even been considered for a spot here. He made multiple solid plays elsewhere, including a big tackle for loss and a tipped interception that got nullified by a penalty. At the end of the day, though, you simply can't put your team in a compromising position like that.

title: Kenneth Walker is Rushing Past Reasonable Expectations, Straight Into Chiefs History
full_text:
It keeps getting more and more difficult to write about Kenneth Walker III.
Not because I'm bored of talking about Walker's unbelievable dominance—quite the opposite, in fact. Walker has been so outstanding that even a measured evaluation of his 2026 season sounds like the ravings of a madman.
The remarkable stats help tell the story, but even those feel insufficient. Still, they're worth knowing: Walker's 133 rushing yards per game are the most for any running back through six weeks since at least 2016 . He has a 40% forced missed tackle rate , the best in the NFL by more than 10%. He's the first player since 2002 to have 750+ scrimmage yards and 8+ touchdowns through the first five games of the year. The player who did that in '02? Chiefs Hall of Honor member Priest Holmes.
Many excellent running backs have starred throughout Chiefs history, as good-but-not-great teams often relied on dominant runners to carry their respective squads.
Christian Okoye—"the Nigerian Nightmare"—thundered into Chiefs history in the late '80s and early '90s. Marcus Allen left the rival Raiders to finish his career in Kansas City, taking the baton from Okoye. Holmes was the running back of my childhood—a workhorse that thrived behind a remarkable offensive line, instilling a love of smashmouth football in so many young Chiefs fans. Larry Johnson followed as a quintessential bellcow back, the engine of Chiefs offenses that relied on him to take on a superhuman workload.
Then came Jamaal Charles, my favorite running back of all time. Charles was a gamebreaker. He moved unlike anyone I've ever seen on a football field, skating past defenders with a smoothness typically reserved for athletes on ice.
In recent years, the Chiefs briefly had a true No. 1 back with Kareem Hunt, found excellent role players like Damien Williams and Jerick McKinnon, invested a premium pick in Clyde Edwards-Helaire, got two productive years from Isiah Pacheco, and patched up the weaker seasons with relative success until the wheels fell off the running back room in 2025.
But with all that history, all those legacies, and all of those yards... Through five games, Walker has been in a league of his own.
Walker's second touchdown against the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday might have been the most on-brand run of his still-young Chiefs tenure. Look at this snapshot of Walker's situation moments before scoring a touchdown.
This was a touchdown. pic.twitter.com/uYSK1YJkof
By any NFL standard, that play is dead. The body is cold. The Chargers had the beat on the play. All they had to do was, y'know, tackle Walker. But that's been a problem for every team the Chiefs have faced through five games.
My favorite nugget from the Chiefs' win over the Chargers comes from Next Gen Stats .
"Walker gained 53 yards and 2 TDs on 6 carries against stacked boxes (8+ defenders). He leads the NFL in yards (183) and TDs (6) on those runs."
Kenneth Walker III forced 7 missed tackles against the Chargers, bringing his NFL-leading total to 52. Walker gained 53 yards and 2 TDs on 6 carries against stacked boxes (8+ defenders). He leads the NFL in yards (183) and TDs (6) on those runs. @LACvsKC | #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/fsnBre5Mn5
One of the surefire selling points of Walker's contract with the Chiefs was that he would be able to take advantage of light boxes while opposing defenses respected Patrick Mahomes and the KC passing game, allowing Walker's life to get easier while the rushing attack got more productive. Instead, Walker is just slicing through heavy boxes, too. It's remarkable.
Can Walker keep up this outrageous standard of performance through 17 regular season games and a playoff push? Who knows. But at some point, we should probably stop asking “Can he keep doing this?” and start asking, “What if this is just who he is?”
I'm still struggling to flip that particular switch myself. Even if he does this for 15 more games, can he do it in 2027? 2028? Is his legacy evolving from “very good running back who won Super Bowl MVP on a team with a questionable quarterback” to a future Hall of Famer who truly evolved into a superstar once he joined the Chiefs? Will the rest of his prime be spent as a perennial Offensive Player of the Year finalist? Is he the most impactful non-quarterback in the league?
This is why it feels so difficult to properly talk about Walker through five games. The truth sounds like hyperbole, and hyperbole still isn’t strong enough to explain what Walker has done throughout the start of this season.

title: Chiefs WR Xavier Worthy Finally Stepped Up When Kansas City Needed Him the Most
full_text:
Amid the ongoing injuries to the Chiefs' receiving corps, there were concerns about how the wideouts would fare against the Chargers. Kansas City was without Tyquan Thornton whose fractured ankle will force him to miss most of the season, and Rashee Rice was also sidelined with a hamstring injury.
Third-year speedster Xavier Worthy had caught a lot of flak in recent weeks due to his mediocre start to the season. Through the first three weeks of the campaign, Worthy ranked in the bottom three in the NFL in yards per catch and was primarily used in the short game. The Chiefs weren't necessarily playing to his strengths , which include his ability to stretch the field as a long-ball threat. Worthy finally silenced those concerns in the game where KC needed him the most. He finished the 22-6 victory over the Chargers with a season-high seven receptions for 73 yards, hauling in all of his targets from quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Going into the contest, Worthy knew he'd have to take on an extended workload to help make up for the team's injuries. He couldn't have asked for a better opportunity to show that he was ready for it.
"They told me all week that [WR1] was going to be me," Worthy said in the locker room after the win. "I got to step up for the receiving room guys who went down, so I did my job."
It has been a long road for Worthy, whose progress during his 638-yard, nine-touchdown rookie season was derailed by a subpar sophomore year. He dislocated his shoulder in the 2025 season opener, and although he returned to action a few weeks later, he never had the same explosiveness or burst moving forward.
Regardless, head coach Andy Reid maintains that Worthy has always been capable of this kind of production and should be able to reach his full potential now that he's fully healthy and being given a more featured role in the aerial attack. "We had some injuries, and all of a sudden, he becomes the primary guy," Reid stated in his media appearance this afternoon. "But he's always had this ability and can do all of this. He's a good football player. It's just a matter of there's only so many plays, and so many times to spread the ball around."
All of the questions about whether Worthy's speed had diminished since his first year in the red and gold were put to bed in Week 6. His highlight of the night came on a blazing 19-yard catch that helped Kansas City tack on another three points before halftime.
Xavier Worthy hit 21.07 MPH on this play per @NextGenStats the 2nd fastest ball carrier of the week. https://t.co/XOmGcJ36nR
The length of Rice's absence remains to be seen, but Worthy should have plenty of confidence after finally getting a chance to show what he can do. If this version of Worthy sticks around, Kansas City's receiver room may not be as dire as it once appeared.

title: The Chiefs Have a Harrison Butker Problem, Whether They Care to Admit It or Not
full_text:
It's hard to go directly to nitpicking after a win, especially for a team that returned from the bye and improved to a perfect 5-0 . If there's one thing the Kansas City Chiefs have shown through five games, however, it's that multiple areas of the team are imperfect as the season's midpoint draws near.
For every instance in which the Chiefs' dominance of old has flashed, there's been a reminder or two that this is a new era. There's no greater example of that than the roller coaster ride that is the play of kicker Harrison Butker.
I will repeat again, Harrison Butker came into this game as one of the bottom 10 Kickers in the NFL to start 2026 and this performance in Kansas City is going to send him tumbling down the list.... Chiefs must look for replacements. pic.twitter.com/v0YSLh6u48
With data mounting that this is a new era for Butker as well, should that come with new expectations? It's clear that he isn't the same player right now, yet special teams coordinator Dave Toub preaches patience and sample-size variance for the entire special teams unit. Following Sunday's victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, head coach Andy Reid also danced around any Butker-related concerns.
"Butker, he's as consistent as anybody," Reid said. "He had a couple of misses in there, and that's not normally him, so he'll continue to work on that."
It'd be one thing if Kansas City admitted Butker isn't meeting the bar that's been set. A plan to establish more consistency — actual consistency, not the perceived press-conference backing provided by the team — would be a nice first step.
Instead, the club is paying Butker more on a per-year basis ( $6.4 million ) than all but three kickers in NFL history to provide negative value. Doing so while denying that is even worse.
The three-time Super Bowl champion is now several years removed from his last legitimately good effort. In 2023, he drilled 94.3% of field goals and didn't miss an extra point. In 35 regular-season outings since then, though, those respective accuracy marks are 84.2% and 91.4%. Last year saw the former seventh-round pick finish just 1.2% above the league average on field goals and 7.3% worse on PATs.
Following the Chargers game, Butker's missed one extra point in 2026 and is sporting an ugly 76.9% conversion clip on field goals. According to Pro Football Focus , his average starting field position on kickoffs (30.2 yards) is 18th out of 33 kickers with five or more tries. Last year, his 30.3 figure sat 26th among 44 players with double-digit kicks. That does, in fairness, have something to do with coverage.
There's also the question of long-range kicking. Something that was once a calling card for Butker has turned into another high-variance component, evidenced by him going 5-for-8 in 2025 and being off to a 1-for-4 start in 2026. The 31-year-old can still be relied upon to have a clutch gene, which is a damn good plus to have in the toolbox, but the positive traits are dwindling .
He was erratic on other kicks this preseason, too, which was followed by Reid saying he'll "learn from it and move on" and "make an adjustment."
Butker has been through a similar stretch before, connecting on 76.9% of field goals and 84.6% of point-afters entering Week 6 of 2025 and finishing the year strong. That doesn't mean it didn't impact him, as he admitted in June :
"I think when you start the season off with misses, your back's kind of against the wall [and] mentally, it kind of takes a toll on you," Butker said. "It's just not great. I climbed out of it; I finished the season, I think I was above middle-of-the-pack. Obviously, you don't even want to be there, but you don't want to start out the season missing as much."
Butker is held in too high of regard and making too much money to be an up-and-down player at best and a diminished version of himself at worst. An in-season change is mostly unrealistic, although the Chiefs coming to terms with their current reality and future salary cap flexibility shouldn't be. The glory days of not having to question whether KC had an elite kicker are over.
Now, both the team and those watching it should be questioning whether Butker's even good anymore.

title: Biggest Winners and Losers From Chiefs’ Week 6 Win Over the Chargers
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are 5-0, and you'll never apologize for a double-digit win in the NFL. Sunday’s 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers was dominant in the ways that mattered most, and the next two weeks will get a whole lot stiffer against the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks and the reigning AFC West champion Broncos.
The Chargers never posed a genuine threat to Kansas City’s win column, but the Chiefs left enough on the field Sunday afternoon that the locker room will know there is plenty to clean up before the real tests arrive.
Here is a full breakdown of the biggest winners and losers from Week 6.
Running back Kenneth Walker deserves his flowers, once again. With the Chiefs struggling to punch it into the end zone for much of the afternoon, he took matters into his own hands twice. The first came on a third-and-one when he bypassed the red zone entirely, ripping off a 33-yard touchdown on a straightforward up-the-gut call.
The second came at the end of an eight-play, 80-yard drive, where he was met in the backfield by Chargers defenders, bounced off them, and dove into the end zone from two yards out. Walker now has 665 rushing yards and six touchdown runs, the most rushing yards through a player’s first five games with a franchise in NFL history.
With Tyquan Thornton on IR and Rashee Rice still sidelined with his hamstring, Xavier Worthy was the player the team needed most to step up in Week 6 and beyond. He answered the call in his first real audition as the team’s primary wide receiver option in 2026. Mahomes targeted him seven times, and Worthy caught all seven for 73 yards.
His longest gain was 19 yards, which suggests this wasn't a splash-play performance but a consistent, reliable one. With Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen still finding their footing, Worthy’s ability to be a dependable option for Mahomes was the afternoon's most encouraging development.
The sack drought is over. After three straight games without getting home, the Chiefs recorded four sacks Sunday, and no pass rusher performed more impactfully than George Karlaftis. Karlaftis secured his one sack on the Chargers’ final offensive drive, the second of back-to-back sacks that sealed the 22-6 victory.
In PFF’s preliminary grades, he finished with nine pressures and a sack, following up his 11-pressure performance against the Raiders with another dominant afternoon. He also batted down two of Justin Herbert’s passes, adding a dimension to his game that the traditional box score doesn't always show. Karlaftis has been the most consistent performer on the defensive line over six weeks, and Sunday was no different.
Special teams was once again a theme in the losers column, and Harrison Butker was the central figure. He missed a 52-yard field goal and an extra point on the Chiefs’ first touchdown, giving Kansas City a 9-3 lead instead of 10-3.
The misses beyond 50 yards are understandable, but Butker is the league's fourth-highest-paid kicker. Over five games, he has three missed field goals and one missed extra point, and as the schedule tightens, those points will matter enormously at times. It didn't cost the Chiefs this time, but in Seattle and Denver over the next two weeks, misses can matter.
Nikko Remigio is on the 53-man roster for one thing: to be reliable in the return game. It would be unfair to call him unreliable at this point, but he fumbled a punt return while trying to extend a gain.
Luckily, the Chiefs allowed a combined negative yardage on the two Chargers drives that sandwiched the turnover, but they can't afford mishaps like that moving forward. Against Seattle or Denver, that kind of fortune is unlikely to repeat. Remigio is a trusted Dave Toub player, and his roster spot isn't in immediate danger, but Chiefs Kingdom, who is growing tired of special teams woes, won't forget the fumble.
Walker’s 33-yard third-and-one touchdown was the lone bright spot in an otherwise brutal day in the red zone and short-yardage situations. The Chiefs failed to convert a separate third-and-one, turned the ball over on downs on a fourth-and-goal at the one-yard line, and Mahomes threw an interception on a third-and-goal at the Los Angeles two.
In total, Kansas City went 1-for-4 inside the red zone, 3-for-10 on third downs, and 0-for-1 on fourth downs. That's why a team that outgained the Chargers 422 yards to 259 won by only 16 points. Mahomes threw for 9.1 yards per attempt in a quietly brilliant performance, but the team's inability to execute in key moments kept a bad Chargers team within two scores for the all game.

title: Patrick Mahomes Explains Chiefs’ Inconsistent Offensive Execution in Win Over Chargers
full_text:
The Chiefs were in command for the entirety of their 22-6 win over the Chargers tonight, but Patrick Mahomes would be the first person to tell you Kansas City left some points on the board.
It wasn't exactly a vintage outing by the superstar quarterback's standards, as Mahomes didn't throw a touchdown for the first time this season and tossed a red-zone interception in the second quarter. The Chargers' anemic offense couldn't capitalize on the miscue, but Mahomes knows that won't always be the case against better opponents. The three-time Super Bowl MVP took responsibility for the interception during his postgame press conference and explained what he saw before the throw. It was an awkward in-between decision, as he was partially trying to throw the ball away while also giving his intended target, Andrew Armstrong, a chance to make a play.
"It happened faster than I expected it, so instead of just staying with it and throwing it to the end zone, I tried scrambling and did what you're not supposed to do. I was trying to throw it away but trying to give him a chance..You just can't do that, especially with how our defense was playing," Mahomes said.
Cam Hart picks off Mahomes in the end zone ‼️ LACvsKC on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/zWLXiWFXZb
There were also a handful of stalled possessions, including a goal-line sequence where KC ran Kenneth Walker up the middle four straight times and came away empty-handed. The Chiefs also had multiple drives fizzle out after halftime, making execution a major talking point for Mahomes after the game.
"Missing the field goal and stuff like that, you got to execute at a higher level in the second half like we did in the first half," Mahomes stated. "That's stuff we have got to continue to work... For me, it's just about how can we be consistent for an entire game and not have those droughts, a quarter here and there where we're not playing to our standard." When asked what the offense needs to clean up to become more consistent, Mahomes pointed to the little things and specifically mentioned the fourth-and-one stop. It marked the third consecutive week Kansas City was stuffed on fourth-and-short with Walker pounding it up the gut.
"Little things here and there," he continued. If one guy makes a mistake in a moment and that just ruins the drive. Obviously, you want to be able to punch it in on that fourth-and-one at the goal line. That's a big one."
Still, Mahomes isn't going to dwell on a few missed chances after a 16-point victory. He reflected on his devastating injury last season and the grueling recovery from a torn ACL , explaining how the experience has changed his perspective and allowed him to enjoy playing football even more.
"Last year, to me, put football in perspective," Mahomes said. "We have played in so many Super Bowls, and especially those last few, we didn't play our best football in the regular season and just turned it on in the playoffs. Even last year, when stuff wasn't going right, I thought we were going to figure it out. Having to go through that rehab process and not play football, it's really made me enjoy the process of it. I try to have fun out there and enjoy the wins, because you never know when it's going to be your last one."
The Chiefs will head to Seattle next Sunday night for a much tougher test against a top-ranked Seahawks defense. That matchup should provide a better gauge of where Kansas City's offense stands, especially after Mahomes and Eric Bieniemy spend the upcoming week identifying the little things that need to be cleaned up.

title: Andy Reid Drops Chiefs Injury Updates on Jaylon Moore, Travis Kelce After Week 6 Win
full_text:
Despite being shorthanded, the Kansas City Chiefs found multiple ways to take down the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday and came away with a 22-6 victory that didn't feel as dominant as it truly was at times. The club did see some players go down with injuries in Week 6, although most of them escaped the outing without anything too significant.
The offensive side of the ball, in particular, was already missing talent and dealt with additional adversity throughout the afternoon and into the evening. Speaking to the media after the final whistle, head coach Andy Reid provided his usual injury roundup.
The only injury that forced someone out of the game long-term was to right tackle Jaylon Moore. Reid confirmed it's a concussion for his first-string lineman, also dishing out context for tight end Travis Kelce, wide receiver Jalen Royals and left guard Kingsley Suamataia.
"As far as the injuries go, Jaylon Moore has a concussion," Reid said. "That's the one that probably stands out the most there. Kelce tweaked his ankle there; he continued to play. He might be a little sore tomorrow, but he did a nice job tonight. The rest of that, everybody worked. Royals went to be checked for a concussion, but he was good there. And then Kingsley, he got kicked in the calf, but he should be OK."
The Moore news shouldn't come as too much of a surprise. Kansas City acknowledged via social media that he was in concussion protocol during the game, then downgraded him to out less than an hour later. At the time of his departure, according to Pro Football Focus , he'd played 31 snaps and been credited with a pair of pressures and one quarterback hit.
In Moore's place, Joshua Ezeudu finished out the game. Ezeudu, a former New York Giants draft pick, primarily had experience playing on the left side of the offensive line but held his own given the circumstances. The 27-year-old was acquired via trade prior to August's mandatory roster cutdown deadline.
Kelce, the biggest name who got dinged on Sunday for KC, sustained an ankle injury in the first quarter when his foot bent at an awkward angle on a tackle. He received an initial sideline examination and tape job with his shoe off before coming back into the game, then getting his foot/ankle spatted and finishing the tilt. Kelce split time with fellow tight end Noah Gray; each pass catcher had 53 receiving yards.
Suamataia appeared to be in severe pain and discomfort in the second half of Sunday's win, but he ultimately returned to the contest and finished with PFF 's highest preliminary pass block grade for anyone on the roster.
For a team that was down left tackle Josh Simmons ( back ) and wideout Rashee Rice ( hamstring ) before kickoff even happened, this is far from the worst case for the Chiefs. Moore's progress in return-to-play protocol will be worth monitoring this week.

title: 10 Instant Observations From the Chiefs’ Commanding Week 6 Victory Over Chargers
full_text:
It wasn't particularly pretty by either team, but the Kansas City Chiefs emerged victorious tonight in a 22-6 triumph over the winless Los Angeles Chargers . Despite special teams miscues and multiple turnovers, KC pulled away late as its defense clamped down. The Chiefs picked up right where they left off from their bye week and now sit atop the AFC West with a 1.5-game lead over the second-place Broncos. Here are 10 instant observations we gathered from the win.
This was a trivial moment in what was otherwise an impressive win, but the Chiefs have now been stuffed on fourth-and-short in three straight weeks with a Kenneth Walker run up the middle. It happened on a fourth-and-one opportunity against the Dolphins, again on the opening drive against the Raiders when Kansas City turned it over on downs, and once more today when the Chargers stopped Walker at the goal line in the third quarter.
Walker mentioned earlier this week that he and the coordinators were looking to correct this issue, but it nearly proved costly again. There has to be more creativity in those situations than simply handing it off to Walker and hoping the offensive line can create enough separation.
There was once a point in the AFC West where it looked like Justin Herbert would be a fierce competitor to Mahomes for years to come. We can safely say those days are no more. The seventh-year signal-caller was dreadful in this showing, tossing his eighth interception of the campaign and completing just 59.5% of his passes. He was bailed out by having a pick called back due to a penalty, only to throw another one a few plays later.
Herbert finished the afternoon with 204 passing yards, no touchdowns, and a turnover. The Chargers' anemic offensive attack looks beyond the point of repair, and it's honestly quite disheartening to see how quickly Herbert has fallen from a once-promising quarterback.
Cornerback Nohl Williams was solid through the first four games, but he took his play to another level in this one. It was easily his best performance of the season and one of the strongest showings we've seen from the second-year corner. Williams finished with three solo tackles, two pass deflections, a tackle for loss, and two huge open-field stops. Despite briefly exiting the game with an injury during the opening defensive series, he'd return and put together a standout performance as the best player in Kansas City's secondary.
Tight end Travis Kelce stepped off the field to have his ankle worked on multiple times throughout the contest. That's the product of being 37 years old and lugging 250 pounds around on your lower body.
Kelce still looks as elite as ever when he's out in open space, but an ankle injury for someone his stature is worrisome. Even after his first catch of the afternoon in the second quarter, he exited the game for one play and was slow to get up.
Travis Kelce is having his ankle worked on. pic.twitter.com/IFQ9nsp2dG
His target share had significantly dipped in the two weeks before the bye — two and four, respectively — and clearly can't be relied upon as often as he once was. Other contributors must take on more responsibility, especially if Rashee Rice's absence extends beyond this week.
While the Chargers' struggles didn't allow this to matter, Mahomes had an uncharacteristically bad interception on the goal line when the Chiefs were winning 9-3 in the second quarter. Theoretically, it could have turned the tide if Los Angeles responded with a touchdown and retook the lead.
Cam Hart picks off Mahomes in the end zone ‼️ LACvsKC on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/zWLXiWFXZb
He was trying to throw it away to the back of the end zone but didn't get enough air under it, and the ball fell right into Cam Hart's hands. Those kinds of blunders aren't expected from Mahomes. It was only his third pick of the year, but history would suggest he'll clean those things up heading into the next matchup.
Trying to stay as neutral as possible here, Nikko Remigio's days as the punt returner simply have to be numbered. He had a horrendous fumble on a punt return that gave the Chargers the ball near midfield in a two-score game. He had a rare invalid fair-catch signal penalty on a punt return two weeks ago and somehow found a way to make another head-scratching mistake today. At this point, it's tough to justify holding a roster spot for a special teams "guru" when guys like Brashard Smith have been far more effective in the return game this season.
The sales pitch for Nikko Remigio is that he’s trustworthy. If he’s gonna do this, what use is he?
As people online have pointed out, Remigio's entire selling point is supposed to be his reliability. If that has gone out the window, what exactly is he bringing to the table over other deserving roster candidates?
This would've been higher on the list had it resulted in points, but we witnessed one of the worst roughing calls in recent history today. Ashton Gillotte was inexplicably flagged to wipe away a Chiefs interception despite hardly making any contact with Herbert. You make the call yourself:
Roughing the passer for barely touching the quarterback. This took away a #Chiefs INT. pic.twitter.com/KxdolOrGZx
Luckily, the Chiefs were able to snag another pick off LA's mistake-prone quarterback later in the drive, but in what world is this a penalty? Gillotte clearly does his best to minimize the contact and keep Herbert out of harm's way. If a gentle bear hug is roughing the passer, the NFL might as well turn into a flag football league.
In a matchup where Xavier Worthy had to step up in the absence of Rice and Tyquan Thornton, he did just that. The speedster out of Texas followed up his best showing of the year with a seven-catch, 73-yard outing.
Worthy's best moment came at the end of the first half when he took a ball up the sideline for 19 yards to put KC in field goal range, allowing Harrison Butker to drill a 50-yarder right before the clock expired. He looks a lot more explosive than he did during the opening weeks when he was struggling , and he should continue to be a key weapon in a Chiefs offense that lacks playmakers outside of Walker.
Cue the Kenneth Walker music, because there's no way we could write one of these 10 observations articles without giving him his flowers. His dream inaugural season in Kansas City continued with two more scores on the ground today and 139 yards from scrimmage.
Walker was the first Chiefs player to find paydirt this afternoon with a 33-yard burst up the middle on a third-and-one opportunity in the opening quarter. He's now up to 665 rushing yards and eight total touchdowns on the year, keeping him on pace to make a run at AFC Offensive Player of the Year in his first year with the red and gold.
KENNETH WALKER III DOES IT AGAIN LACvsKC on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bo0Vpy9A29
The best thing to come from today is that the Chiefs' defensive line can finally exhale after snapping its ugly three-game stretch without getting to the quarterback. Ashton Gillotte broke through in the third quarter, recording KC's first sack in more than 15 quarters of football. Earlier in the second quarter, the broadcast panned to defensive line coach Joe Cullen getting into it with Chris Jones on the sideline. Jones apparently took the message to heart, because he got into the sack column for the first time this year, splitting a takedown with rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods. George Karlaftis also got his first of the year as well.
CBS broadcast shows the discussion between #Chiefs DL coach Joe Cullen and Chris Jones. pic.twitter.com/z8NB0VnS4U
This had been a weekly talking point for a while, so perhaps the Chiefs can finally put it in the rearview mirror and get back to making opposing quarterbacks uncomfortable.

title: Jim Harbaugh Ruining Justin Herbert Rumblings Keep Increasing
full_text:
There’s a concerning, budding idea around the hapless Los Angeles Chargers right now: Jim Harbaugh is doing more harm than good for Justin Herbert.
Most of the attention for the 0-6 Chargers at the bye week falls on offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel . His complexity of the scheme, proper talent for the scheme, all that stuff has come under fire with McDaniel so far.
But that’s overshadowing another uncomfortable topic around the Chargers when it comes to how Harbaugh actually fits Herbert, too.
And no, this doesn’t have anything to do with Harbaugh’s gushy exaggerations about Herbert, such as declaring him on the way to being one of the best ever or that he dreams of getting a Lombardi Trophy with his star quarterback.
In fact, this idea about Harbaugh hurting Herbert goes back to 2024.
While examining the Chargers’ issues, The Athletic’s Mike Sando put Harbaugh himself under the microscope.
Sando’s most crushing point: “Herbert ranked seventh in expected points added per pass play under two other head coaches and three offensive coordinators across his first four seasons. He ranks 23rd under Harbaugh, and the trend is unmistakable (12th in 2024, 21st last season and 32nd this season).”
We can bemoan how the Chargers spend money or how general manager Joe Hortiz builds out a roster. But that roster has input from Harbaugh.
And it’s Harbaugh who went with his friend Greg Roman for multiple years as coordinator, taking Herbert and placing him in a conservative offense that asked him to play hero ball far too much.
And it’s Harbaugh who had an uncanny loyalty to middling players like Bradley Bozeman in the heart of the offensive line.
And now it’s Harbaugh leaving his comfort zone and dramatically over-correcting with the hire of McDaniel, which is currently doing far more harm than good. Credit for trying to right the ship by doing something that was widely accepted as a good move, but it’s a byproduct of the prior mistakes.
Make no mistake, Herbert deserves some blame too. The overarching franchise and Hortiz, especially so.
But it does feel like Harbaugh isn’t getting enough criticism for holding back Herbert because a few years ago, nobody would have expected a regression for the star quarterback compared to the Brandon Staley days.

title: Chargers Could Use Unexpected Veteran Trade Option Before Deadline
full_text:
With the Los Angeles Chargers securing the first overall pick for the 2027 NFL Draft order for now, they are expected to be a team looking to "sell" or, in other terms, trade away valuable assets to teams who are looking to "buy" or to improve their roster for a playoff run.
Even with the team being the worst in the NFL, the Chargers still have plenty of players under contract who could be potential trade candidates. The biggest of those names is the veteran, future Hall of Fame EDGE rusher, Khalil Mack.
With Mack swirling in trade rumors, one name has been largely forgotten until a recent CBS Sports article by Carter Bahns named the Chargers veteran CB, Donte Jackson, as a possible candidate to be moved to a different team.
In Bahns' article, he discusses Jackson's possibility of being traded: "Teams with holes on the back end of the defense could call about Jackson and his expiring contract, too. He racked up nine interceptions across the 2024 and 2025 seasons, after all."
Jackson has been a long-time starting-caliber corner since he was drafted in the second round of the 2018 NFL Draft by the Carolina Panthers. After six seasons with the Panthers, Jackson spent a year in Pittsburgh, where he began to earn his ballhawking moniker, which he replicated in his first season in Los Angeles under defensive coordinator Jesse Minter.
Now in year two with the Chargers, Jackson has only played in four games, recording two pass deflections and eight tackles. While he has been on the field, he has been a solid contributor for Chris O'Leary's defense, but a hamstring injury has kept him off the field for nearly half the season.
If a team needs a veteran presence who is known for turnovers in their back seven, adding Jackson is a good idea. He would likely only cost a Day 3 selection, with a fifth-round pick being within reason for a player of his caliber.
The Chargers have not exactly found options behind Jackson as starting-caliber cornerbacks in the defense, as Deane Leonard and Rodney Shelley have been either hurt or lackluster, but at 0-6, having strong CBs is somewhat of a luxury, considering the season is just about over.
It should be noted that Bahns' article also mentions Khalil Mack, Quentin Johnston and David Njoku as other trade candidates for the Bolts to "sell."

title: 3 Chargers Who Had Standout Performances Against the Chiefs
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers dropped to 0-6 on the season after dropping their week six game against the Kansas City Chiefs. The Chargers offense has not been playing winning football but to make matters worse, the football gods have been cruel with injuries through the first six weeks of the season for Los Angeles.
The week leading up to the game was loaded with questions in the media over which coaches could potentially be on the hot seat and which players would be the subject of trade rumors. At 0-5, it was clear the Chargers were set to make their final stand of 2026 in Arrowhead.
The Chargers defense, despite injuries across the board battled and gave the offense every chance they could have asked for. For the first time all season, the special teams unit looked sharp, productive and play complementary football.
The offense may be in a purgatory of confusion and ineptitude but there are several players who gave performances worthy of recognition against the Chiefs. Let's dive into a few of the best standouts from week six.
Tony Jefferson and the Chargers make a goal line stand! LACvsKC on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/WjY5BbzBPJ
Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs have transformed their offense into a typical play-action unit relying heavily on running back Kenneth Walker and short throws. Mahomes was consistently hitting short throws to the outside and safety Tony Jefferson was flying downhill to make sure every pass catcher was not getting a free pass.
In addition to delivering imposing hits on the outside, Jefferson was an integral part of the run defense and was the playmaker on the field when the Chargers needed it. Jefferson was in on the goal line stop on fourth down to keep the Chiefs out of the endzone.
The Chargers cornerback room is thin right now. Third-year cornerbacks Cam Hart and Tarheeb Still are battling week in and week out but it was Hart this week who stood out. Cam Hart gave up one reception for four yards against Kansas City and had a phenomenal interception of Patrick Mahomes in the endzone to prevent the Chiefs from capitalizing on Justin Herbert's own interception.
The Chargers punt return unit had not been effective before week six. Derius Davis and the return unit completely changed that narrative against the Chiefs. Davis perfectly faked as if he was going to receive a punt and let it bounce behind him into the endzone giving the Chargers the ball at the 20 as opposed to inside the ten.
Additionally he decisively returned a punt for 21 yards and wasted no time getting upfield once he corralled the punt. The positive field position gains were a welcome change for the Chargers.
The Chargers special teams units have been terrible to start the season. There was a substantial change from week five to week six. Derius Davis was more decisive, Troy Dye forced a fumble on a punt return and Genesis Smith as a gunner nearly caused another by blocking and nearly throwing cornerback Kristian Fulton into returner Nikko Remigio. title: Los Angeles Chargers Rising Falling Ahead of NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are once again looking for any sort of positivity after losing big to division rivals, the Kansas City Chiefs. This drops the Bolts to 0-6, the worst in the NFL, with the Miami Dolphins as the only other winless team in the NFL.
With this depressing fact that the Chargers are the worst team in the NFL, who are some players who are raising their stock for the future after Week 6? Who is losing stock and contributing to this horrid season?
Cam Hart is in a crucial season for his future as an NFL pro, at least with the Chargers. He is a fifth-round pick who has been a borderline starter since his drafting in 2024. He has shown major flashes, with highs of shutting down Ja'Marr Chase and lows of missing weeks at a time multiple times throughout a season. If he can stay healthy and play as he did in Week 6 (four tackles and a red zone interception), expect Hart to stick around.
Dalvin Tomlinson was brought in to help the Chargers run defense, a unit that was in need of a veteran nose tackle who could help add some real fight to a group that is under a new leader, defensive coordinator Chris O'Leary. With this, Tomlinson has been generally solid, with his first game returning from injury being Week 6, being his worst. He had a missed tackle for loss in the red zone, allowing Kenneth Walker to score and extend the lead. Tomlinson is an easy bounce-back candidate for next week.
KeAndre Lambert-Smith has not seen any offensive action this season, returning from injured reserve earlier this week. In his first action back, he was expected to handle a full workload as one of the team's only healthy pass catchers left. In his return, he recorded five catches for 32 yards. While this was a nice boost for the room, his late fourth-quarter fumble essentially ended the game for the team. He looks to get into the winners column next week.
Oronde Gadsden II's 2026 season has been so weird, dating back to the offseason. Going from TE1 to TE3, back to TE1 due to injuries. Even during this stretch, he has not played like his rookie-year self, dropping multiple passes and becoming a non-threat i n an already bad Chargers offense.
Gadsden II in Week 6 recorded 3 receptions for 17 yards, but his drop in the end zone looms large. He desperately needs to turn it around if he wants a role in 2027.
Omarion Hampton , like Gadsden II, has had a weird 2026 season. With a fumble in back-to-back weeks to start the season, his workload dropped, making him another non-threat in the Chargers' offense (and for your fantasy leagues).
In Week 6, Hampton finally saw his workload return to a somewhat reasonable amount, even getting work in the receiving game. He totaled 18 rushing yards and 21 receiving yards, giving some optimism for the rest of his 2026 season.
Ladd McConkey has been one of the saddest stories of the Chargers season, with multiple injuries holding him out for weeks at a time. Against the Chiefs, he was expected to finally be back at full capacity...then was quickly ruled out with a concussion early in the first quarter. McConkey needs a healthy stretch to end off the 2026 season if he wants to begin discussing a contract extension.

title: 5 Realistic Trade Targets for the Chargers Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have several needs to address before the NFL trade deadline on November 10th. Injuries are creating problems along the offensive line and the team struggling to find consistency. The need for more reliable playmakers is growing at a fast rate. General manager Joe Hortiz could potentially explore affordable additions to strengthen the roster.
Rather than surrendering premium draft picks for established stars, the Bolts should target players whose teams have reasons to consider a trade.
Estimated trade cost: A sixth or seventh-round pick
If the Chargers move on from veteran pass rusher Khalil Mack, they could need additional depth on the edge. Malik Herring offers a relatively inexpensive option who could compete for rotational snaps.
Herring began the season with the Titans before joining the Dolphins, where he has contributed as a rotational defender. Herring could help replace some of the depth lost if Mack departs, giving them another option against the run and pass.
Miami is rebuilding, and Herring could be available for a late-round pick if the Dolphins are willing to part with him. The Chargers should explore this move without investing significant draft capital.
Estimated trade cost: A fifth or sixth-round pick
The Chargers could use another receiver capable of creating separation and giving Herbert a dependable option in the passing game. Jerry Jeudy would bring experience and a different skill set to the receiving group.
Jeudy’s route-running ability could complement Ladd McConkey and give the Chargers another option on intermediate routes and underneath concepts. He could also help create more space  Jeudy has appeared in trade-deadline speculation, making him worth monitoring. The Browns would still need to be willing to move him, and his remaining contract would factor into negotiations. A mid to late round pick is a projected price, not a confirmed asking price.
Estimated trade cost: A sixth or seventh-round pick
Dylan Cook is a potential low-cost option after losing his starting opportunity to Steelers 2026 first round pick, Max Iheanachor.
Cook could provide additional competition and depth at a position where the Chargers need more reliable options to protect Herbert. He should be viewed as a developmental or depth addition rather than an assumed starting-caliber solution.
Pittsburgh could consider moving Cook if its offensive line depth allows it. A late-round pick would be a reasonable starting point. Provided the Steelers are willing to negotiate.
Estimated trade cost: A fifth or sixth-round pick
Calvin Ridley is another receiver the Chargers could monitor as the deadline approaches. The veteran has demonstrated the ability to threaten defenses downfield, potentially giving Herbert another weapon in the passing game.
Ridley could stretch opposing defenses and create opportunities for McConkey and the other receivers. His experience would also give another established option in their passing attack. Tennessee has been identified as a potential seller, and Ridley’s contract makes him a name worth watching.
Estimated trade cost: A fifth or sixth-round pick
With injuries exposing the team’s offensive-line depth, acquiring another experienced tackle could be a more valuable move than adding another running back. Austin Jackson is a potential option. The Miami Dolphins have been identified as possible sellers ahead of the trade deadline, and Jackson has emerged as a player worth monitoring.
Jackson could provide additional competition at tackle and give Los Angeles another option for protecting Herbert. His experience would be valuable for an offensive line that needs more dependable depth, particularly if injuries continue to affect the starting lineup. Miami could consider moving Jackson if it prioritizes future draft capital and believes it has sufficient replacements.
The Chargers should prioritize protecting Herbert before pursuing another offensive playmaker. Dylan Cook would offer a potential low-cost depth addition, while Jeudy and Ridley could provide different options in the passing game.
Herring meanwhile, could be worth pursuing if the Chargers lose key players on the defensive line. Joe Hortiz should avoid overpaying for short-term help. The best deadline move will be one that addresses a genuine roster need without sacrificing valuable draft capital.
