title: Buzz About Chargers Firing Mike McDaniel is Getting Hard to Ignore
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers might not wait long to make Mike McDaniel the scapegoat of a horrific 0-6 start.
At 0-6 heading into a bye week, the Chargers have looked like one of the worst teams in modern times. Year 3 of the Jim Harbaugh experience derailing this terribly is, frankly, worse than the infamous 63-21 moment in franchise history.
That demands accountability . And for Harbaugh, that probably means cutting ties with McDaniel .
Justin Herbert’s Chargers just generated six points in Kansas City. He threw for 204 yards and an interception and the ground game ran for 73 yards on a 3.3 average.
For those keeping count, the Chargers now have a -98 EPA , the sixth-lowest over this span since 2016.
"We're going to look at everything, “Harbaugh told Noah Furtado of The Athletic after the game. “I feel bad for our players, our team, our coaches, our fans. And (the offense) needs to be addressed."
Let The Athletic’s Mike Florio tell it, this move is already making buzz around the NFL.
“There’s a growing buzz that the Chargers will be making that move, soon,” Florio wrote. “Pass game specialist Adam Gase, a former head coach of the Jets and Dolphins, is expected to take over, if McDaniel is fired.”
NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport followed the next morning, echoing many of the same sentiments:
From @gmfb : The #Chargers are considering everything with regards to how to fix their offense. pic.twitter.com/HBtqfoibUu
At this point, it’s not just onlookers connecting the dots and stating the obvious. There’s a little smoke around the fire, as there should be.
This isn’t what anyone envisioned when the Chargers made the apparent slam-dunk hiring of McDaniel. Something went deeply wrong with Herbert’s fit in the offense and the franchise’s acquisition of talent to make the scheme work, to name a few factors.
Alas, canning McDaniel as soon as possible gives the Chargers an extra week to get back to basics while tearing up, or at least deeply modifying, the plan.
The Chargers aren’t making the playoffs at 0-6 and could very well be looking at a fire sale before the trade deadline. But self-preservation mode is a go in Los Angeles, but likely without McDaniel.

title: Jim Harbaugh's Biggest Strength as Chargers' Head Coach Has Disappeared
full_text:
Three weeks into the 2025 season, head coach Jim Harbaugh and the Los Angeles Chargers were not only 3-0, but had completed a three-game sweep of the Kansas City Chiefs (27-21), Las Vegas Raiders (20-9), and Denver Broncos (23-20), respectively.
They had not only taken an early lead in the AFC West, the opening week victory over Andy Reid’s team in São Paulo snapped the Bolts’ seven-game losing streak in that rivalry.
The Chiefs are already FLYING! Kenneth Walker III with the touchdown and the Chiefs are 9-0 up against the Chargers. pic.twitter.com/Pa5zKxeE6q
Six weeks into this season, Harbaugh’s team has yet to win a game. And that includes Sunday’s ugly 22-6 setback at Arrowhead Stadium, as well as home losses to the Raiders (26-14) and Broncos (23-17) in Weeks 2 and 5, respectively. The Chargers were outgained 422-259 by Andy Reid’s team, failed to score a touchdown, and committed two more turnovers.
During his first two seasons at the helm of the Bolts, which included a pair of wild card appearances, Harbaugh compiled a combined 22-14 overall record. What stood out was the fact that while the team had its problems outside of their division (13-11), the Chargers were an impressive 9-3 vs. their AFC West rivals. That included a 4-0 record vs. the Raiders, a 3-1 resume vs. the Broncos, and a four-game split with the Chiefs.
Justin Herbert threw this one right to a Chiefs defender. pic.twitter.com/mhxilirBgn
This season, Harbaugh’s club can’t be accused of playing favorites. The disappointing Bolts are 0-3 vs. their division neighbors and 0-3 vs. the rest of the league—which includes the Arizona Cardinals, Buffalo Bills, and Seattle Seahawks.
Against their AFC West rivals, the disappointing Chargers have scored a combined 37 points and only four touchdowns (none vs. the Chiefs) while turning over the football eight times. The club has been limited to 17 or fewer points in each of their divisional setbacks. And to make matters a bit worse, the losses to the Raiders and Broncos were both at home.
Hence, there’s been a lot of finger pointing when it comes to the offense, in particular new coordinator Mike McDaniel and seven-year signal-caller Justin Herbert. The team has generated just 287.2 total yards per game, has just as many field goal as touchdowns (9), and has committed a whopping 15 turnovers in a half-dozen contests. However, the defense has also had its shortcomings when it comes to stopping the run, allowing 123.8 yards per game on the ground.
There’s some very sad symmetry here. The last time this franchise lost its first six games was the start of this century. The 2000 San Diego Chargers opened 0-11 and finished 1-15 under head coach Mike Riley. And the third of three different starting quarterbacks for the Bolts that seasons was Jim Harbaugh. In his second season with the team, he appeared in seven contests and made five starts in what proved to be his final NFL campaign as a player.

title: The Morning-After Thunder: Chargers' Loss puts McDaniel and Hortiz on Chopping Block
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers enter their Week 7 bye week beaten, battered and bruised. Their roster is in injury purgatory , their offense is lifeless and their personnel is weak in many spots.
The Chargers defense has been going to absolute war week in and week out trying with their entire might to keep the Chargers in games. Against the Chiefs on Sunday, Cam Hart intercepted Patrick Mahomes in the endzone, Justin Egboigbe and Tony Jefferson stonewalled Kenneth Walker on a four-and-goal run and the defense forced multiple stops to give the offense the ball back. The offense appears to be the walking dead and incapable to reciprocating the defenses efforts.
The Chargers offense isn't just bad, it's historically bad. The franchise is off to its worst start since the 2000 season, ironically a season in which Jim Harbaugh went 0-5 as a starter alongside Ryan Leaf and Moses Moreno. This was supposed to be a team primed to be Super Bowl contenders. Even the most cynical media pundits never imagined the results would stray this far from success. What happened?
The most obvious elephant in the room is that despite the excitement for the pairing of offensive genius Mike McDaniel and franchise quarterback Justin Herbert the two are not meshing. Herbert seems to be struggling with his post-snap reads and his confidence in what he is seeing is causing uncharacteristic errors and an explosion in his turnover-worthy play rate, plays in which he puts the ball in danger.
Justin Herbert has a career average of 2.2 percent with his highest rate hitting 2.6 percent. The high of 2.6 percent occured last season in 2025 while he was playing behind an injury-decimated offensive line that he dragged to the playoffs.
Herbert has a 6.7 percent turnover-worthy play rate through the first six weeks of the 2026 season. He had four different offensive coordinators from 2020-2025 and was consistent, 2026 is an absolute and undeniable outlier.
Mike McDaniel is a branch off of the Shanahan coaching tree and not all quarterbacks are best suited for that style of offense. McDaniel is likely on his way out of LA with how the offense has performed. It very well may be purely a water and oil situation where the two do not mix. Herbert has been elite at pre-snap analysis and post-snap execution, the sudden collapse is more than likely the shift in emphasis in a Shanahan-based system for which he is not suited for and McDaniel was unwilling to adjust his offense to match the quarterback.
The Chargers offense is not just bad, they are also dealing with a massive gap in talent and experience. For the second season in a row, the offensive line, particularly the interior has been the catalyst for Justin Herbert running for his life, being pressured and hit at historically bad rates, again.
Chargers general manager Joe Hortiz and the Chargers front office was tasked with retooling the interior offensive line after horrific play on the offensive line in 2025. Los Angeles frustratingly did not treat the guard position with the intent and importance that they should have. They did sign quality veteran center Tyler Biadasz to replace retiring Bradley Bozeman. But to replace left guard Zion Johnson and right guard Mekhi Becton, they signed journeymen or former first-round busts to compete for the starting guard positions.
Joe Hortiz believes in and fully uses the Baltimore Ravens philosophy of believing that they can find cheaper guards and elevate them with scheme and quarterback play. Hortiz fully expected and banked on McDaniel being able to elevate the interior with scheme, when Biadasz went down with injury, the results were catastrophic.
The 2026 offensive line was built to be functional in a best-case scenario, the Chargers have started their sixth option at left guard the past two weeks with rookie Logan Taylor and have backup rookie tackles as well. The lack of investments in the offensive line for the past two years in the draft and this past offseason in free agency have had catastrophic results.
On the flip side of the ball, the cornerback room was thin entering training camp. The position group generally experiences high rates of injury and Los Angeles entered the season with only five cornerbacks with one being a career special teams ace and another was an undrafted rookie.
Due to injuries, a practice squad cornerback had to be thrown into the fire against the Kansas City Chiefs. Injuries happen, but the glaring lack of depth in the cornerback room was evident from the start of training camp and was not addressed, that falls on the front office.
Watching the franchise quarterback take an absolute beating week in and week out behind a catastrophic injury circumstance along the offensive line only to repeat the problem the following season while hoarding excess cap space is not a good look. By all objective statistics, the offensive line for the 2026 Chargers is worse than the 2025 version.
The failures of the offense and the personnel decisions that have lead to the current offensive line situation, should put both Mike McDaniel and Joe Hortiz in the crosshairs to be potentially fired by the Chargers. The Chargers are 0-6 and the entire offense is playing terribly and something has to change. Los Angeles enters week seven on a bye, if change is coming, this is the time to do it.

title: Jim Harbaugh Post-Game Quote Spells Doom for Mike McDaniel Following Chargers Loss
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers dropped to 0-6 after losing a clunker to the Kansas City Chiefs. The battle in Kansas City was clearly the Chargers final stand of the 2026 season but their injury-ravaged and ineffective offense could not put anything together and scored only six points.
The offense has been the Chargers' Achilles heel this season. Their defense has performed well and kept games close and have provided opportunities to the offense to attempt to mount a comeback.

title: 5 Rams Overreactions After Disastrous 2-4 Start: Which Ones Are Actually Justified?
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams opened the season as Super Bowl favorites, and through six weeks, they sit at 2-4 with a 41 percent chance to make the playoffs. After losing to the Cardinals, t he Rams hit rock bottom and the season continues to spiral.
Naturally, the overreactions have started pouring in. Sean McVay should give up playcalling duties and needs to be on the hot seat. The Rams blew it with a super team. The list goes on. Let's break down five of the biggest overreactions surrounding the Rams and determine which ones are justified.
Following the loss to the Cardinals, one of the primary talking points is how Sean McVay needs to give up playcalling . McVay certainly hasn’t been perfect, and his call on 4th-and-1 against the Cardinals wasn’t good. However, he’s still one of the NFL’s best offensive minds and playcallers. It simply doesn’t make sense to take that away from him and give it to an offensive coordinator in his first season. McVay may be part of the problem right now, but he’s also a big part of the solution. Overreaction Validity: 2/10
For much of the offseason, the Rams were labeled a super team. To be fair, nobody on the team mentioned that phrase. The Rams understood that they looked good on paper, but still had to prove it on the field. With that said, the super team that the media has referred to hasn’t played a single snap together. Myles Garrett wasn’t 100 percent in Week 1 and Aaron Donald didn’t make the trip.
Garrett was immediately placed on injured reserve and the Rams have been managing injuries ever since. We may not see the “Super Team” at full strength this season, but it’s unfair to call the experiment a failure the vision of the roster never came to fruition in the first place. Overreaction Validity: 1/10
It might not be time to start Ty Simpson, but it’s time to at least make him the backup. Much like McVay, Stafford deserves some blame for the Rams’ early-season troubles, but he’s also a big part of the solution. An argument can be made that the game against the Eagles isn't close with Simpson under center, given that Stafford threw two ill-advised interceptions. The Rams may have beaten the Cardinals with Simpson. A time may come when the Rams do decide to start their rookie quarterback, but the only player capable of digging this team out of the current hole it's in is Stafford. Overreaction Validity: 5/10
We’ve been doing the same exhausting dance with the Rams’ defensive coordinators going back to Raheem Morris. This isn’t to say that the defense is faultless. However, they made a play that should have won the game against the Buffalo Bills. They held the Cardinals to 18 points and 0-for-5 in the red zone. A McVay-led offense should be expected to score 20 points against the worst scoring defense in the NFL.
Through six weeks, the Rams’ defense ranks 10th in defensive DVOA and third in yards allowed per game. That’s without Garrett and other key pieces in several games. Shula has implemented the exact style of defense that fans wanted early in the season. Overreaction Validity: 4/10
It’s going to be interesting to see what the Rams do at the trade deadline. With that said, Les Snead isn’t known to sell assets and call it a season. The Rams could certainly trade Byron Young and get decent draft capital in return. However, it’s hard to see them going that route.
It’s more likely that the Rams stand pat or make a move to improve the roster. While the Rams didn’t make the playoffs in 2019, they traded for Austin Corbett and Jalen Ramsey. In 2022, they made calls on Christian McCaffrey and Brian Burns. The Rams may not make a splashy move, but Les Snead will likely be actively working the phones. Overreaction Validity: 6/10

title: Grading Rams Signing of Brandon McManus: The Latest Chapter in a Never-Ending Nightmare
full_text:
When the Los Angeles Rams put kicker Blake Grupe on injured reserve on Monday, it was reported that they worked out veteran kickers Brandon McManus and Matt Prater. After holding a competition, the Rams have opted to sign McManus according to NFL Media’s Ian Rapoport.
The #Rams are signing veteran kicker Brandon McManus, per me and @MikeGarafolo , the latest in Los Angeles’ kicker saga. He worked out today, along with FA K Matt Prater. McManus most recently kicked for the #Packers and #Broncos . pic.twitter.com/eyzO9QmQjt
Speaking to the media on Monday, head coach Sean McVay said that they were in the process of replacing Grupe. The group of Assistant GM John McKay, Special Teams Coordinator Bubba Ventrone, and General Manager Les Snead worked on different options and eventually opted with McManus.
McManus made just 80 percent of his field goals last year in the regular season with the Green Bay Packers, going 24-for-30. In the playoffs against the Chicago Bears, McManus went 0-for-2 on field goals, missing from 55 and 44 yards. He also missed an extra point in what was a 31-27 loss. T he Packers cut McManus in May.
Brandon McManus had only missed one playoff kick in his career going into tonight (11/12 on field goals, 4/4 on extra points). He's missed THREE kicks against the Bears: Two field goals and an extra point. #Packers #Bears #NFLPlayoffs pic.twitter.com/IdnJrdd6dQ
The Rams will hope that McManus can provide some immediate stability at the kicker position. At 35 years old, he’s at least a veteran presence and a known commodity. Even if he isn’t the kicker that he was in his prime, he still made a kick from 56 yards last year and is one season removed from making 95.2 percent of his field goals in 2024.
At this point in the season, there aren’t a plethora of great kicking options available.. This remains something that the Rams should have done in July rather than having to do it now in October. It’s a similar approach to the one the Rams took in 2023 when they signed Brett Maher.
No matter who the Rams signed at kicker, it would be an ‘is what it is’ situation. Matt Prater went 18-for-20 on field goals last year and 5-for-5 in the playoffs. Both options are simply putting a Band-Aid over a bullet wound, and neither provides a long-term solution. It still seems odd that the Rams won’t sign a player like Tanner Brown to their practice squad just to give them a younger option to develop.
The Rams’ handling of their special teams and field goal unit has been a disaster . Even if they had confidence in Harrison Mevis, he didn’t perform well enough to not have any competition this offseason. Grupe finally gave them some upside if he had worked out but got injured on his first kickoff because the coverage unit didn’t do its job.
Even with McManus, the Rams will likely be searching for another kicker during the offseason. Given how they handled Joshua Karty and the lack of development with Mevis, it’s fair to question whether this coaching staff and front office can identify and then develop a kicker that finally resolves the issues.

title: The Rams Have a Sean McVay Problem, But Giving Up Play-Calling Isn't the Answer
full_text:
As the Los Angeles Rams have started to lose, the calls for head coach Sean McVay to give up playcalling have begun like clockwork. The Rams are at 2-4 and just scored 16 points against one of the worst defenses in the NFL. McVay came under the microscope for his fourth-down play call to Davis Allen, and the demands for McVay to give up play calling duties have only grown louder.
This isn’t to say that McVay is perfect, but as much as some might not like to admit, he’s still one of the NFL’s best playcallers. At times, it’s easy to get caught in an echo chamber during the NFL season. It’s important to take a step back and look at the NFL through a wider lens.
While the offense needs to be better, not all of that is on McVay and the playcalling. This offseason, The Athletic’s Ted Nguyen ranked McVay as the second-best playcaller in the NFL behind only Kyle Shanahan.
“McVay is more systematic in his approach than playcallers who tailor their game plans more week to week,” wrote Nguyen. “He isn’t reinventing the wheel with flashy play designs. McVay runs his core concepts, but his system has answers for whatever defenses throw at him. His genius lies in his ability to force defenses into the calls that he wants them to be in.”
FantasyPoints came up with six “hacks” that make a good playcaller this offseason. Taking in data from 2021 to 2025, McVay ranked first among all playcallers based on his tendencies with early-down passing, utilizing play action on early downs, getting the quarterback under center, creating a box advantage, downfield passing, and fourth down aggressiveness.
Back in March, McVay was quoted saying that he wasn’t necessarily married to calling plays . However, it seems odd to take playcalling duties away from someone who is among the best in the world at it. In today’s NFL, the best head coaches call their own plays.
Mike Macdonald, Kyle Shanahan, Ben Johnson, Andy Reid, and Matt LaFleur all call their own plays. The days of the CEO head coach are limited. There are only a few of them in existence in the modern NFL in Mike Vrabel, John Harbaugh, and Dan Campbell.
Heading into the 2025 season, Sean Payton was still considered a top-10 playcaller. In 2025, the Broncos still ranked 10th in offensive EPA per play. Payton had the Broncos’ offense rolling with Bo Nix at quarterback.
This offseason, Payton made the decision to give up playcalling duties to first-year offensive coordinator Davis Webb. Through four weeks, the Broncos ranked 20th in EPA per play on offense. After the Broncos lost to the San Francisco 49ers in Week 4, Payton took back playcalling. Webb was the primary playcaller for the Broncos for a whole four weeks.
"We know we have to improve our balance in running the football," said Payton when he made the change. "It's changing things up and really trying to reduce some of the calories to get back to getting some things really well. That's going to be the focus."
The biggest issue with taking away playcalling duties from McVay is that it would remove his main connection to his players. It would take away what makes McVay great as a head coach and part of what he does best.
McVay has given up playcalling one time, and it was during the disastrous 2022 season when he was at his lowest of lows. McVay gave playcalling duties to Liam Coen against the Kansas City Chiefs. The Athletic’s Jourdan Rodrigue described the situation at the time .
“Careful observers can see the ebbs and flows of his brain call by call — and they can also see when creativity and collaboration morph into frustration and angst. When he calls a game, he feels connected to his players and they to him,” wrote Rodrigue. “As McVay stood on the sidelines in Kansas City, his shoulders knotted and his jaw set, he could hear the game unfolding in his headset and see it on the field. But not calling the game made him feel more distant than ever from his players — and from himself.”
Just because McVay is calling the plays doesn't mean there isn't a collaborative effort. Throughout the game, McVay is taking input and getting information from his coaching staff such as Nate Scheelhaase.
Again, this isn’t to say that McVay has been perfect. Sunday was a primary example of that. Facing a 4th-and-1, McVay called a dive play to tight end Davis Allen . Allen had never taken a hand-off in his four years with the Rams or his four-year career at Clemson. When the options include Kyren Williams and Puka Nacua, going to Allen seems odd.
This is the Rams play call that I have an issue with...but it's also poor execution. Not sure why Parkinson isn't going up to the second level like Greg Olsen described. Is plan for Allen to run over a LB to get a yard? If Parkinson goes at Wilson, maybe Allen has a chance. pic.twitter.com/dYNcZRJFvr
In Week 6, the Rams had a 50 percent rushing success rate. While 20 percent of their runs had been stuffed, only one of those came in 13 personnel. This season, Kyren Williams has an 81.8 percent success rate on third or fourth down with less than three yards to go. He is 9-for-11 in those situations. Among players with at least five such attempts, that ranks third.
There’s also been a lack of balance in the offense. The Rams have the fifth-highest pass-rate over expected at +4.9. Pass rate over expected measures how much a team passes compared to the expected rate in every situation. It’s a good way to tell how balanced a team is, rather than just looking at the basic run-pass rates. Over the last four games, they have the highest at +7.7.
A positive pass rate over expected isn't necessarily a bad thing. However, the Rams are still passing at an extremely high rate. For comparison, the San Francisco 49ers are at +2.5 and the Kansas City Chiefs are at +3.6. Both are still inside the top 10.
As expected, the Rams have generally always had a high pass rate over expected. Last season, their +5.8 pass rate over expected ranked third. The Rams were extremely low in 2024 at -1.2 and were down at -1.6 in 2023. When the Rams won the Super Bowl in 2021, their pass rate over expected ranked sixth at +4.0.
The issue isn’t necessarily with the Rams’ +4.9 on the season. However, their +7.7 pass rate over expected over the last four games is extremely high. In three of the last four games, Matthew Stafford has 50 or more passing attempts. In two of those games, the Rams never trailed by double digits to warrant passing that much.
Buffalo did present a mismatch in the passing game due to the injuries at cornerback, but the Rams still had a +9.9 pass rate over expected. Throwing 55 times against the Broncos was more egregious as the Rams led by 16 points in that game. Against the Broncos, the Rams had a +9.3 pass rate over expected.
So far this season, the Rams have a neutral pass frequency of 62.6 percent, which is the second-highest rate in the NFL. Their 62.6 percent pass rate in neutral situations is 10 percent higher than the league average at 52.5 percent. It’s also the highest it's been since 2021 through six weeks.
At the end of the day, the buck stops with McVay. It is up to him to get the offense on track. However, how much is the playcaller at fault when the offense still ranks 10th in EPA per play and sixth in success rate? The offense ranks sixth in DVOA. Those numbers would suggest that the overall infrastructure and health of the offense is in good shape.
Players also hold some responsibility and need to be able to execute. That’s also where the Rams are lacking consistency.
“The consistency of execution from phase-to-phase is really what we're hunting up,” said McVay on Monday. “Sometimes it just comes down to not executing on a play here or there, but there are a lot of things that lead up to those moments. We're hunting up consistency on a snap-to-snap basis, on a play-to-play basis.”
Again...we can complain about play calls, but the plays aren't being executed consistently enough. McVay calls an easy pass to get some yardage on 2nd-and-9 to…

title: Week 6 Consensus NFL Power Rankings: Rams' Super Team Experiment Is Falling Apart
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams entered the 2026 season as Super Bowl favorites. However, the issue with super teams is that they typically aren’t looked on favorably by the football gods. In 2011, the Philadelphia Eagles went 8-8 after building an offseason dream team on paper. After losing to the Cardinals, the Rams have hit rock bottom .
Through six weeks, the Rams sit at 2-4, and everything is crumbling around them. They are a team without an identity. Additionally, the injuries are starting to pile up and they didn’t have a lot of depth to begin with. Wide receiver Davante Adams will be out for two months and they also lost Poona Ford and Kobie Turner. The Rams still can’t figure out special teams and they are now onto their third kicker.
For much of the season, the Rams deserved the benefit of the doubt. They had a long trip to Australia and then faced a grueling schedule. With that said, after an 18-16 loss, this Rams team might just be what their record says they are. Right now, they are an inconsistent, below-average team still trying to figure out who they are.
After being ranked at the back of the top 10 in last week’s power rankings, the Rams have dropped significantly. Maybe the Rams needed to be counted out before they could start proving people wrong. However, they are running out of time. Let’s jump into this week’s consensus power rankings.
The Rams dropped six spots from No. 8 to No. 14 in ESPN’s power rankings . An argument can be made that they should have dropped further. ESPN is the highest on the Rams, as it is the only outlet that has them ranked inside the top 15. Sarah Barshop noted the team’s lack of an identity.
“Coach Sean McVay tried to describe why the Rams are beating themselves with penalties, turnovers and "so many unforced errors" at critical times on offense,” wrote Barshop. “But ultimately, he said he's "not really sure" why the Rams can't get out of their own way.”
The fact that even the head coach seems lost and unsure of how to fix it is concerning. In 2021, McVay had a conversation with Raheem Morris that changed the course of the season. When the Rams were 3-6 in 2023, it was Cooper Kupp who had that conversation. McVay needs that from someone right now or this could spiral very quickly.
It’s hard to pinpoint exactly what has gone wrong with the Rams. They could arguably be 5-1 right now. They should have beaten the Denver Broncos, Harrison Mevis should have made the kick to beat the Buffalo Bills, and they should have beaten the Cardinals. However, all this Rams team is right now is a series of “what ifs,” and that doesn’t win football games. The Rams dropped 10 spots in Connor Orr’s power rankings with Sports Illustrated this week.
“I don’t know what is happening with the Rams, but I know that we’ll all wish these takes vanished when the team beats the Raiders, Chargers, Commanders and Cardinals in successive weeks,” wrote Orr. “There’s still time for the “trade Sean McVay to the Jets for three firsts” fan forum post to come down!”
The Rams stay inside the top 20 in The Athletic’s Power Rankings , but only just. Last week, the Rams ranked 10th and were still ranked fifth two weeks ago. With each passing week, the media is losing faith that this Rams team can turn it around.
Nick Shook from NFL Media has been much lower on the Rams this season than most and that’s reflected in his rankings. Shook continues to be proven right, though, and now has the Rams ranked in the bottom 10 at No. 24. He’s the only analyst to have the Rams outside of the top-20. It may seem harsh, but it’s hard to blame him. The Rams just lost at home to a Cardinals team that has essentially waved the white flag on the season.
“The offseason darling and preseason Super Bowl favorite is now 2-4. The Rams will be without Davante Adams for more than a month (if not longer), Myles Garrett still isn’t back and they’re down two defensive tackles after Sunday’s loss to Arizona,” Shook wrote. “Los Angeles lacks an offensive identity, can’t take care of details and is already in need of a third kicker in 2026. This is a mess that Sean McVay needs to start to clean up quickly.”
As the Rams continue to lose and suffer injuries at key spots, the narrative will continue to fall back on how they should have drafted a wide receiver in the first round. As Mike Florio wrote , “The 13th overall pick should’ve been used on a receiver.”
It’s a fair criticism, but if the Rams believed in Ty Simpson, there was still a process behind that pick. The one that still doesn’t make sense is Max Klare in the second round. Antonio Williams was drafted shortly after and continues to produce for the Commanders.
After watching the Rams on Sunday, it’s hard to look at the product on the field and not come to the conclusion that they look broken. A team ranked No. 29 in defensive EPA per play and last in scoring defense held a Sean McVay offense to 16 points. Again, as the Rams lose, a narrative will likely surface that the Rams and McVay blew it with a super team. However, the core of that super team still hasn’t played a single snap together.
“I have now officially lost all faith in the Dream Team. I was willing to write their early struggles off to jet lag and a mostly brutal stretch of opponents in the first five weeks,” wrote Ralph Vacchiani. “But their hideous 18-16 loss to the Cardinals this past Sunday broke me. It might have broken the Rams, too.”
Finally, the Rams dropped from No. 10 to No. 18 in Pete Prisco’s rankings with CBS Sports. It’s very possible that the Rams can turn it around over the next four games and still end up at 5-5 at their bye week. Given how this team has played up to this point, there isn’t a lot of confidence in their ability to string wins together.
The Rams enter Week 7 with an average ranking of 17.7 and will take on the Las Vegas Raiders this week, who have an average ranking of 18.4. However, while the Raiders have lost three in a row, they have played teams close. Two of their last three losses are by just three points.
While the Rams may be favored to win this game, as seen last week, nothing is a guarantee. The Raiders played the Bills close and the Rams will need to be sharp if they're going to leave Vegas with a win.
After losing to the Cardinals, the Rams have officially dropped out of my top 10 as well. It's hard to justify them being there until they earn it. The top three are pretty solid, with the Chiefs and 49ers interchangeable. With the Seahawks losing to the Broncos, they could start to drop. The next two weeks should start to provide some more clarity.

title: 5 Wide Receivers Rams Should Trade For to Replace Davante Adams, Including One Who Could Save Their Season
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams are in need of a wide receiver with Davante Adams rupturing his hamstring and going on injured reserve. It’s possible that the Rams could just go to the next player on the depth chart, but that could be problematic.Coming into the season, the Rams lacked depth at wide receiver and didn’t have a reliable WR3. With Adams’ injury, they don’t have someone who can step into the WR2 role.
Entering the season, the Rams gambled that they could stay healthy at the wide receiver position. With Puka Nacua having missed two games and Adams now out for two months, that has not been the case.
When Nacua was hurt, the Rams were able to turn to Terrance Ferguson. However, Ferguson is out for at least the next game as he is also on injured reserve. As the Rams sit at 2-4, it’s hard to see them making a trade. Still, it’s something they will have to explore . Given their cap space of $989,000 and the fact that they don’t have a first- or third-round pick next year, it would also need to be for the right price.
Here are five wide receivers who make the most sense.
Most of the Rams’ wide receivers lack speed outside of Tutu Atwell. With that said, it’s clear how the Rams feel about Atwell as he’s rarely included in the offense and was inactive last week. The Rams don’t have a legitimate downfield threat, a role that Adams filled to an extent.
Outside of Atwell, Adams led the Rams with an average depth of target of 15.5 yards. The next closest Rams wide receiver is Konata Mumpfield at 13.7 yards. Adams also led the Rams with an average depth of catch of 11.9 yards. That still only ranked 29th, but the next closest Rams wide receiver is Mumpfield at 10.8 yards.
Which WRs are getting open and how accurate are the passes coming their way? Per @FantasyPtsData - As good as Matthew Golden has been... could he be even better? - Josh Downs is a demon - Mike Evans is as good as ever pic.twitter.com/mqXkoW60sk
On Monday, the Indianapolis Colts fired general manager Chris Ballard, potentially opening the door for a fire sale. Downs has always been a talented player, but the Colts haven’t had the quarterback to consistently get him involved. He’s in the final year of his rookie contract, and after just extending Alec Pierce, it’s not likely that Downs is brought back this offseason.
Downs brings good speed and explosiveness, allowing the offense to get creative. He is everything that the Rams have wanted Tutu Atwell to be. One thing that the Rams will miss with Adams is his ability to beat man coverage. This season, Downs has 2.43 yards per route run against man coverage, which ranks 23rd in the NFL. Last season, he had a 75.3 percent success rate against man coverage, which cleared the 80th percentile. Downs is also very good against press.
Josh Downs is down there! 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/q5It4TblNk
Downs also fills a void on special teams. This season, the Rams have struggled to find a punt returner. They started the season with Xavier Smith and have since shifted to Alex Bachman. Downs was used as a punt returner in his first three years and averaged more than 10 yards per return in his first and second seasons.
In his final year, Downs fits the profile of a trade target for the Rams. Downs is cheap and the Rams would only take on around $2 million in a trade. While the Rams would still need to open up cap space, it’s manageable. Additionally, Downs’ value would only be around a fourth-round pick. The Rams have a 2027 fourth-round pick but could potentially negotiate it down to a fifth-round pick and a conditional Day 3 pick in 2028.
If the Rams are looking for a prototypical “X” receiver to replace Adams, Jeudy makes a lot of sense. Given that the Browns drafted Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion, Jeudy isn’t part of their future at the position. The question is whether the Browns, at 4-2 and in first place in the AFC North, would be willing to trade contributing players.
Big play Jerry Jeudy! BALvsCLE on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/pnEoVVFag4
Much like Downs, Jeudy is a cheap option. The Rams would only take on around $1 million in cap space, which is manageable for this season. As an aging veteran, he’d also be cheaper to acquire. The issue with Jeudy is his future contract.
He has a $13.5 million cap hit in 2027. While the Rams could move on, they would also take on $25 million in dead cap because of his four void years. If Jeudy were to rework his deal, the Rams may consider a move as he would also only cost a fourth-round pick.
It may be more wishful thinking, but it’s hard not to include Brian Thomas Jr., considering how great of a fit he’d be in the Rams’ offense. He’s exactly what they need as an “X” receiver and also gives them a future at the position.
As a rookie, Thomas had 1,282 yards receiving and 10 touchdowns.However, he hasn’t shown himself to be the same player since. Trading for Thomas would be much like the Houston Texans trading for Marvin Harrison Jr. A team would be paying a premium in hopes of getting that level of production out of the player.
A wide open Brian Thomas Jr. makes it a two-score game! JAXvsCIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/uXT47Yp4vh
Thomas fits the Adams prototype, but he ranks 85th out of 86 wide receivers in adjusted catch percentage, which is the percentage of catchable targets converted into catches. He has not been the same player that he showed as a rookie.
It’s possible that the Rams could get that out of him again, but it is a huge risk for the price they’d have to pay. Harrison Jr. was acquired by the Texans for a second-round pick and a seventh-round pick. That’s likely where Thomas’ value would start. It is worth pointing out the relationship between Les Snead and James Gladstone here as well.
If the Rams trade their 2027 second-round pick, their first selection in next year’s draft wouldn’t come until the fourth round. The Rams would only take on around $700,000 of Thomas’ contract and he only has a $4.6 million cap-hit next season. They would also have the fifth-year option. For as good of a fit as Thomas might be, the Rams aren’t in a position to give up the draft capital that it would take to get him.
Jennings would be in a similar tier as Jeudy, but would the Vikings trade him at 5-0? He would be a great fit for what the Rams need as a dependable option. He could slide into the WR2 role and then be the reliable WR3 that the Rams have been missing once Adams returns.
Due to Jennings’ age and contract, he’s a cheaper option and would only cost a Day 3 pick. The Rams may be able to get him for a Day 3 pick swap. With that said, the Rams would take on around $4 million in cap space. If the Rams were to go this route, they would need to adjust some contracts.
If the Rams are looking for an immediate solution at their “X” wide receiver spot, calling the Eagles on Dontayvion Wicks could make sense. As seen with the Cam Jurgens trade, the Eagles may be punting on 2026 and looking at next year. Jalen Hurts is out for the rest of the season and they sit at 2-4.
Wicks would only cost the Rams around $700,000 in 2026, and he only has a $4 million cap hit in 2027. He also has experience in a McVay-style offense, having played in Green Bay with Matt LaFleur and playing under Sean Mannion this season. The Eagles traded a fifth- and sixth-round pick to acquire Wicks, and he would likely have similar value if they were to part ways with him.
Dontayvion Wicks' first TD as an Eagle 🦅 WASvsPHI on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/O4iz070w2o

title: How the Rams Can Replace Davante Adams, Kobie Turner, and Poona Ford
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams got some unfortunate injury news on Monday. Head coach Sean McVay told the media that the Rams will be without wide receiver Davante Adams, defensive lineman Kobie Turner, and defensive lineman Poona Ford for an extended period or the entire season.
You feel terrible for these guys because they put in so much work to try to be able to bring some stuff to life. Those guys are key contributors for us," said head coach Sean McVay. "The next thing is make sure that we figure out what's the best way for our team to be able to move forward in the absence of some critical factors for us. That's part of it. That’s an unfortunate part of this game. We’ve taken some shots this year and we have to be able to get up and keep swinging. This is a good test."
When it comes to the NFL, it’s a next-man-up mentality. The Rams will need their depth to step up in a big way if they are going to come back from a 2-4 start. Let’s take a look at the players the Rams will be relying on.
Out of the injuries that the Rams suffered on Sunday, the loss of Davante Adams may hit the hardest . Stafford and Adams were clicking this season. Adams had back-to-back 100-yard games when Nacua was out of the lineup. He also already had six touchdowns through four weeks. Coming into the season, there were questions around the Rams’ WR3 situation. Now they don’t have a legitimate WR2 for the next 6-10 weeks.
“It's significant when you don't have a player like Davante, but we have to be able to adjust," said McVay. "His contributions can't be measured. You don't replace somebody like him so what you do is you have to be able to figure out, what's the next right thing? What does that look like in terms of our vision?"
The clear answer as to who steps up in place of Adams is Konata Mumpfield. Mumpfield isn’t a true ‘X’ receiver, but he is someone that the Rams have used frequently as the lone wide receiver in 13 personnel. The Rams seem to like what Mumpfield can do, but he still remains inefficient. Mumpfield has caught just eight of 17 targets this season. After playing just six snaps in Week 5, he was back up to 27 against the Cardinals. The Rams may rely on Mumpfield more with Adams out.
It will be interesting to see if CJ Daniels finally gets an opportunity. Daniels’ name came up a lot during training camp. During the preseason, Daniels had 15 receptions, which was tied for the most in the NFL. Daniels lined up out wide on 72.9 percent of his snaps during the preseason and would be a seamless fit in that spot. It’s unfair to ask Daniels to replace Adams and his productio n, but he could slide into that role. Adams spoke highly of Daniels this summer.
“I'm proud of him,” said Adams. “He came to me and asked what I thought he needed to work on. We talked about a couple of small things. I saw a lot of good stuff from him during the offseason program and he came back and did exactly those things.”
It’s been a surprise that Daniels hasn’t been active in six games, but this could be his opportunity. Daniels obviously isn’t the next Puka Nacua, but the Rams have been able to get a lot out of rookie wide receivers in the past. They may need that from Daniels.
The Rams could try and trade for someone. However, at 2-4, it feels unlikely. They don’t have a lot of cap space and, right now, they need to keep their already limited draft capital. If the Rams do make a trade, Josh Downs and Jauan Jennings make a lot of sense. It’s possible the Rams could look into Brian Thomas Jr., but his price is likely too high.
Kobie Turner is going to be a huge loss on the Rams’ defense . In four years, he’s grown to be the heart and soul of that defensive line. Turner may only have 13 pressures this season, but he was having an impact as a run defender as well. He had a nine percent run stop rate with 10 run stops, according to Pro Football Focus. The Rams will hope to get Turner back soon from his groin injury, but he’ll be missed.
The obvious replacement for Turner is Ty Hamilton. However, this is a huge drop-off. The Rams traded up for Hamilton last year, giving up a future fourth-round pick. In six games this year, he has an overall defensive grade below 50 via PFF.In three of those games, he recorded a grade below 40. Hamilton doesn’t have a single pressure this year in 24 pass-rush snaps. He’s supposed to be good against the run, but only has one run stop. The Rams are going to need Hamilton to step up. It will likely be a rotation here, but Hamilton will be the primary player in that spot.
Fiske has been rotating with Aaron Donald throughout much of the season, but without Turner, he could see more playing time. The issue with Fiske is that he isn’t as effective against the run due to his size. Still, he does have an 11.8 percent run stop rate, which ranks eighth in the NFL. He also leads the Rams with 16 pressures this season. In three years, Fiske has been labeled as a “JAG”, and this will be an opportunity for him to show that he is more than that.
Ford hasn’t been as good as he was last year, but he’s still an important piece of the defensive line. The Rams added Ford after 2024 to be a space eater in the middle of the defensive line and help stop the run . He played an important role in making the Rams one of the best run-stopping defenses last year. Not having him in the middle of the defensive line for the rest of the season will be felt.
Tyler Davis played very well last season. While technically listed as Kobie Turner’s backup, he can play at nose tackle. The Rams have mostly used him on early downs next to Ford or alongside Turner on either side of the center. It wouldn’t be surprising, though, to see Davis used in place of Ford because of his size.
With Ford out, the Rams will likely elevate Bill Norton from the practice squad. Norton is a player the Rams have been developing, but he has struggled in the preseason. He had just a 49.3 run defense grade via PFF last year. Norton has size and could be brought up to add some depth.

title: Rams Dealt Devastating Injury News on Davante Adams, Kobie Turner, Poona Ford
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams received a series of bad injury updates on Monday afternoon. According to Sean McVay, wide receiver Davante Adams will be out for six to 10 weeks, while defensive lineman Kobie Turner will miss several weeks as he heads to injured reserve. Poona Ford will also be out for the season.
Adams left Sunday’s game against the Cardinals in the final minute, seemingly pulling up at the end of the play. A non-contact injury is rarely good and McVay said on Monday that Adams had ruptured his hamstring.Adams will be out for a minimum of six weeks and could miss up to 10. Depending on where the Rams are at, they could opt to shut him down for the year.
Non-contact injury for #Rams WR Davante Adams. Came out of the game pic.twitter.com/wSh2CYsLuD
Last season, Adams suffered a strained hamstring that forced him to miss the final three games. Given Adams’ age, re-injuring his hamstring was always a risk. With Adams out for the next two months, the Rams are extremely thin at the wide receiver position. Puka Nacua is the only legitimate option, especially until Terrance Ferguson returns. The Rams drafted CJ Daniels in the sixth round, but he’s been inactive in every game to start the year.
The Rams took a significant hit to their defensive line with Monday’s news. Turner played a career-low 23 snaps, and the injury explains why. Turner injured his groin and is expected to go on injured reserve, but could return later this season.
Ford is another big loss for the Rams’ defense. Over the last two seasons, Ford has played a large role in stopping the run as the starting nose tackle. Ford hadn’t played as well this year but was arguably one of the most important players on the Rams’ defense in 2025.
While the Rams have depth on the defensive line, the injuries to Turner and Ford will call for those players to step into roles that they may not be ready for. The Rams have been developing Tyler Davis and Ty Hamilton over the last two years. However, Hamilton has struggled again in year two and Davis has been better in a rotation.
The slew of injuries is reminiscent of the 2022 season, when the Rams were decimated by injuries on their way to a 5-12 record. In 2022, the Rams lost Cooper Kupp, Matthew Stafford, Aaron Donald, and nearly the entire offensive line.
With Adams, the Rams lose a player who has been a threat in the red zone. Adams and Stafford seemed to have a much stronger connection than they had at times last year. Turner has been a staple on the defensive line and Ford will also be missed. That’s three starters who played significant roles that the Rams won’t have available as they try to recover from a 2-4 start. That also doesn’t mention the Rams placing Blake Grupe on injured reserve .
Tucked away in all of this is the fact that Myles Garrett still hasn't been cleared to practice. Garrett was held out for much of training camp before being placed on injured reserve after Week 1. It was reported last week that Garrett could practice as soon as this week . While Garrett was initially given a six-week recovery timeline, that was always viewed as a worst-case scenario.
At 2-4, the Rams were already facing an uphill battle to turn their season around. With several key players now unavailable, that challenge has only gotten more difficult.

title: 5 Kickers the Rams Could Sign After Placing Blake Grupe on Injured Reserve
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams will be searching for another kicker this week after placing Blake Grupe on injured reserve Monday. After cutting Harrison Mevis last week, the Rams signed Grupe as his replacement. Grupe made a 44-yard field goal on Sunday, but on the ensuing kickoff, he got injured trying to tackle returner Devin Duvernay.
Placing Grupe on injured reserve is a continuation of the special teams drama that the Rams have endured this season. Just when they thought they may have resovled the issue, they have to find another solution.
LA Rams Transactions: • Reserve/Injured K Blake Grupe pic.twitter.com/eiyLAZ82GF
Without Grupe, the Rams turned to Ethan Evans to kick extra points. Evans made his lone extra point in the fourth quarter to briefly give the Rams the lead. Now that Grupe is on injured reserve, the Rams are right back where they started last week. Here are five options the Rams could turn to.
Brown remains one of my favorite options to come in and at least try out for the Rams’ kicker spot. The Rams signed Brown as an undrafted free agent in 2023, but he was cut before the start of the regular season. Brown went 25-for-28 last year in the UFL and was 7-for-9 from 50+. He made field goals from 60 and 63 yards in the playoffs last season.
ANOTHER 4-POINTER 🤯‼️ Tanner Brown is good from 63-yards 🔥 @DynastyFP 4-Point Field Goal pic.twitter.com/Jqp63Ed7Ks
McManus is a veteran kicker and wasn’t brought back by the Green Bay Packers in the offseason. McManus was 24-for-30 last season with a long of 56. He was also 32-for-33 on extra points. All six of McManus’ misses were from beyond 40 yards, and he was just 3-for-7 in the 40- to 49-yard range. It’s not ideal, but it’s an option.
Not many will want the Rams to bring back Joshua Karty after last season. At one point, Karty showed plenty of talent. Karty finished his rookie year strong before his struggles in 2025. It would be hard to trust Bubba Ventrone to get that out of him again, but he may be worth a look. Karty was let go last season before the Rams made changes to their field goal operation as a whole.
Gano is another veteran kicker at 39 years old. He kicked for the New York Giants last year and went 9-for-10 on field goals in five games, with a long of 55 yards. He was also 9-for-9 on extra points. A veteran like Gano may bring some stability to the position.
At this point, the Rams are running out of proven options. Sauls was signed as an undrafted free agent by the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2025 and has since bounced around with the Atlanta Falcons and New York Giants. Sauls is a left-footed kicker and went 8-for-8 in three games with the Giants last season.

title: Rams Report Card Reveals Major Offensive Failures in Loss to Cardinals
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams lost another one-score game this season , falling 18-16 to the Arizona Cardinals. It’s the type of loss that shouldn’t happen to a Sean McVay-led team. The Rams didn’t get a good performance from Matthew Stafford, and Sean McVay didn’t coach a clean game. While the defense kept the Rams in it, they also allowed six scoring drives. Let’s grade each position group’s performance.
The Rams can’t keep having Matthew Stafford not show up until the fourth quarter. Through the first three quarters on Sunday, Stafford was 12-for-19 for 96 yards. While Stafford picked it up in the fourth quarter and gave the Rams the lead at the end, it’s just not sustainable. The Rams need Stafford for 60 minutes. In two of the last three games, the Rams have gotten the version of Stafford that they need for less than 15.
Sean McVay could have done a better job getting the running backs more involved in the offense. Sunday’s game should have been one where Corum and Williams combined for over 30 carries. Instead, they had 19 carries for 92 yards. Both averaged over 4.5 yards per carry in the game. Corum seemed to pick up where he left off last year against the Cardinals, forcing three missed tackles. He even got involved in the passing game, scoring on a screen.
When the wide receivers got involved, they were good. Stafford simply didn’t give them enough opportunities.Puka Nacua had three targets in the first three quarters and then matched that on the final drive alone when the offense finally came to life. Konata Mumpfield was efficient with two catches and Nacua had six receptions on seven targets and should have had a touchdown if Stafford hits him wide open in the third quarter.
For an offense that is supposed to feature the tight ends, that position group hasn’t shown that it is good enough for that to be the case. Davis Allen was featured on a fullback dive on 4th-and-1 that came up short. Additionally, Tyler Higbee fumbled with the Rams nearing the red zone. It’s his second fumble this  year. Colby Parkinson scored the go-ahead touchdown late, but it can be argued that it hurt the Rams in that situation and that he would have been better off going down.
For the most part, the offensive line played well. The Cardinals certainly took advantage of Alaric Jackson’s absence by blitzing more, but David Quessenberry wasn't the reason the Rams lost. He only gave up two pressures. Where the Rams have struggled is on the interior, which is supposed to be their strength. Still, Warren McClendon had an untimely penalty that pushed the Rams back five yards on 4th-and-3.
Aaron Donald made a few splash plays against the Cardinals and Byron Young was dominant in the first half. However, no player had more than three pressures and they struggled against the run. One can certainly hope that the return of Myles Garrett provides a boost here, but this group overall needs to be better.
Nate Landman missed two tackles and both he and Omar Speights allowed three receptions on three targets. Landman was exploited in coverage a few times. The Rams need better linebacker play.
Josh Wallace continues to play very well when given opportunities. He was targeted eight times against the Cardinals and allowed just four catches. His big penalty at the end can certainly be argued. Quentin Lake had the interception on the first drive as well. That’s where the positives end, though. Kam Kinchens missed two tackles along with Kam Curl. The inability to tackle at the second and third levels is a big reason why the Cardinals were able to run the ball as successfully as they did.
Sunday didn’t come without its special teams errors. On the Rams’ first kickoff of the game, the coverage unit once again didn’t execute well, allowing a big return that led to Blake Grupe getting injured. Jordan Whittington also had a chance to down a punt inside the five and missed it. Due to the lack o confidence in the coverage unit, the Rams opted to kick the ball into the end zone in the fourth quarter, setting up the Cardinals at the 35-yard line. However, Ethan Evans gets some props for making the extra point that gave the Rams the lead.
McVay was severely out-coached in this one by Mike LaFleur and Nick Rallis. The fullback dive playcall on 4th-and-1 isn’t acceptable given the other options on offense. McVay and Stafford are two of the biggest problems right now. That doesn’t mean either needs to be benched or fired, but the Rams need better from both of them. The good news is that both are part of the solution.

title: Rams 10 Takeaways: Identity Crisis Deepens After Inexcusable Loss to Cardinals
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams lost to the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, 18-16, to fall to 2-4. It’s only been six weeks, but the Rams are already facing an identity crisis . A month and a half into the season, the Rams still don’t know who they are as a team, and that’s evident in the inconsistency of their results.
“We won't win a game unless we figure out how not to beat ourselves,” said head coach Sean McVay. “So many unforced errors, so many things that are not in alignment with what we want to do, specifically on the offensive side of the ball.”
This isn’t where the Rams had planned to be at the beginning of the season, but it is their current reality. Let’s jump into this week’s 10 takeaways.
For a moment, it appeared as if the Rams had solved their kicking issues. Blake Grupe made his first field goal from 44 yards out and it was right down the middle.On the ensuing kickoff, the Rams’ coverage unit allowed Devin Duvernay to break through, and Grupe went in for the tackle, only to injure his knee. The Rams may need to bring in a Witch or Catholic priest to solve the special teams issues at this point, because they are cursed. McVay didn’t have an update on Grupe after the game, but noted the knee injury.
Rams New Kicker Blake Grupe Tried To Tackle Somebody On The Kickoff And Ended Up Injuring Himself. The Rams Just Signed This Guy After Cutting Harrison Mevis. Rough Start. 😬 pic.twitter.com/0BDZRD1hzh
This isn’t to say that the Rams need to bench Matthew Stafford. We aren’t at that point yet. However, he does need to be better . Stafford had a -0.14 EPA per pass against the Cardinals. That was worse than Daniel Jones and Tyler Shough in Week 6. It was only slightly better than Cam Ward. In the first three quarters of games this season, Stafford’s 0.07 adjusted EPA per play ranks 17th. However, in the fourth quarter, he ranks seventh at 0.32. Stafford is part of the solution to get the Rams’ offense out of this rut. With that said, right now, he’s also part of the problem.
It’s fair to have an issue with both fourth down play calls. With that said, there was at least some logic with the screen on 4th-and-8. A good way to beat a blitz is with a screen. The more inexcusable call was the fullback dive to Davis Allen. Allen had never taken a handoff in his four-year NFL career or in college. When options such as Kyren Williams and Puka Nacua exist in the offense, going with a hand-off to Allen is confusing to say the least.
A big reason the Cardinals were able to dictate the tempo of the game was their success running the ball. The Rams didn’t stop the run consistently throughout the game as the defensive backs got run through. Chris Shula likes to operate out of dime, but those lighter packages aren’t working. Poona Ford isn’t as dominant in the middle as he was last year, and the Rams are getting washed away at the second and third levels. If there’s an adjustment to be made on defense, this is it.
Aside from special teams, Chris Shula and the defense continue to be the scapegoats for the Rams’ struggles. However, at some point, the offense has to do its part. Had it not been for Shula’s defense, this game wouldn’t have been close. They held the Cardinals to 0-for-5 in the red zone and got stops in the fourth quarter to give the offense a chance. It’s true the Cardinals were able to play ball control as they held the ball for almost 35 minutes. At the same time, if the Rams had scored points against a defense ranked No. 29 in EPA per play and forced the Cardinals to play from behind, Arizona wouldn't have been able to rely on that approach.
The Rams continue to have crucial mistakes in big moments. Facing a 4th-and-3, Warren McClendon jumped to make it a 4th-and-8. With the Rams in the red zone, Matthew Stafford stumbled for a loss of 11 before Tyler Higbee fumbled on the next play. The Rams continue to out-gain opponents, but haven’t been able to turn the yards into points consistently.
“We've had some really critical errors at really unfortunate times,” said McVay. “That's what our narrative has been for this year. We can't keep saying, ‘Oh, that we haven't done that before.’ Well, this year we are doing it.”
The Rams have out-gained their opponents by a league-best 644 yards this season. They are 2-4.
For most of the game, Cardinals defensive coordinator Nick Rallis had McVay and Stafford in a blender. The Rams’ offense made Rallis look like Vic Fangio coaching the 2018 Chicago Bears. There was certainly an element of execution, but McVay was out-coached by Rallis and Mike LaFleur. McVay gave the Cardinals a chance late because he didn’t drain the clock. There were too many questionable playcalls. If you had said before the game that the Cardinals wouldn’t score a touchdown, nobody would have thought the Rams would lose.
“There were other instances that we could have made them pay. We just didn't execute, simple as that,” McVay said. “Had an idea of what they were doing. We have to be able to execute in some of those instances and that wasn't the case today.”
Both McVay and Stafford were asked what the identity of this team was after six weeks. “We're figuring it out. I can't answer that right now,” McVay answered. Stafford added, “We are what our record is. We have to try to find a way to be better.”
The Rams don’t have an offensive identity that they can lean on. Culturally, they are also lacking an identity as they seemingly implode after yet another close loss. The frustration is starting to set in and that’s starting to make its way around the locker room.
It’s hard to say that this isn’t rock bottom for the Rams . That was one of the worst losses of the McVay era. It’s right up there with losing to the 0-13 New York Jets in 2020. Beating the Cardinals under McVay has been about as much of a ‘sure thing’ as it gets. This Cardinals team had essentially waved the white flag, and the Rams gave them life. Instead of sitting at 3-3 and second place in the NFC West, they are 2-4 and in last place. While 2022 was bad, the expectations of this season might make it worse.
During his post-game press conference, Sean McVay used the phrase “I’m not really sure” twice and “I can’t answer that right now” one other time. The Rams don’t have answers for how to get out of this. In 2021, Raheem Morris helped McVay recover from “No Win November.” During the 2023 season when the Rams were 3-6, it was Cooper Kupp. There is still an opportunity for the Rams to climb out of this, but there isn’t much reason to be confident that they can.

title: Hondo’s Mailbag: Raider Nation Agrees on One Thing
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) are about to host the Los Angeles Rams (2-4), and while the Silver and Black are overachieving, the preseason unanimous Super Bowl favorite (Rams) is limping into Allegiant Stadium.
With a roster that looks more like an episode of M*A*S*H* than a Super Bowl contender, led by certain Hall of Fame QB Matthew Stafford and a roster full of talent at every position, the Rams are the favorite, but the Raiders have upset on their mind.
While Klint Kubiak has shined this season, GM John Spytek has as well.
The Raiders GM may have painted himself into a corner , according to another NFL executive, but that is not what fans want to talk about.
Each week, I ask Raider Nation on my social media to sound off on their team.  Every week, Raider Nation never fails to deliver, and by the tone and tenor of your comments, the Silver and Black, who see their fandom as a way of life and part of their identity, are all thinking the same thoughts.
Or, as my four-year-old son Dexter Ernest Wayne Carpenter says, “Are you thinking what I am thinking?”
OL giving time and making holes. DL getting pressure on the QB
I am not pretending that Ashton Jeanty has looked like Barry Sanders; he hasn’t, but he also can’t block for himself while toting the rock.
The offensive line will face a stacked box each week until they beat it.  There are many ways to do that, like the play-action pass, but this Tweet nails it.
For the Raiders to upset the Rams, the offensive line will have to have a good day.  Not great, and not even elite, but a good day.
The Rams are primed for an upset here, but the OL has to deliver a much better run-game performance this weekend.
Give Washington the rock 20 times.
I believe the Raiders will not take long to get Mike Washington Jr. more reps this weekend, should Ashton Jeanty struggle early.
I in no way, and neither do the Raiders, place the blame for the lack of a successful running game on Jeanty, but there is no secret that the rookie Arkansas Razorback has delivered some spark.
Kubiak was asked this week about Washington and his role heading into Sunday, and his answer was telling.
"I think we have to get production from all three of our backs, and Mike Washington [Jr.] did some good stuff yesterday, and I thought overall our backs, they ran harder yesterday. I thought they broke tackles. I thought they moved the line of scrimmage when things weren't there. I thought Coach Omar [Young] did a really good job of challenging our guys. I thought they had one of their better games, and I expect that to continue to improve."
No Penalties Finish The Game Score 7 In The Red Zone Not 3 Need A Running Game ☠️🏴‍☠️
This Tweet tells a story that all goes back to the run game.
Penalties kill the running game because you aren’t going to run on third-and-long.  An anemic running game also causes teams to falter in the red zone because of the aforementioned inability to run the ball.
The subsequent lack of a running game turns a seven-point touchdown into a three-point field goal, essentially a loss of four points.
Kirk Cousins said it best after Sunday's loss about the red zone woes: “Anytime you leave points on the board in the red zone, it's hard."
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Raiders' Biggest Needs Ahead of NFL's Trade Deadline Are Painfully Obvious
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders have looked for ways both big and small during this offseason and the early part of the 2026 regular season.
With the trade deadline approaching, below are the position groups the Raiders should consider trading for.
The Raiders invested heavily in Tyler Linderbaum this offseason. He has already gotten the unit headed in the right direction, but Sunday confirmed that Las Vegas needs additional help along the offensive line. The Raiders started Caleb Rogers over Jackson Powers-Johnson on Sunday.
As expected, Rogers had his ups and downs. Kolton Miller, while still playing well overall, is not quite what he once was. The jury is still out on Spencer Burford. If the Raiders make a trade, finding additional help for their offensive line has to be at the top of that list.
The Raiders are thin at both guard positions. They lack dependable options behind their starting interior offensive linemen. Las Vegas does not know for sure whether the starters they currently have along the interior offensive line are dependable.
Las Vegas kept Cousins clean again on Sunday against the Bills, but still allowed several pressures. They also struggled to run the ball, partly because of issues along their offensive line. Kubiak shared his thoughts on the unit after the Raiders' Week 6 loss to Buffalo.
"I think Spencer has been a really great addition for our team. I think he's a guy that's continuing to improve. Overall, as an offensive line, I really like what we're doing protecting the quarterback,” Kubiak said the day after the game.
“I like how our quarterback's getting the ball out on time, and he knows Spencer and Tyler [Linderbaum] and Kolton [Miller] and DJ [Glaze] and Caleb [Rogers] and the whole offensive line knows that we have to improve in the run game blocking if we want to get to where we want to get.”
If the Raiders were to trade for a player, an offensive lineman would be nice.
The Raiders have a young defensive backfield they trust. Still, Las Vegas' front office and coaching staff knew that the position group was undoubtedly the roster's most vulnerable entering the season.  If they were to make a trade, adding another cornerback would be ideal.
There are few, if any, position groups on Las Vegas' roster that a trade would make more sense for than a trade to boost their defensive backfield moving forward. Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak explained his thoughts on the group.
“I think the best advice you can give them is that you just keep playing. Especially as a defensive back, you're going to get beat, and when you get beat everybody in the free world is going to know it because it's on TV,” Kubiak said.
“When a defensive lineman misses his gap, they're going to show the guy that missed the tackle. So, you got to have thick skin, and you got to move on to the next play. Just keep playing, keep competing,”
Veteran wide receiver Jalen Nailor returned to the Raiders' lineup on Sunday against the Bills. Tre Tucker had a solid overall day that was capped off by an impressive long touchdown pass from Cousins late in the game. Still, the unit leaves much to be desired.
The Raiders still sorely miss Jack Bech, and likely will aim to add another receiver or two next offseason. However, until then, wide receiver will continue to be an issue for Las Vegas unless something changes. If the Raiders were to trade, a receiver may be the top option on their list.
With Nailor back in the fold, Las Vegas' offense seemed to have much more of a chance of moving the ball and scoring points than they did without him in the field in Week 5. Kubiak explained how Nailor impacted the game despite his stats.
"He had targets. He got called on. We threw a double move to him, and they had a penalty on him. He caught a choice route. I thought Jalen [Nailor] was great to have him back. You could feel his presence out there and just got to keep finding ways to get him the ball because he's a really good player. He's a player that I'm counting on, that we're counting on, that's going to continue to ascend," Kubiak said.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Hondo's Raiders Report Card: Roadmap To Ending the Losing Streak
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) fell short on Sunday in their upset bid against the Buffalo Bills (5-1). The 33-30 loss hurt, but perspective is important.
In their last three games, the Raiders have faced the two favorites to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl: the Kansas City Chiefs and the aforementioned Buffalo Bills.
In both games, the Raiders' upset bids ended not when their opponent beat them, but when they beat themselves.
In the other game, against the reigning AFC representative in the Super Bowl, the New England Patriots , it was a brutal butt-whipping.
That said, the overachieving Raiders continue to move forward with GM John Spytek making roster moves, and Klint Kubiak shining brightly as an NFL first-year coach.
Each Tuesday, throughout the season, I offer you my weekly report card from inside the franchise. An honest assessment, not based on fandom or hatred, no hyperbole, just an honest look at your team. Let’s dig in.
At first glance, a struggling offensive line and no running game may make this seem far-fetched, but let me explain.
The reality is that part of the reason (and no, not the only reason) for the terrible rushing attack is that the opponents know Kubiak’s system. They know his system is built on running the ball, and defenses are selling out to stop it.
It doesn’t mean anemic run game is acceptable; it is not. It needs more attention, but Kubiak discussed his thoughts on the effort on Sunday.
"I think we have to get production from all three of our backs, and Mike Washington [Jr.] did some good stuff yesterday, and I thought overall our backs, they ran harder yesterday. I thought they broke tackles. I thought they moved the line of scrimmage when things weren't there. I thought Coach Omar [Young] did a really good job of challenging our guys. I thought they had one of their better games, and I expect that to continue to improve."
The red zone offense is not good. The Raiders are leaving far too many points on the field with their inability to score in the red zone. Something Kubiak is very aware of.
“Penalties, lack of execution. It's not one thing. But I think mainly when you want to be a good red zone team, you got to run the ball well in the red zone. We didn't do that."
The point is, against a team many feel is on its way to the Super Bowl, the Raiders put up 30 points, and you have the NFL’s leading touchdown-throwing QB, Kirk Cousins.
It isn’t pretty, but the Raiders offense is finding ways to score. It isn’t a beauty contest. Al Davis said, “Just Win, Baby.” He said nothing about pretty. Kubiak agrees.
“The object of the game is to score points, and whether you're getting it done from the ground or from the air, or they're coming from special teams or defensive scores as a team. Obviously, it's a team game, and it's about outscoring the opponent. So, we're never going to – we always want to be great in all facets, okay, but you're going to play to your strengths."
"So, moving the ball and scoring points was good yesterday. However, what do you got to do to get over the hump? You've got to score on all five possessions in the red zone, not just two of five.”
At first, once again, that grade may seem too high. Trust me, it isn’t.
Robbie Leonard, despite a thin DL, a young defensive backfield, and a high-powered offense led by a certain Hall of Fame QB in Josh Allen, did give up 30 points.
But when you look at them holding Allen to one rushing yard, and some of those points coming off offensive mistakes, it was more than impressive; it was outstanding.
Chris Shula, the DC of the Los Angeles Rams, is rightfully discussed as a future head coach in this league, but Leonard just put on a clinic controlling what many consider the best offense in the NFL, and he's had only one bad week this year.
Leonard is an emerging star who can only coach with the roster he's been given, but his head coach trusts him, and they've formed a special tandem.
With John Spytek and his staff building a brilliant roster for the future, the outlook is bright.
Matt Gay, AJ Cole, and long-snapper Alex Ward were great, but still, problems exist.
The Silver and Black special teams unit, for lack of a better term, self-destructed on Sunday through a myriad of costly penalties and, to be kind, poor coverage. They surrendered multiple big returns—including a 40-yard kickoff return to Ray Davis and a 22-yard punt return to Greg Dortch—while committing crucial veteran penalties that repeatedly gave Buffalo prime field position.
I am 100% a supporter of STC Joe DeCamillis, and you should be as well, but this is a rebuilding team, and special teams has been a consistent struggle this season.
DeCamillis will fix it, but it is really ugly.
First-year head coach Klint Kubiak made a rookie mistake when he challenged a play that he shouldn’t have, and that is part of the learning curve. The amazing thing about Kubiak is that, as a first-year coach, he should have had a plethora of mistakes; he hasn’t. You could count his mistakes on one hand and not even need all your fingers.
Robbie Leonard was outstanding, and while Kubiak’s staff has some real stars, this is a rebuilding roster. It is thin, young, and, in many places, void of talent.
Credit the Raiders for not panicking and building the right way.
Without this staff, there's no way the Raiders are 3-3 today, but they are.
This fan base sold a lot of their tickets well before preseason games started. I had several family members and friends who are Bills fans, bought their tickets months ago, and were in town.
That said, I have been to every Raiders game and practice in Allegiant Stadium. The crowd was conservatively 75-25 Bills fans, and I have never seen a crowd that lopsided.
Credit Raider Nation, however: with far more Bills fans in attendance, the crowd was never overwhelming for the Bills, and Raider Nation was loud at all the appropriate times.
As one season ticket holder who sold their tickets told me, “I love what Klint and Spytek are doing; I won’t be selling tickets next year if they keep this up.”
If I had told you back in June that the Raiders would play the Bills as they did, most reasonable people would have laughed.
This loss hurt, because the Raiders beat themselves.
But in the long run, there were a lot of positives you can take from it. If the true direction the leaders of this franchise want to take is a Super Bowl, then Sunday was a yardstick. Reading it, this team may not be as far off as once thought.
The Rams, I suspect, are coming into a buzz saw, a Silver-and-Black buzz saw. If the Raiders play the Rams as they did the Bills and Chiefs, next week we will be talking about an upset.
Can you hear that noise? It’s called optimism, Raider Nation.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience.
