title: Saints vs. Giants: Can New Orleans Snap Its Losing Streak? Our Staff Predicts
full_text:
The pressure continues to mount on the New Orleans Saints as they head to the Meadowlands for Sunday's Week 6 showdown against the New York Giants , desperately searching for answers amid a disappointing start to the season.
Following a frustrating 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , the Saints (1-4) have dropped three consecutive games, raising questions about the team's direction under second-year head coach Kellen Moore.
The struggles have even drawn the attention of team owner Gayle Benson , who recently expressed frustration with the organization's performance and made it clear that continued losing would not be tolerated without consequences.
With expectations rising and patience wearing thin, New Orleans faces another difficult challenge against a surprising Giants team that has emerged as an early contender in the NFC East.
Here are our predictions for Sunday's game.
This is the Saints' first road game since Week 2, and it’s a strategic one at that, as the Saints will immediately fly out of New York for their game against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris next week. However, this is a critical game for coach Kellen Moore , and maybe even longtime general manager Mickey Loomis .
I don’t think Tyler Shough will have many games like he did last week in the loss to the Vikings, but he will have another matchup against a top-10 defense as the Giants are ninth in total defense. The strength of the defense is its ability to defend the pass, allowing only 199.7 yards per contest, which is good for seventh in the NFL, and have forced six interceptions, which is good for fourth.
While I think Shough will do much better, the Giants have the players needed to at least limit Shough, and New Orleans’ rushing attack is one of the NFL’s worst and will be ineffective. While the Giants have struggled to stop the run, they will have no trouble stopping the Saints.
Defensively, I think the Saints will do enough to keep the game close but not enough to win. The Giants aren’t the greatest offense in the world, but Cam Skattebo is a decent running back, while the receiving threats of Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely are going to give the Saints’ defense a heap of trouble.
I predict a one-score game in the Meadowlands with the Giants pulling it out.
Which Saints club will show in the Meadowlands today? Will it be the one from the first three weeks of the season, or the one from the last three?
We know this: those leading this organization have been put on notice by the woman that holds the checkbook. For the first time as owner of the Saints, Gayle Benson is faced with a situation that will require resolve and a possible move that will force her to make decisions that will be uncomfortable. She has put her trust and belief in those in charge. After seeing where her club has gone in the last few weeks, and the fan reaction to that direction, Mrs. Benson is having to rethink that trust.
Meanwhile, a two-week road trip followed by the Saints open/bye week may be just what the doctor ordered for Moore and his troops: a chance to regroup and rethink where things are.
Being a "glass-half-full" kinda guy, I'm getting this feeling this may be the first step to Moore, his coaches, and his players turning things around. However, don't bet the house on who I choose to win today. I've only been right once in five prognostications this year.

title: Saints vs. Giants: Three Things New Orleans Must Do to Win at the Meadowlands
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints enter Sunday's Week 6 matchup with a trip to the Meadowlands against the New York Giants looking to avoid their fourth consecutive loss, but a familiar face stands in their way and remains a fan favorite in New Orleans.
Former Saints quarterback Jameis Winston will lead the Giants against his former team as New Orleans attempts to rebound from a disappointing 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings .
The Saints (1-4) have struggled to find consistency on both sides of the football, particularly offensively, where turnovers and an ineffective rushing attack have contributed to their disappointing start.
Meanwhile, the Giants (3-1-1) have emerged as one of the NFC's early surprises under first-year coach John Harbaugh , overcoming injuries and inconsistent quarterback play to remain atop the NFC East.
Beyond Winston's reunion with New Orleans, the Saints must contend with two dangerous receiving threats in Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely while finding a way to exploit New York's ball-security problems.
A persistent issue for New Orleans throughout Kellen Moore ’s tenure has been their inability to build early momentum.
Across 22 games with Moore at the helm, the Saints have managed a mere 35 points in the first quarter. During this stretch, they have logged 29 three-and-outs—the highest tally in the league—and have yet to top seven points in any opening period.
These early-game woes have persisted into the current season. Atlanta built a 14-0 first-quarter cushion against New Orleans in a 45-24 Saints loss. The following week, Minnesota held New Orleans scoreless in the opening frame as the Saints were limited to 142 total yards.
Finding an offensive rhythm from the opening kickoff must be a top focus for Moore.
Achieving this requires steering clear of costly penalties, executing on third down, and keeping quarterback Tyler Shough in manageable down-and-distance scenarios.
With a playmaking Giants offense on the horizon, another slow start risks burying New Orleans in a hole too deep to climb out of.
Containing wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely—quarterback Jameis Winston's primary targets—presents the New Orleans defense's most formidable task, even as Winston draws significant focus.
Together, Nabers (29 receptions, 329 yards, two TDs) and Likely (33 receptions, 284 yards, four TDs) account for most of the team's targeted passes and 58% of its overall offensive yardage.
Nabers, the former LSU standout, has successfully recovered from a season-ending knee injury. His recent performances include a six-catch, 112-yard game with a touchdown against Arizona in Week 4, followed by an 11-reception, 121-yard, one-touchdown outing on 20 targets versus Washington.
Over-focusing on Nabers creates chances for Likely, the former Baltimore Raven who has emerged as Winston's top redzone option. Against Washington, Likely caught 11 passes for 94 yards and two scores, becoming the first tight end in Giants franchise history to record at least nine catches and two touchdowns in a single game.
Standing 6-foot-4, Likely poses significant coverage challenges due to his size and athleticism. Following recent difficulties against Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers , limiting Likely will be a critical test for the Saints' defensive scheme.
New Orleans must balance its coverage duties to avoid exposing defensive backs to disadvantageous single-coverage looks against either receiver.
Despite their contrasting records, both the Saints and Giants have struggled with ball security this season.
New York has committed seven turnovers through five games, including three interceptions and four lost fumbles. Meanwhile, New Orleans enters Sunday's matchup with a minus-six turnover differential.
However, the Giants have compensated for their mistakes by intercepting six passes, tied for third-most in the NFL, while the Saints have recorded just one interception.
That discrepancy could prove decisive, particularly with quarterback Tyler Shough coming off a disappointing performance against Minnesota.
Shough completed 16 of 25 passes for just 96 yards and two interceptions, finishing with a 38.1 passer rating. Through five games, he has thrown for 1,299 yards, nine touchdowns and five interceptions.
For the Saints, protecting the football, forcing Winston into difficult throws and capitalizing on New York's mistakes could determine whether they snap their three-game losing streak.

title: Giants Rookie Report Card Week 6: J.C. Davis Impresses in Limited Action
full_text:
The New York Giants squandered much of the trust they built early in the campaign after a rough 34-27 loss to the visiting New Orleans Saints. While there were some thrilling moments and impressive performances, the overall picture was quite ugly.
Big Blue’s rookies were largely underwhelming. First-year players will experience growing pains, and those can happen even against a sub .500 squad at home. Let’s take a look at where the rookies stand after a frustrating Week 6.
The Giants were cautious with left tackle Andrew Thomas after he was evaluated for a concussion , so they gave sixth-round draft pick J.C. Davis an extended look.
The former Illinois standout picked up where he left off in the summer and made many fans wonder why he wasn’t already on the active offensive line.
Davis allowed no sacks, pressures, or hurries in 25 offensive snaps , according to Pro Football Focus. He also stayed penalty-free, which was not an easy thing to do on this day.
The Giants still have run-blocking issues, but Davis’ pass-protection skills could be invaluable if Thomas misses time again.
Even when the No. 5 overall pick has a down game, he still manages to produce at least one memorable play. Arvell Reese’s highlight against the Saints came when he effortlessly forced offensive lineman David Edwards to the ground, which in turn caused running back Kendre Miller to trip about midway through the second quarter.
Reese posted four total stops, but he showed his inexperience with two missed tackles . While the combination of speed and strength is eye-catching, he is still learning what it means to be an NFL linebacker.
The sixth-round linebacker has not seen the field on defense, but he remains a consistent presence on special teams. Jack Kelly logged a season-high 31 snaps against the Saints, per PFF, and has now totaled at least 24 in three straight games.
He is doing the unglamorous work that is helping the Giants become a more balanced team. The special teams unit was far from its best, but Kelly has earned a weekly role, which is more than coaches can reasonably expect from a Day 3 selection.
The Giants traded back into the third round to snag Malachi Fields, so the former Notre Dame wide receiver is under pressure to make worthwhile progress this season. He has recorded exactly two catches in every game and has exceeded 50 yards only once.
Perhaps a quarterback change could boost his production. Fields may have a better chance to manufacture offense with J.J. McCarthy taking snaps, especially given the fireworks in the fourth quarter.
They didn’t appear to be on the same page during an interception, but the duo flashed a bit of chemistry afterward.
Maybe they can build on their rapport against the Houston Texans, assuming McCarthy starts ahead of Jameis Winston . Regardless of who is at quarterback, the 6-foot-4 Fields needs to offer more as a blocker.
New York took a risk by converting the Miami Hurricanes tackle to guard , banking on his power and versatility. The decision may yield excellent results in the long run, but for now, there will be scuffles.
Mauigoa surrendered two hurries and two pressures against New Orleans, and a roughing-the-passer penalty negated a big sack he allowed to Vernon Broughton. He will have to improve his timing moving forward, but it is far too early to panic.
Like fellow sixth-rounder J.C. Davis, defensive tackle Bobby Jamison-Travis took the field for the first time on Sunday. He didn’t make the same impact, though.
The 6-foot-3, 328-pounder was part of a porous Giants run defense that gave up 175 yards to New Orleans. He finished with two tackles and valuable experience. Given the lack of depth at defensive tackle, Jamison-Travis may get another chance to prove himself soon.
Undrafted free agent Dominic Zvada did not miss any kicks in the traditional sense in Week 6, but he made an extremely costly miscue.
The 2024 Big Ten Kicker of the Year was tasked with launching the kickoff out of the back of the end zone before the two-minute warning, which would have saved the Giants about 40 seconds for one last comeback drive. He came up short.
The ball was returned, and the clock whittled down to 2:00. Young J.J. McCarthy indeed needed that additional time to score a touchdown. Zvada should be able to come through in that spot, but he is a rookie. Harbaugh could also have ceded five yards by kicking the ball out of bounds, keeping the clock the same.
Zvada nailed modest 41- and 34-yard field goals, so there was not much else to evaluate.
The No. 37 pick suffered a concussion against the Washington Commanders and was inactive for the Saints game. He hopes to clear the concussion protocol for Sunday’s game in Houston.

title: Should the Giants Trade for Colts RB Jonathan Taylor to Fix Their Backfield?
full_text:
Legendary NFL head coach-turned-broadcaster John Madden once said, “If you have two quarterbacks, you have none.”
While the New York Giants are still figuring out what to do at quarterback, Madden’s words could just as easily apply to the team’s situation at running back.
After releasing Najee Harris, the starter in Sunday’s loss to the New Orleans Saints, head coach John Harbaugh is still waiting for one of the team’s remaining backs (Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy Jr., or Devin Singletary) to step up and claim the RB1 job.
Each running back has had his own issues that have kept him from claiming the job.
Skattebo, who began the year as the RB1, has struggled with ball security. He has fumbled four times this season, including one on a critical scoring drive against Washington that ended the team’s chance to win. Over two seasons, he fumbles once every 36.4 carries.
Tracy, seeking his third straight season with 1,000 all-purpose yards, has also struggled with ball security, along with questions about his pass protection. Those are two big factors that usually keep a running back on the sideline.
To his credit, he has improved in pass protection, if Pro Football Focus’ grades are to be believed: Tracy has a team-leading 84.1 grade (on 17 pass-blocking snaps) and has allowed no pressures thus far.
Singletary has been the odd man out in the rotation, inactive for three consecutive weeks. He does a lot of little things well, but he's taken a back seat because Skattebo and Tracy are viewed as longer-term options, and he lacks the explosiveness that forces defenses to really account for him when he’s in the game.
The situation at running back, combined with the loss of quarterback Jaxson Dart’s mobility, has seen the Giants’ rushing attack, a top-five unit last year, drop to 16th in rushing yards (629) and 22nd in yards per carry.
As if that hasn’t been enough, opposing defenses this year have loaded the box with eight or more defenders on 77 of the Giants’ rushing attempts, the sixth most in the NFL.
All of this raises the question of whether it’s smart for the Giants to trade for a legitimate RB1. We don’t think they will make that move because we think defensive line depth is a bigger need.
But of the four players suggested by SI.com’s Conor Orr , the one who makes the most sense is Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, who is reportedly among the players who could be on the move after the Colts dismissed general manager Chris Ballard this week.
Taylor, 27, recently signed a contract extension worth $44 million in new money, with $39 million guaranteed. If he is traded, the acquiring team would not pick up the prorated signing bonus, which is $7.562 million this year before dropping to $5 million in 2027 and 2028.
He would cost a new team $410,588 per week in base salary, plus another $60,000 for each game he plays, but he could be worth it.
Since 2020, Taylor ranks second in total rushing yards (8,090), behind only Derrick Henry of the Baltimore Ravens (9,719), despite injuries that kept him out of games every season through 2024.
Taylor also has four 1,000-yard rushing seasons (2020, 2021, 2024, and 2025), led the league in rushing yardage in 2021 (his second year in the league), and is a legitimate threat as a receiver out of the backfield.
The closest comparison for a deal to acquire Taylor would be the one back in 2021 when the San Francisco 49ers acquired running back Christian McCaffrey from the Carolina Panthers for a second-round pick plus an additional Day 3 selection.
The Giants currently have six projected picks in next year’s draft, so if they were to swing this kind of trade, they’d almost certainly have to split the assets between 2027 and 2028.
Then there is the question of whether the Giants are better off waiting to see what transpires in the 2027 draft.
Florida’s Jadan Baugh, Missouri’s Ahamad Hardy, and Mississippi’s Kewan Lacy are candidates who could provide the production they seek if they’re willing to wait on adding a running back and stick with Skattebo, Tracy, and Singletary for now.
As much as a balanced offense matters, if the Giants need to make a trade, it should be for a defensive lineman to help stop the run.
Another factor is whether the Giants ultimately decide to roll with J.J. McCarthy at quarterback. Because McCarthy is a mobile signal caller, a quarterback the defense must account for as a potential runner, could open things up for the rest of the running backs and finally allow Harbaugh to declare a winner at RB1.

title: Giants at a Crossroads: Is It Time to Turn the Offense Over to J.J. McCarthy?
full_text:
The New York Giants sit all alone in first place in the NFC East with a 1.5-game lead, a position that they would undoubtedly like to retain through Week 18, preferably with a larger cushion if possible.
For that to happen, though, head coach John Harbaugh faces a crossroads at the most important position on the team: quarterback.
After losing starter Jaxson Dart seven snaps into what became the team’s Week 2 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, the offense has been placed in the hands of 12-year veteran Jameis Winston.
But in doing so, the offense has had to move away from the RPOs and designed runs built into the playbook to capitalize on Dart’s mobility and shift toward a more traditional dropback, downfield offense that has changed the entire complexion of the Giants.
Adding to that is what’s become known as the “Jameis Winston Experience,” which in football terms means that while Winston can deliver some big-time throws, with that comes a high degree of risk.
According to Pro Football Focus’ advanced data, this season, Winston has had eight turnover-worthy plays in 178 dropbacks, or one for every 22.25 dropbacks. J.J. McCarthy, in an admittedly smaller sample size (23 dropbacks), has had only one such play.
Harbaugh told reporters Monday that the team was still working through who to start against Houston this coming weekend, leaving the door open for a potential change.
But should that change happen this week? Let’s look at both sides of the coin.
A big issue Harbaugh and his staff need to balance is the urgency to make a change (if they feel one is warranted) versus McCarthy’s readiness to handle not only a full game plan, but enough of the playbook if adjustments are needed.
“To me, that’s got to be maybe the main thing. I mean, you can never be ready,” he said. “You just got to go out there and play. That’s one part of it.
“But the other part of it is you got to be able to be successful and protect yourself. If it’s a performance-type situation, you’ve got to be able to perform at a high level, give yourself a chance to be successful, but also the team, right, to be successful.
“So, with a quarterback, since that’s what we’re talking about, what kind of a grasp does he have on all the things he’s going to need to do with just operating the offense, and understanding the terms and its cadences and the checks and all those kinds of things, and to what degree are you able to do all those things? Is it enough to run your offense? And that’s something that we have been grappling with.”
Based on that point alone, it’s fair to wonder whether it makes more sense for the Giants to stick with Winston against a very difficult Texans defense and plan for a softer landing spot for McCarthy, such as what he’d likely get after the bye against the Eagles.
The other factor is that the Texans are an AFC team. If the Giants lose to the Texans, it shouldn’t cost them much in the NFC East division standings because the Commanders have their bye this week and the Cowboys and Eagles go at it on Monday Night Football .
Even if the 2-4 Cowboys win that game, the Giants, if they lose to Houston, would still be in first place in the division in part because they hold a 1-0 advantage over Dallas thanks to their Week 1 win.
There’s no really good time to make a switch, nor, as Harbaugh admitted, is there ever a time when one can say for certain that a guy is fully ready for a bigger role.
But with that said, McCarthy gives the Giants something they don’t have with Winston: a mobile quarterback who can not only move the pocket but also extend plays with his legs.
McCarthy’s ability to operate the RPO game gives the opposing defense another potential running threat to account for. It can also reduce the number of stacked boxes the Giants face.
To put that into perspective, this season the Giants have faced a stacked box on 77 of their rushing attempts, the sixth most in the league. They average 3.0 yards per rushing attempt against stacked boxes, which is 17th in the NFL.
Putting in a quarterback who can run should theoretically loosen things up and let the running game find success again.
There are many other reasons for and against a change at quarterback, including locker room reaction. Winston is not solely to blame for everything that has gone wrong with the team so far.
The question also creates a distraction if the debate continues to linger. If Winston stays as the starter, the players are all but certain to get questions as speculation grows about how much longer he has in the job.
Winston was signed as the backup and had his contract extended before the season to remain in that role.
While Harbaugh is no rookie when it comes to controlling the narrative, he can only do so much. Agree or disagree all you want, but this might be one of those situations where, if the change is inevitable (and it seems it is), you might as well rip the Band-Aid off now and roll with McCarthy.

title: Giants Releasing RB Najee Harris
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh admitted he wasn’t a fan of the team's four-man running back rotation Sunday against the Saints, saying he wanted someone to take the bull by the horns.
That running back room just got smaller by one member, as the Giants are releasing veteran Najee Harris , who was one of four running backs, along with Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary, vying for the RB1 role.
Harris, who got the start Sunday against the Saints after Skattebo’s snaps were significantly reduced that week, questioned the team’s decision to rotate running backs.
Asked about Harris’ frustration and whether he felt the need to pare down the number of players at the position, Harbaugh, during his Monday video call with reporters, said, “Do understand it. Respect it. Also understand that that’s earned."
Harbaugh also said that he would love for the Giants to have a RB1 they could count on emerge from the current group.
“I would love for us to be in that kind of circumstance. A (Baltimore Ravens running back) Derrick Henry circumstance, a (Philadelphia Eagles running back) Saquon Barkley circumstance, or whatever it might be. That would be great, and we haven’t. Our run game hasn’t earned that yet, and none of those guys have.”
Harris, who is trying to come back from a season-ending Achilles injury suffered three games into his first season with the Los Angeles Chargers, previously posted four straight 1,000-yard rushing seasons with the Pittsburgh Steelers.
He signed a one-year deal in August, a curious move at the time given how similar his downhill running style is to Skattebo’s.
In five games with the Giants, Harris carried the ball 31 times for 99 yards, a career-low 3.2-yard average. His 2.61 yards after contact per carry is also a career low. He also caught one pass for five yards.
With one less competitor for the role, Harbaugh offered public advice to Skattebo, Tracy and Singletary about the still-up-for-grabs RB1 spot.
“Make the most of those opportunities, and you’re sure to get more opportunities,” he said. “Do something. I get it that you want to get out there and get a rhythm, but that rhythm is earned too, and it just hasn’t happened yet.
“My advice is to go out there and take the job when you get the ball. Take the job.”

title: Giants Releasing DL/OLB Jihad Ward Three Weeks After Signing Him
full_text:
The New York Giants’ search for defensive line help this season apparently will continue.
Big Blue is planning to release defensive lineman Jihad Ward, whom they signed off the Vikings’ practice squad three weeks ago to fill the hole left by Chauncey Golston’s neck injury and to help with the pass rush after outside linebacker Brian Burns suffered a season-ending knee injury in Week 3.
Ward, who was in his second stint with the Giants, was no stranger to the team’s current coaching staff. He was with Giants head coach John Harbaugh in Baltimore from 2019 through 2020, and with Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson in Tennessee last year.
In his first stint with the Giants, during the 2022 and 2023 seasons, Ward appeared in 34 games with 20 starts in then-defensive coordinator Wink Martindale’s defense. He posted 67 tackles, 12 tackles for loss, four pass breakups, and 8.0 sacks, five of them (a career high) in 2023.
In his most recent stint with Big Blue, Ward was inactive for the team’s Week 4 game against the Arizona Cardinals after just arriving from Minnesota. He then played the next two games, against Washington and New Orleans, but registered only one tackle in 41 defensive snaps (he also played four snaps on special teams).
The Giants have been trying to bolster their defensive line depth ever since trading Dexter Lawrence to the Cincinnati Bengals before the draft.
The team most recently held a tryout for a pair of nose tackles: Jahmeer Carter, whom the Los Angeles Chargers originally signed as an undrafted free agent, and Taki Taimani, an undrafted player who was with the Vikings from 2024 until he was waived with an injury designation this past summer. It’s unclear whether either player will sign soon.
The Giants’ run defense has been a season-long problem, with Big Blue allowing 120-plus yards in four of its six games. In the last two games, Washington gouged the unit for 202 yards and the Saints for 175.
The problem has been depth. When starters D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris have both been on the field, the Giants’ run defense has held opponents to 4.9 yards per rushing attempt.
When they have not been on the field together, that average has swelled to 6.2 yards per rush attempt.

title: Giants Defense and Special Teams Grades: Charlie Jones’ Fumble Turns the Tide in Loss to Saints
full_text:
Let’s dive into this week’s New York Giants defensive and special teams player grades from the Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints.
The defense’s best interior player continued to produce this week with a whopping 7 total tackles from the nose tackle position.
Reader made plays in short yardage, stayed home to handle cutbacks, and regularly stood up blockers and double teams. Too bad he can’t rush the passer, because he does most everything else, primarily between the tackles.
In his first pro game, the big rookie recorded 2 solo tackles simply by standing his ground and letting the play come to him.
Alas, he was pushed around a bit too easily and washed out of his lane without putting up enough of a fight. At times he seemed light on his feet but never heavy-footed enough to hold his ground.
Though he managed 3 total tackles this week, we thought Harris had a barely visible game, which is something we’ve seen from him lately. He started the season slowly and picked it up over the last two weeks, but this week he took a step back, got pushed around too much, and couldn’t find his way to the ball.
After what we thought was a more visible and combative game last week, Alexander was regularly pushed around and abused out there this week in the pit.
We saw several pancakes and a whole lot of too-late-to-the-party arrivals from the defensive tackle, who was rarely engaged at the point of attack without taking abuse.
Getting some rotational edge snaps, both standing up and in a 3-point stance, Ward proved too slow to close in space and not very physical between the tackles. He got in on 1 tackle, but his presence was negligible at best.
Carter started the game fast with several pressures and two drawn pass-blocking penalties, but the Saints quickly adjusted and threw bodies at him, which slowed his impact.
In the second half, Carter played less and seemed slowed by the calf injury he suffered last week, which perhaps stiffened up at halftime.
Though he played physically throughout the second half, he lacked his typical explosiveness and never could find the ball. He finished the game with a solitary quarterback hit, his only mention on the stat sheet.
Without Carter’s big playmaking, the defense sagged, especially in the second half, when Carter didn’t appear until the seventh snap of the Saints’ opening third-quarter drive.
Playing most snaps at outside linebacker this week, Thibodeaux got most of his 5 total tackles late in the game.
That was when the Saints pulled in the reins on their offense, and he physically closed down inside runs without a care in the world about containing his edge.
He was a complete non-factor on the pass rush all game long, unless you want to call his third-quarter roughing-the-passer penalty on a bootlegging quarterback a successful pass rush; it wasn’t.
Six games into his contract year, Thibodeaux hasn’t had a single impact play for his defense, despite getting plenty of playing time and opportunities.
Getting another elevation from the practice squad, Ford got a heavy dose of outside linebacker snaps (especially with Carter struggling).
Like so many of his teammates, Ford did not impress. His 2 tackles came in pursuit and were flash plays, but when he couldn’t make plays on his edge, he showed a lack of the quick twitch and athleticism required.
Ford was sucked to the inside on a handful of edge contains that went around him too easily; his inside move is his go-to reaction, but it leaves the wide stuff too vulnerable. Ford’s pass rushes were easily neutralized.
Edmunds played another impactful game in the middle, and each of his 9 total tackles came at an important moment to stop the bleeding.
As the Saints extended their second-half lead, Edmunds’ tackles started to come farther downfield as the defensive pit crew wasn’t holding up.
There were no flash plays from the inside linebacker, but it was another solid effort from a free-agent signing who hasn't disappointed.
The Giants’ dynamic rookie continued to show improvement week to week. This week, his pass coverage really stood out. Reese not only recognized his reads and reacted quickly, but he stayed with them as the plays stretched and consistently blanketed his man.
On one edge play, Reese annihilated an O-lineman who flew backward into the ball carrier’s back for the tackle. The physicality is consistent from this kid. He made several face-up tackles between the tackles that shook the rafters.
Though he somehow finished with only 5 total tackles, Reese also recovered a second-half fumble that contributed to the team’s exciting but aborted comeback.
After playing another positive, aggressive game, Newsome had to leave with a concussion and did not return. The injury came early in the third quarter and really affected the defense.
A player like Newsome may play the game too hard; he’s just not built for the physicality that he tries to play with.
Playing too hard doesn’t seem like something you want to tell an athlete competing at this or any level, but if it keeps taking you off the field, you may have to learn to play smarter. Newsome finished with 3 total tackles and a pass defensed.
Banks played another stellar cover game on the edges, and the coaches eventually moved him to cover the Saints’ best receiver, Chris Olave, after Newsome left the game.
Banks finished with 4 total tackles and another pass defensed as his coverage game continues to thrive in this aggressive scheme.
Put Banks in a zone, and he’s not the same player. Put him in the face of the opponent’s best receiver, and he’s psyched.
Unlike Newsome, Banks has the goods to hold up in a physical game, even though he does NOT play a physical game. If only he and Newsome could trade personalities.
The defense’s Top Dawg continues to play fine up and down the line of scrimmage. When a tackle needs to be made, and several others shy away, count on Phillips to step in and do the dirty work.
He recorded 4 more tackles this week, but he got lost in coverage in the end zone and gave up a fourth-down touchdown that really hurt.
Phillips was also beaten deep on a second-half all-out blitz, but the pass was overthrown. He did well to run with his man rather than grab him, and the blitz forced the quarterback into an early throw, ergo the miss.
After Newsome went down with a concussion, Jones got all of Newsome’s snaps and was eventually targeted on a fade to Olave, who hauled in the perfect pass despite Jones’ tight coverage; Jones just missed knocking the ball away.
It’s tough to criticize Jones’ coverage here. We thought he played well otherwise.
Tying for the team lead with 9 total tackles, the team’s top safety played a quiet game, mostly a deep contain game that kept the Saints’ receivers in front of him.
He is a real asset whenever the defense calls one of those zero max-blitz things, as he is so alert and plays with such great instinct that the offense rarely beats the coverage.
A bunch of his tackles came early in run-support contain while the Saints gouged the defense on the ground.
Getting the start, Pinnock was sharp on several of his early blitzes (a Pinnock specialty). In fact, we thought his alertness in coverage was a big plus for the Giants defense. He forced the second-half fumble and finished with 2 tackles and 1 pass defensed.
We’d have to say Pinnock is more of a coverage safety than a run-support one. His fall-off missed tackle on the Alvin Kamara 31-yard touchdown catch-and-run — a boundary tackle Pinnock had to make — should have been just a 3-yard gain.
Instead, it gave the Saints the third-quarter lead, and they never looked back.
The uber-aggressive Washington, a blood brother in style to Dru Phillips, finished with 4 solo tackles, and each one seemed big. It’s hard not to like the way that Washington plays this game; not just hard, but fast. If he were just a few inches taller, he’d be an unquestioned starter in this league.

title: Harbaugh Leaves Door Open to Quarterback Change as Giants Weigh Winston, McCarthy
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh, in his Monday video call with reporters, said the team is currently “working through” its options on whether to stick with Jameis Winston at quarterback or switch to J.J. McCarthy. McCarthy played an impressive 11-plus minutes in the fourth quarter of the team’s 34-27 Week 6 loss to the Saints and nearly erased a 24-point deficit.
“I would say absolutely like every other personnel decision we make, what gives us the best chance to win the football game at this given time, or what combination of players and schemes and things like that give us the best chance to, in this case, move the ball, score points, protect the football, et cetera,” Harbaugh said when asked what goes into the decision.
The fact that Harbaugh hasn’t come out and endorsed Winston as the team's starter moving forward suggests a switch to McCarthy is very much on the table.
McCarthy’s skill set is believed to be a closer fit for the playbook the Giants built for injured starter Jaxson Dart. He showed some of that on Sunday with his mobility, forcing the Saints’ run defense to account for him as a threat to run.
Winston has been good enough to get the Giants to a 2-1-1 record as a starter since taking over for Dart full time in Week 3. For Harbaugh, though, it sounds like what he sees in the current situation carries more weight than Winston’s body of work.
“You take all that into account, absolutely,” he said. “Jameis has done a great job in so many ways, and I just admire him and respect him for it. He’s helped us win games and did what he had to do to win games, and that’s something you value very much.”
There is never a perfect moment for a personnel switch, regardless of the position. In the case of the Giants’ quarterback spot, Harbaugh admitted there is a balance between urgency and a player’s readiness.
“To me, that’s got to be maybe the main thing. You can never be ready enough. You just got to go out there and play. That’s one part of it,” he said.
“But the other part of it is you got to be able to be successful and protect yourself. If it’s an injury-type situation, you’ve got to be able to protect yourself. If it’s a performance-type situation, you’ve got to be able to perform at a high level, give yourself a chance to be successful, but also the team, right, to be successful.
“So, with a quarterback, what kind of a grasp does he have on all the things he’s going to need to do with just operating the offense, and understanding the terms and its cadences and the checks and all those kinds of things, and to what degree are you able to do all those things? Is it enough to run your offense? And that’s something that we have been grappling with.”
Given the struggles of the Giants’ offense and, in particular, a running game that doesn’t have a Derrick Henry-type back, the temptation to move to the more mobile McCarthy might be too hard to resist.
“Yeah, I’m sure that it’s not a revelation for the Texans or anybody else that if we go that way, that opens up some things that we wouldn’t be doing with Jameis, for sure,” Harbaugh said, noting that the offense is still “a work in progress.”
“There are some things that Jameis does that hit his strengths. So, J.J.’s definitely a better runner, scrambler, those kinds of things, although Jameis has made some scramble plays. So, both guys are capable of doing different things, but that’s definitely part of it.”

title: Giants vs. Saints Film Review: Player-by-Player Takeaways From Week 6
full_text:
The New York Giants offense got itself into another jam this week, this time against a New Orleans Saints team that came in with the league’s 30th-ranked run defense and a host of question marks.
But the Giants' inability to run the ball on offense played right into the Saints’ hands. While Big Blue rallied in the fourth quarter and nearly pulled off a comeback, it still wasn't enough, and it’s fair to say it shouldn't have come down to that.
Then again, that’s what happens when the offense becomes one-dimensional, and you put too much on a quarterback with a specific set of skills that, at least in this case, wasn’t enough to drive the team across the finish line.
It’s not all on Jameis Winston, whose status as the starting quarterback moving forward is in jeopardy. But the Giants clearly need to make decisions if they want to keep their season from going completely off the rails.
Let’s dive into this week’s player-by-player grades, some of which are encouraging, and most of which should worry a team trying to protect first place in the NFC East.
After this week’s choppy performance, the Jameis Winston era has very likely come to an end. Despite leading his offense to a second-quarter 10-0 lead, Winston left too much on the field.
Right off the bat, on his third pass, Winston missed Isaiah Likely, who had run an economical short middle route into open space. If Winston throws the ball where it’s supposed to go, Likely is still running. Instead, the throw was behind the tight end, and a missed opportunity became a punt and one of many uninspired moments.
Winston bounced back with an efficient, 12-play touchdown drive that gave the Giants an early 7-0 lead. A field goal drive made it 10-0 at the two-minute warning, but Winston’s teammates let the lead slip to 10-10 by halftime.
A parade of procedure penalties derailed his first possession in the third quarter, and then Winston was intercepted on his next two drives, which contributed mightily to a 34-10 deficit.
Winston was then subbed out for J.J. McCarthy, who led the inspired comeback that will likely send Winston back to a backup role.
One problem with Winston’s game is his lack of mobility and foot speed. He’s pretty much a statue in the pocket and cannot threaten the defense with his feet, which lets defenses tee off and attack the line of scrimmage, knowing exactly where he’s going to be.
His game lacks variety, which makes his offense much easier to defend. It’s one thing if you’re a pocket passer with top-shelf arm talent, but Winston’s talent is only ordinary.
His release is deliberate at best, and his accuracy is inconsistent. Winston finished this week with a pedestrian 14-of-26 for 152 yards, one touchdown, two interceptions, and four sacks.
It’s probably best that he takes the sacks rather than force throws into traffic, but he is what he is, a limited pocket passer with loads of guts and faith in himself. His limitations make him one of the better backup quarterbacks in the league, but he’s not a long-term starter.
The second-half arrival of this talented thrower was fun to watch, with McCarthy showing off the legit arm talent that made him a top-10 pick.
Down three scores in a likely blowout, McCarthy came out slinging and injected late-game excitement with some big-time throws to a variety of receivers.
We liked that he moved the ball around to all of his receivers, while never ignoring the “Big Two” of Nabers and Likely.
McCarthy took over the reins at 11:31 in the fourth quarter, and after throwing an interception on a misread with rookie Malachi Fields, his offense scored two touchdowns and a field goal to get within 7 points.
He finished the game just missing on a game-tying pass in the end zone to Likely. He went 11-of-21 for 243 yards in that short time on the field. Beyond the big arm McCarthy loves to show off, he also showed his foot speed by scrambling for 26 yards that set up his offense on that last-gasp drive.
A lack of touch on several of McCarthy’s throws is a legit red flag, but otherwise we liked how he moved in the pocket, stood tall, and threw the ball with accuracy and snap downfield. There doesn’t seem to be a throw he cannot make or attempt.
If McCarthy isn’t named next week’s starter, we’d be stunned.
Getting this week’s start, Harris did very little to inspire. Two of his four touches had no chance, but he could have made yards after contact on the other two and didn’t.
Harris pass-blocked reliably, but he didn’t do anything with the ball in his hands. We really don’t like how he tends to run so upright, though considering he had consecutive 1,000-yard rushing seasons, it clearly works for him. Then again, he had better run blocking in those years, so maybe there’s a tradeoff there?
Getting just six snaps, Skattebo never saw the ball and barely broke a sweat. Although Harbaugh said that Skattebo’s lack of touches weren’t by design, it’s hard to envision the coach seeing the other backs struggle as they did and not wanting to stick to his guns in teaching Skattebo a lesson about accountability.
We support elevating Tracy to the offense’s third-down role, where he seems like a natural fit, especially since he’s committed to the blitz pickup responsibility that is so important.
He rewarded his coaches’ faith by scoring two touchdowns this week, a 17-yard catch-and-run and a 5-yard inside run against contact.
We don’t think Tracy is a bell cow, but he’s definitely got the goods to be a rotation piece and third-down receiver on this team.
Getting a uniform after several weeks on the sidelines, this reliable veteran flashed on a fourth-quarter 19-yard catch-and-run checkdown. He also got three first-half touches for minimal yardage, plus what appeared to be garbage-time touches in the fourth quarter, including a 9-yard run.
Reeling off his third straight uber-productive game (112, 121, and 165 receiving yards in the past three weeks) for a guy who says he’s still not 100% just yet, Nabers seems to be getting better week by week.
Talk about being economical: his 12 catches this week came on just 15 targets. He had zero drops and some big-time yards after contact as he competed like crazy.
He could have done more if the O-line had pass-blocked better. With opposing defenses trying their darndest to keep things in front of them, plenty of room opens up in the intermediate areas for players like Nabers to attack.
His big gains this week were 46, 27, and 18 yards, which kept the chains moving. He was reliable, tough, and physical.
We’re still waiting on the word “explosive” to come to mind when we watch him. There seems to be another gear missing, but the way he’s playing without it is pretty darned impressive.
The one blip on his record this week was the rather lackadaisical approach he took on one of Winston’s interceptions. We would have liked Nabers to be a little more proactive by sticking a hand in there for at least a chance to break up the pass, but other than that, it was another solid showing by the Giants’ top receiver.
The rookie seemed to be the culprit on the J.J. McCarthy interception; Fields went right, the ball went left. A handful of throws in Fields’ direction on the boundary were also tightly covered, one nearly becoming another interception.
Fields isn’t a separation guy; he’s a contested, positional kind of receiver. The Giants really need to figure out how to use him best. We think he’s more effective in the middle of the field, where his physicality can thrive.
We haven’t seen him run anything deep against press coverage, as the quarterbacks don’t like throwing the ball to well-covered receivers. Fields has to earn that trust with some tough catches.
His two receptions for 19 yards this week came on an uneconomical 8 targets, an ugly percentage. The rookie’s blocking continues to be hit-and-miss, which isn’t good enough.
Getting his weekly “hospital” ball from Jameis Winston, Mooney had a chance at a tough catch in the middle of the field on…

title: Giants-Saints: The Four Plays That Doomed New York in a 34-27 Loss
full_text:
The New York Giants had all the momentum in an October battle against the New Orleans Saints, only to self-destruct and suffer a stinging loss that showed fans just how far they still need to go to become genuinely respectable. This was the case when these two teams collided in 2025, and it remains true now.
The Giants blew a lead against a flawed Saints squad. While they fought back and nearly pulled off one of the most incredible comebacks in recent NFL history, the attempt fell short when a J.J. McCarthy incompletion on fourth-and-1 sealed a 34-27 defeat .
This game did not come down to just one moment, though. To better understand how the first-place Giants (3-2-1) came up short in a very winnable matchup, let’s take out the microscope and scrutinize the four plays that defined this unsuccessful afternoon.
Thrust into a bigger role after Braxton Berrios’ season-ending foot injury , returner Charlie Jones made a difficult 49-yard reception during New York’s monster fourth quarter. Unfortunately, it wasn’t his most memorable play of the game.
With the Giants due to receive the ball with about 1:18 remaining in the first half, and up 10-3, Jones fumbled on the return and gave New Orleans the shot in the arm it needed. The Saints took over on the Giants’ 28-yard line and tied the score five plays later. What followed was a relentless beating.
After the fumble, New Orleans established control with 31 unanswered points. Momentum eventually swung dramatically back in Big Blue’s favor, but John Harbaugh’s squad never fully recovered from all the self-inflicted damage.
There is a lot of blame to go around, but Jones’ blunder certainly was a key turning point in the outcome.
New York complemented its turnover spree with a penalty-palooza, making for the perfect debacle at MetLife Stadium. Outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux got called for an infraction that encapsulates the lack of discipline this group displayed on Sunday afternoon.
The 25-year-old edge rusher was assessed a roughing-the-passer penalty on first-and-10 from New Orleans’ 41-yard line during the opening drive of the second half. Alvin Kamara scored on a 31-yard reception soon after.
Safeties Jason Pinnock and Jevon Holland missed badly while trying to tackle the longtime Saints running back, an issue that would plague the team throughout the game. Still, one cannot understate the significance of Thibodeaux’s mistake. That error gifted the visitors 15 yards and put the defense in an even more vulnerable spot.
Following back-to-back weeks in which they accrued fewer than 45 penalty yards, the Giants reverted to their old ways. They got slapped with 10 penalties for 73 yards. Yuck.
Fans can question some of the officiating calls, but Thibodeaux’s late hit was one of several slip-ups that should have been avoided.
Trying to shake off three consecutive New Orleans touchdowns, the Giants put together a promising drive in the third. Jameis Winston used both Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely to lead the offense past the Saints’ 40-yard line.
The Giants erased a two-touchdown deficit against the Washington Commanders and could have done the same here.
Instead, Winston threw an interception that plunged New York into a deeper hole. Nabers curiously did not put his hands up or jump for the ball, which was especially odd since he had shown tremendous effort by breaking multiple tackles about a minute earlier.
In any case, New Orleans got the ball at its own 26-yard line with 4:23 left in the quarter and ultimately extended its lead with a 51-yard field goal. Winston would toss another pick and find himself on the bench.
Missed chances have defined the veteran quarterback’s career, and they certainly characterize this loss.
John Harbaugh has helped the Giants begin to develop a new identity, but against the Saints, he did his part to make them look like their old selves.
Cam Skattebo’s limited snaps and zero touches, the latter of which the head coach said was “ not by design ,” was head-scratching enough, but Harbaugh took another risk that did not pay off in Week 6.
Amid a chaotic fourth quarter that saw J.J. McCarthy throw for 243 yards, one touchdown, and one interception, New York actually had a shot to overcome a 24-point deficit and tie or take the lead in the final minute. A prior miscue denied the franchise a legendary finish, however.
Down 34-27 with 2:04 on the clock, and holding two timeouts, the Giants wanted to kick the ball out of the back of the end zone and delay the two-minute warning for one more play. Undrafted rookie Dominic Zvada, known for his big leg at Michigan, failed to produce the requisite power.
Bryce Lance retrieved the ball and returned it five yards, forcing the two-minute warning before the Saints played another snap. The defense did its job, but New York lost about 40 seconds that would have helped on the final drive.
A rushed McCarthy threw an incomplete pass in the end zone on fourth-and-1 in the final seconds, fittingly capping off a Giants slopfest. Harbaugh is not immune to criticism.
Knowing that this 22-year-old posted a rough outing last Sunday and may not be his sharpest, the former special teams coordinator could have instructed Zvada to kick the ball out of bounds. Harbaugh was unwilling to sacrifice the five-yard penalty for the added time.
He may deserve credit for trusting his kicker, but the consequences of that faith were severe. Luckily, this team resides in a substandard NFC East, and the Giants rarely get to learn from crushing losses while still in first place .

title: Winners and Losers From Giants’ Wild 34-27 Loss to the Saints
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ hype train finally went off the tracks on Sunday, as they lost a winnable game to the New Orleans Saints, 34-27.
Although they fought back to close the scoring gap, it wasn’t enough. In retrospect, there may have been signs of trouble even before this game, in their narrow wins over the Tennessee Titans and Arizona Cardinals, and the same problems resurfaced in a tie with the Washington Commanders.
That said, Big Blue remains in first place and did not lose ground in the division thanks to losses by the Cowboys and Eagles. The Giants might have even found fresh legs at quarterback, but a painful afternoon of football shows the John Harbaugh effect isn’t always a given.
It’s time to sift through the good and the bad as we assign our winners and losers in this ugly NFC battle.
Aside from a puzzling decision not to make a play on the ball during a Jameis Winston interception, Giants star wide receiver Malik Nabers was once again excellent. He matched a career high with 12 receptions and totaled a walloping 165 yards, eclipsing the 100-yard mark for a third straight game.
He helped New York mount a miraculous comeback and showed his pre-injury elusiveness. Nabers broke three tackles at one point, displaying strength beyond what his 6-foot frame suggests. The 23-year-old is not just back. He is one of the NFL’s most dangerous receivers.
The other half of this superb offensive duo is also one of the best players at his position through six weeks. Isaiah Likely has notched at least six catches, 90-plus yards, and one touchdown in consecutive games.
He has been clutch as a pass-catcher , using his reliable hands to extend drives. Even with ongoing questions at quarterback, the Giants’ aerial attack should remain competent as long as Likely provides notable production as a receiving option.
Big Blue was a big mess on run defense, surrendering 175 rushing yards and 4.6 yards per carry. DJ Reader offered some nice moments amid the onslaught.
The 32-year-old defensive tackle recorded seven stops , per Pro Football Focus, highlighted by a terrific tackle on Alvin Kamara near the goal line. He also temporarily kept six points off the board, an impressive achievement that will get lost in the shuffle following all the disarray.
Reader is shaping up as a gem of a free-agent signing, but he is not enough to fix the squad’s perennial problems against the run.
A case could be made here for Jason Pinnock, as his forced fumble was a catalyst for the nearly successful comeback effort. Instead, fellow safety Jevon Holland gets the nod after looking active again following a relatively quiet Week 5.
Holland denied end-zone access to Saints quarterback Tyler Shough, played tight coverage on tight end Juwan Johnson, and allowed just two receptions for 13 yards . While both Holland and Pinnock were discombobulated on a 31-yard Kamara TD early in the third quarter, they both produced their share of positive plays.
Holland was a particularly formidable presence in a secondary that has been better than expected.
Jameis Winston’s lack of mobility in the RPO game might very well spell the end of his tenure as the Giants’ starting quarterback, especially as the rushing game continues to struggle.
Enter J.J. McCarthy, who brings that dimension to the game. Despite throwing one interception and nearly tossing another, the young signal-caller put up a staggering offensive output in the fourth quarter. He completed 11-of-21 passes for 243 yards and one TD, while adding 26 yards on the ground.
Simply put, McCarthy helped bring an ailing squad back to life. We can focus on the poor throws or the brutal sack he took, but the former No. 10 overall pick was gutsy and mobile, looked like a better version of himself, and likely earned a start moving forward.
Did Jameis Winston take his final snap as QB1 for the Giants this season? Harbaugh refused to answer that question after the game, but it is hard to imagine the veteran gunslinger getting the nod against the Houston Texans next Sunday.
Winston threw for 152 yards, tossed two picks, and absorbed four sacks on the day. Although the offensive line made him work at times, he still exercised poor judgment far too often. He gets a little leeway on his first interception considering Nabers should have done more to help prevent it, but Winston’s second one was awful.
Winston still has plenty to offer the locker room, to be clear. He is an outstanding vocal leader who can keep teammates energized and focused. He can also make an impact when called upon.
That said, Winston may not be the right man to lead this offense going forward, especially against better pass-rushing teams, where he tends to get more skittish than one might like to see.
We had no problem with how Harbaugh handled the Cam Skattebo situation by reducing the running back’s snaps to just six for the day and, whether by design or not, not putting the ball in his hands. Harbaugh runs a meritocracy, and if you don’t do your job, you don’t get game snaps, end of story.
This is a similar approach he took with center John Michael Schmitz and safety Tyler Nubin, to name a few. So expecting an exception for Skattebo, who has a fumbling issue that needs to be fixed, isn’t fair.
That said, a few developments from this game didn’t sit well with us. For one, the Giants’ special teams unit again had only 10 players on the field , the second time this season. That’s simply inexcusable.
The second thing we didn’t like is this running back rotation. We get that Harbaugh is looking for a guy to step up and take the bull by the horns, but how exactly is a running back supposed to step up if he isn’t allowed to get into a rhythm?
For that to happen, there needs to be a degree of taking the good runs with the bad, and right now Harbaugh’s criteria for that seem muddied, at least outside the building.
There was also the decision to have kicker Dominic Zvada launch the ball into the back of the end zone before the two-minute warning when it might have been smarter just to let him boot the ball out of bounds.
No time would have come off the clock in that situation, and field position may not have mattered since New York had to force a three-and-out regardless.
As the team’s head coach, all of these issues fall under his umbrella.
Jones left an imprint as a wide receiver, making a circus-like catch with less than six minutes remaining. Still, he squandered his team’s momentum on special teams when he fumbled a return late in the first half, giving a scuffling Saints offense a prime opportunity to tie the score at 10, erasing the Giants’ lead, which they never regained.
It’s too easy to point fingers at the Giants running backs for the team’s lethargic run game, but the offensive line has to take its share of the blame, too.
We’re talking about a unit that faced the league’s 30th-ranked run defense entering the game, yet the Giants’ offensive front struggled to open holes for its backs.
Big Blue had 20 rushing attempts in this game, and three runs were tackles for loss. The Giants finished with just 84 yards on the ground, and the numbers look worse once you subtract the yardage gained by quarterback J.J. McCarthy and wide receiver Darnell Mooney, who had the only runs of 10-plus yards on the day.
The running backs had a dismal showing and got very little help from their blockers up front.

title: Faria's Focus Week 7: 5 Final Thoughts From Jets' Disappointing Loss to Patriots
full_text:
It's hard to determine what the Jets are this season. Their record, now 2-4 after a loss to the Patriots, makes it clear that they aren't very good .
But based on how the team looked last season, the quality of play has greatly improved. They have competed in every contest this season, and even when they were outplayed, they found a way to keep the game close.
So what are the 2026 Jets? Just another year of bad football? Or an up-and-coming team going through clear growing pains through their improvement.
After New York's 26-19 loss to the Patriots, it's time to give my final thoughts from last week regarding where the team is, what the Jets could be, and other takeaways as we head into Week 7.
If you told most Jets fans that at the start of the season the team would be 2-4, but would have lost three of those games by one score each, would they be happy? For a fanbase that hasn't seen a playoff appearance in 15 years, most probably wouldn't.
But after a three-win season in 2025, the main push from the fanbase was to see competitive football. They wanted to see a team that could compete with some of the top rosters and not get blown out by others.
For the most part, the Jets are doing exactly that. And somehow, the franchise still seems to screw iy up.
The biggest frustration for Jets fans has to be based on the fact that the team is playing a lot better than they were probably expected to be this year. There have also been moments when the team looks like it could actually pull off upsets in some of its losses, including last week against New England.
But key issues continue to arise . Coaching mistakes, player breakdowns, and mental mistakes have all come at the worst possible time.
Consider this: the Jets are seventh-best in the league in offensive EPA before they cross midfield. They are dead last in EPA after they get into their opponents' territory. It's a sign of the potential this group has as a collective unit, but also the reality of them still finding ways to struggle at the worst possible times.
There's really no other way to put this. In Week 2's loss to the Packers, the Jets' coaching staff made several mistakes, but the players didn't exactly do enough on their own. A Week 3 loss to Detroit had more to do with the injuries suffered in the game than anything else. Week 4 was an organizational failure.
New York's loss to New England was unequivocally a coaching loss . The Jets failed to take points on two separate drives in the first half. The play calls were also a negative, as they didn't take advantage of key parts of the field that the Jets had been targeting all game.
Jets head coach Aaron Glenn has improved the defense as a play-caller. There is no denying that. But the offense's inability to operate functionally in a two-minute situation, and the defense giving up eight third downs on 15 tries, is never something that is just about the players.
Glenn's whole calling card is being someone who can rally a locker room together and can call a great defense. But how long will both points continue if they are unable to get each in-game decision right throughout a game?
In New England, it seemed that the Jets' coaching staff were the reason they lost that game, not the players. And it could only get worse if things don't improve.
Jets linebacker Jamien Sherwood has been a lightning rod for the fanbase's frustration over the last two years. After becoming one of the highest-paid linebackers in the sport during the 2025 offseason, Sherwood struggled mightily under heightened expectations. This season didn't start much better either.
Over the last three weeks, though, a switch has been turned for Sherwood.
In Sunday's loss to the Patriots, he recorded a team-high 11 tackles, had a quarterback hit, and recovered a fumble. His best play, though, came when the Patriots were seemingly running away with the contest after Drake Maye completed a 39-yard pass. Sherwood didn't give up on the play and ran a total of 50 yards downfield to force a fumble, giving New York a chance to get back in the game.
That hustle play endeared Sherwood not only to the coaches but to the fanbase as well. The 26-year-old linebacker is back to being an above-average player at the position and one of the better cover linebackers this season , per Pro Football Focus .
It seems like his confidence is only growing as well. If he continues to play as he did against New England, the Jets will be thrilled with their future at linebacker.
The best offenses in the NFL know how to adapt their system and scheme to the roster, not to who is coaching the team. New York does not do that, though. Since Glenn was first hired, the team has pushed the notion that they want to be a run-first offense.
There's no issue with that, of course. The problem comes with the fact that isn't what the Jets' current roster is built to do. New York has run the ball effectively in each of the last three games. The point totals in those games?
Well below the league average. New York may want to be a run-first team, but their collection of receivers and tight ends shows they are more than capable of being a pass-first unit that uses short throws as an extension of the run game.
It is clear the offense has struggled to get the ball to their full collection of weapons in the passing attack. The way to fix that isn't more plays or just simply better execution. It's about shifting the game plan in a way that maximizes the talent on the roster.
Nothing D'Angelo Ponds is dealing with this year is very fair. At Indiana, the 5'8" corner played primarily on the outside with sparing nickel snaps. Since being drafted in the second round by the Jets, those nickel snaps have increased as his primary way to get on the field.
It would be one thing if Ponds had a full training camp and was struggling. But an injury suffered in July kept him off the team for the entire camp session, including preseason action. The last couple of weeks have been Ponds' first game action since his final game in Indiana.
It's no wonder why the stats aren't kind to him. Ponds has been targeted four times and has given up three receptions for 48 yards and a touchdown on just 17 coverage snaps. He's also been penalized twice.
New York is not concerned about Ponds, nor should they be. He hasn't gotten the same kind of ramp-up period that thousands of rookies were given. If anything, his struggles this season should be considered nothing more than a gap year—one that isn't judged too harshly on the Jets or the player.
Next season will be a big test, but it's hard to judge Ponds fairly when he hasn't received the same process as others.

title: Biggest Decision Aaron Glenn Got Wrong vs. Patriots (And What Needs to Change in Week 7)
full_text:
The Week 5 win over the Browns was short-lived on Sunday as the Jets came crashing back down in a 26-19 loss to the Patriots that served as another reminder that Gang Green's season is still in deep trouble unless something changes in a hurry.
Even though the Jets were without RB1 Breece Hall (right quad) once again and still faced some injury concerns going into the Week 6 AFC East matchup, they could not have asked for a better start, with points on their opening drive and a quick three-and-out defensively. It was also clear that running back Braelon Allen was going to be utilized again in place of Hall .
While Allen did his part with 17 carries for 78 yards and two receptions for 26 yards, a lot of the blame for Sunday's loss falls on the shoulders of Aaron Glenn and the rest of the coaching staff. Sure, offensive coordinator Frank Reich's continued struggles getting WR1 Garrett Wilson more involved in the offense are highly concerning, and his egregious play-calling in short-yardage situations was costly, but a familiar tactic continues to overshadow Glenn on the sidelines.
Game management and end-of-half execution have plagued Glenn since his Jets tenure began last season, and those issues do not seem to be going away soon.
Look no further than a challenge he made late in the opening quarter, when the Jets held a 3-0 lead, which came back to bite him later in the half and set the tone for a lack of execution the rest of the way .
After what was initially called a nine-yard completion from quarterback Drake Maye to wide receiver A.J. Brown, Glenn decided to challenge the play and ended up successfully winning the challenge to wipe away the nine-yard gain. However, Maye responded on the next play with a 42-yard touchdown strike to WR Romeo Doubs (h/t NFL), and the Patriots took a 7-3 lead.
42-yard touchdown from Maye to Doubs! NYJvsNE on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/tKpDzX136o
Up to that point, the Patriots had gone three-and-out and had a nine-yard catch overturned in their first four plays of the game. To be fair, this specific challenge decision did not cause the Jets to lose this game by itself, but it certainly changed how Glenn coached the remainder of the first half.
Later in the second quarter, when the Patriots still held a 7-3 lead, QB Geno Smith was ruled short on a fourth-and-one sneak with the ball on the Patriots' 39-yard line. Given the spot on the field and how close Smith was on the play, this would have been a more challenge-worthy moment for Glenn to throw the flag, but the team would have been down a timeout and a challenge if he were unsuccessful.
That challenge earlier in the game completely impacted his decision-making the rest of the half, and this was a reminder of how bad that decision was on a play that had little impact on the game to begin with.
The Patriots would go on to add a field goal and another TD before the half, while New York went three-and-out and once again struggled in end-of-half situations. To be fair, the Jets came out of the locker room with a TD or field goal on four of their five second-half possessions and even forced a pair of Patriots fumbles defensively. The biggest hiccup was a costly interception from Smith—his first of the season—with the ball across midfield, trailing by 10 in the fourth quarter.
While he later clarified that he was conceptually speaking about the offense's mindset, assuming the defense forced a stop out of the half, Glenn even went viral during his halftime interview with CBS Sports sideline reporter Aditi Kinkhabwala when he said (h/t Ari Meirov), "The good thing is we get the ball," although the Patriots had already deferred to the second half.
#Jets HC Aaron Glenn told CBS coming out of halftime that his team was getting the ball to start the second half. One problem: The #Patriots were getting the ball to begin the half. pic.twitter.com/bqiDfGKI97
While you can also point to Glenn's lack of defensive alignment adjustments and the decision to keep the offense on the field twice in the first half instead of attempting a pair of field goals, the early challenge definitely stood out as Glenn's biggest miscue in Sunday's game, and it certainly impacted how he coached the game from there on out.
As the Jets return home to MetLife Stadium for back-to-back games against the Dolphins and Raiders, their season and Glenn's future in Gotham could be hanging in the balance with a 2-4 record. It is no secret that New York has struggled against AFC East competition dating back to the 2011 season, but the game against an 0-5 Dolphins team tied for the lowest-scoring offense (14 ppg) is a clear must-win.
The Jets were just 3-of-10 on third down against the Patriots, as well as a combined 0-of-5 on fourth-down and red-zone opportunities. They cut back on the costly penalties with just five for 35 yards, but the lack of execution throughout the game and inability to finish drives on both sides of the ball continue to prove costly for Gang Green.
Granted, the Dolphins only lost by one score to the undefeated Vikings and the Bengals in their last two games, but this offense has only scored 20 points once in five games and shouldn't scare the Jets by any means. That said, Glenn must learn from his mistakes and improve his game management going forward if he wants to keep his job and show that he is willing to adapt under the highest pressure.

title: Newly Released RB Could Help Jets Continue to Survive Breece Hall's Absence
full_text:
Although the Jets were a lot more competitive against the Patriots this time around than they were the last time the two divisional opponents squared off last season, they still came up short in a 26-19 loss that dropped them to 2-4 on the season.
While offensive coordinator Frank Reich continues to be one of the biggest letdowns to begin the 2026 season due to an inability to distribute the ball to his best players, third-year running back Braelon Allen has been a bright spot over the last two weeks as RB1 Breece Hall recovers from the right quad injury he suffered in the Week 3 loss to the Lions.
However, while Allen was a stud in the Week 6 loss to the Patriots with 17 carries for 78 yards and two catches for 26 yards, the Jets only had 97 combined rushing yards and provided no balance at all to support Allen's effort. A recent development on Tuesday, though, could present an opportunity for Gang Green to address that issue.
According to ESPN and NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport, "the Giants are releasing RB Najee Harris."
Source: The #Giants are releasing RB Najee Harris, another RB shakeup. pic.twitter.com/N9C5GIIpeh
While the sixth-year back struggled in just five games with the Giants, with 99 yards on 31 carries and one lost fumble, he could be a complementary option alongside Allen and take some of the load off the third-year RB in Gang Green.
Allen has been good in relief of Hall, but Sunday was the RB1's third consecutive game missed due to injury , and Isaiah Davis has not looked good at all in limited action.
If anything, Harris deserves some attention if the Jets want some more stability in the backfield if Hall's injury keeps him out a little longer.
While Harris has not been his usual self since he suffered a torn left Achilles during Week 3 of the 2025 season with the Chargers, this is a player who rushed for at least 1,000 yards and six rushing TDs in his first four NFL seasons with the Steelers, all while never missing a game during that stint.
At 6'1", 232 lbs, Harris would give the Jets another bruising option in the backfield who could step in for short-yardage and goal-line situations. He may only have an average of 3.9 yards per carry throughout his career, but Harris has only committed five total fumbles and is an elite pass-protecting RB.
Given the struggles the offensive line has had giving quarterback Geno Smith enough time in the pocket, Harris could be a huge safety net when a first down needs to be picked up.
Assuming Hall remains out of action, Harris could come in and take at least eight to 10 snaps away from Allen to keep him fresh for the duration of the game. After all, Davis was given an uptick in playing time with seven carries against the Patriots, but he only had 16 yards— a huge disappointment .
New York's grades were all over the place after the frustrating loss to New England, but Allen has already demonstrated why he deserves to remain a key contributor on this offense even when Hall returns to action. His physicality has been on display each week, and it is clear how he fits into the Jets' offense moving forward .
That said, there is no guarantee when Hall will be back. He may return for Sunday's game against the Dolphins, or he may sit out another game or two as he looks to get back to full strength. At the same time, this upcoming stretch at home against the Dolphins and Raiders is a crucial point in the Jets' season, and they could use any help they can get, even if it comes in the form of someone like Harris.
Considering how quiet Harris has been since the Achilles injury last season, his stock has plummeted from what it once was. He was only playing on a one-year, $1.215 million contract (h/t Spotrac ) with the Giants, so the Jets could sign him to a team-friendly, low-risk veteran minimum deal if they choose to. They could even sign him to the practice squad.
Regardless of when Hall returns, Harris would give the Jets a three-headed approach in the backfield with no salary cap strain. Davis has already been someone who could be on the trade block , and his lack of production so far backs that up. Hall may also not be 100%, or at least in a more limited role, when he comes back, so having a more proven body to turn to could prove beneficial.
There is no doubt that Allen has earned himself some additional playing time, but there is still no reliable RB3 on this roster through the first six games. Should the Jets look into signing Harris, it could add some insurance in the backfield and provide a complementary approach to give Hall and Allen a breather when the snaps are coming the offense's way.
