title: Frank Reich Headlines the Jets' 3 Biggest Letdowns to Begin the 2026 Season
full_text:
It's hard to truly judge what the Jets are as an organization right now .
The team is playing much better than they were last year. An improved quality of play was something the Jets needed to show, and they have clearly done that. The problem, though, is that with each passing week, key issues show up at the worst possible time and cost the roster a win.
In Sunday's 26-19 loss to the Patriots, New York's coaching had a lot to do with the defeat. At 2-4, there's certainly reason for optimism, but many Jets fans feel let down by the team's lack of wins.
Today, we dissect each of the three biggest letdowns to begin the Jets' season, beginning with...
No person has been a bigger disappointment this season than Jets offensive coordinator Fran Reich.
The Jets hired him to run their offense because 1) he has past experience dealing with a lot of talent at receiver and running back, 2) because he has a history of developing quarterbacks and 3) because he's a steady hand for a young overall unit.
In each way, he has failed at the reason why he was brought in. None so more than the first point.
Reich was thrilled when the Jets drafted Kenyon Sadiq with the 16th overall pick in the draft, even though it was the second tight end taken by the team in the first two rounds of back-to-back drafts. He believed that he had a plan to get the ball to everyone through the air, including first-round rookie Omar Cooper Jr. and star receiver Garrett Wilson.
The results on Sunday? New York's tight end room made five catches for 45 yards. Wilson saw just six targets and four receptions . Head coach Aaron Glenn's response after the game?
The answer wasn't good enough. It showed Reich has been unable to get his best players the ball consistently. And it's a reason why the team's offensive unit has struggled. New York's offensive grades are in the bottom 10 in almost every category except for turnovers.
A coach who is incapable of scheming his best players open and getting a plethora of targets to their stars is one who is going to struggle. So far, Reich has been a massive letdown .
Last season, the Jets' special teams unit was the best in football at all levels. They tied the league lead in return touchdowns; they had an excellent rookie punter and an aging kicker seemed to turn back the clock for one year.
This year has been a different story. This year has been nothing but a letdown.
In Sunday's loss to New England, kicker Jason Sanders was 4-for-4 on field goals. Austin McNamara punted only twice.
And yet the group was a massive disappointment. That's because kick returner Kene Nwangwu averaged just 21 yards per return. The kick return unit also gave up over 25 yards per kick return, including a 37-yard return to give the Patriots a short field. Making matters worse, the Jets even gave up a 10-yard punt return.
This group needs to play a lot better, and Glenn knows it.
The Jets aren't good enough have their offense and defense play solid and still find a way to win games. It has to be all three levels. And so far, that hasn't been the case.
New York signed captain Demario Davis in free agency to stabilize the defense and provide quality play at the linebacker position . Leadership-wise, Davis is as strong as ever.
On the field, though, the 37-year-old hasn't just lost a step. He's almost unplayable.
Right now, Davis is the eighth-worst-graded linebacker (50.0) in football this season , according to Pro Football Focus . He's given up a 103.4 passer rating when targeted in coverage and has been charged with 9 missed tackles over the course of the year.
On Sunday, Davis recorded seven tackles and one pass deflection. He was a liability in coverage and wasn't quick enough against the run. In total, his return has been a major misfire so far.

title: One Thought on Every Top Jets Rookie Heading Into Week 7
full_text:
Not a ton has gone right for the Jets so far this season. The team is 2-4 and has been outcoached in key moments of almost every game.
Despite the doom and gloom, one part of the Jets should have fans thrilled about the future.
New York's rookie class has excelled in several key areas. The Jets spent three first-round picks on pass catchers and pass rushers. In the later rounds, it was about bolstering the defense in April's draft. The early returns couldn't be better. Almost every rookie has come away with a standout game , play, or stretch that underscores Gang Green's bright future.
Here's what the Jets are saying about some of their top rookies' early success.
The mark of a special defensive player is that, when an opposing team is taking him away from making an impact, he's still able to make a play that can change the outcome of the game .
New England chipped David Bailey for most of the day on Sunday. He wasn't able to do much as a pass rusher. That said, he still made an impact, forcing a fumble early in the third quarter (h/t NFL) to give the Jets a chance to tie the game.
David Bailey forces the fumble, @nyjets ball! NYJvsNE on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/VMzO9ynfhK
Head coach Aaron Glenn was encouraged (but not surprised) by what he saw.
"That's something again that we felt like he would be able to do for us when it comes to being disruptive," Glenn said. " The thing is, we hope that we continue to get those things."
The fact that the Jets offense could only muster a field goal is irrelevant. The second overall pick remains an excellent player who is only getting better.
The 30th overall pick saw action in the first quarter of the first game of the season for the Jets, caught a 30-yard pass, and promptly sprained his ankle. He had been on short-term injured reserve for the last month.
On Sunday, Omar Cooper Jr. played his first full game in the NFL . The stat line? Six catches, 103 yards, one touchdown. He could have had two, but his first score of the day was called back because of a penalty.
This was an awesome game from a really good college player. If Cooper continues playing like this, he will be a major weapon in New York's offense.
When discussing D'Angelo Ponds, context is extremely important .
This is a player who spent most of his college career as an outside corner. Despite his size, he was one of the best in college football. Then, he was drafted by the Jets, who wanted him to learn the nickel—a completely different position in the secondary.
Unfortunately, Ponds misses his entire rookie training camp, so there aren't any reps to learn and build off of. Instead, he is thrust into game and practice scenarios without a true baseline on what to do for his new position.
That explains Ponds's struggles, right? So far, he has allowed 3 catches for 48 yards and a TD on 4 targets despite playing just 17 coverage snaps, and he also has two penalties. His 25.0 coverage grade ranks dead last among 160 cornerbacks , according to Pro Football Focus .
Still, Glenn has a logical take on the situation.
"When it comes to playing time, I always say you have to earn it," Glenn said. "You have players playing now that are fighting to continue to play. (D'Angelo is) playing nickel and outside corner. But each week he's getting better and better."
Ponds was targeted whenever he was on the field on Sunday. It's not fair to truly judge him until he gets a feel for the defensive scheme and for the NFL in general.
It was a quiet game for the fourth-round rookie defensive tackle. Darrell Jackson Jr. had a quarterback hit and three tackles, but wasn't as productive as he was against the Browns in Week 5. That said, Jets defensive coordinator Brian Duker is still high on the rookie defender.
"(Darrell) has grown a lot,"  Duker said. "He has certainly always been big and strong, but now he's kind of doing a better job of playing with the technique and doing those things."
Jackson is graded as an above-average interior lineman for the Jets so far this season, with a 62.6 PFF grade that ranks 51st among 128 qualified players at his position. As the year goes on, he is going to get plenty of chances to stand out.
Sunday was a quiet day for Kenyon Sadiq in the same way it was for Jackson. The first-round tight end caught just one pass for 12 yards. He was also targeted a second time, but the pass was poor and intercepted on the play.
Still, the word on Sadiq is the same one the Jets have been talking about for over a month:
The Jets need to do a better job of distributing the ball to their tight ends, but Sadiq remains a quality cog in this offense.

title: Jets Week 6 Awards: 5 Winners After Coming Up Short in Divisional Loss to Pats
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, M.A. — The last time the Patriots and Jets faced off, it was such a blowout that Drake Maye didn't even play the final quarter of action.
On Sunday, the Jets were able to be more competitive, but the outcome didn't change either .
Gang Green failed to take advantage of several opportunities on both sides of the ball, and Maye threw three touchdowns in the Patriots'  26-19 win. The loss bumped the Jets to a 2-4 mark, with their fourth loss in the last five contests.
After every game, we have awards to give out. Let's go to the five biggest ones now.
In Week 2, Kenyon Sadiq recorded 100 receiving yards in a breakout performance. David Bailey's best game came last week against the Browns with three sacks. This week was all about their other first-round rookie.
Omar Cooper Jr. had missed the last four weeks due to an ankle sprain suffered on opening day. There were questions about how good he would be without getting reps over the last several games.
Those questions were answered quickly . Cooper caught six passes and recorded his first 100-yard game to go along with a deep touchdown reception . He could have had two touchdown,s but one recorded in the first quarter was called back due to a penalty.
The rookie Omar Cooper Jr. makes the 48-yard touchdown catch! NYJvsNE on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/y88N5gruHa
Still, Sunday was an awesome debut for Cooper, and even quarterback Geno Smith was impressed.
"I think Omar did a tremendous job of coming back from injury, fought just to get back out there," Geno Smith said. "What he did is showcase who he is. He's a playmaker. He's a guy who finds ways to make catches, and the tough catches, he makes them look easy. Really impressed with the way that he performed and looking forward to building on that."
New York's defensive line was dominated all game. New England recorded 148 yards in the ground and over 5.6 yards per play. Even more alarming was the fact that the Jets were unable to get any pressure on Drake Maye throughout the contest.
That said, two players stood out to me defensively in a positive way : David Bailey and Jamien Sherwood.
Let me explain. While Bailey did not make a major impact as a pass rusher, he still found a way to affect the game in a good way. By forcing a fumble early in the third quarter, Bailey showed he did not have to have a  big game on the stat sheet to make an impact.
Then there was Sherwood. The veteran linebacker struggled for the first four games of the season. But he was very good against the Browns and had his best game in years on Sunday. Sherwood recorded 11 tackles, one for a loss, a quarterback hit, and a fumble recovery.
More importantly, though, he forced a fumble on a deep completion in which he ran from one side of the field to the other to make a play. By not giving up on the play, Sherwood kept New York's hopes alive.
Both Sherwood and Bailey weren't perfect in this game, but it's clear they played with plenty of heart and hustle, which will make their coaching staff happy.
Not every loss is the same. Some games are lost due to bad coaching decisions mixed with poor execution. For a majority of the season, it felt like the Jets' losses came from the coaching staff and players not being good enough together.
That didn't happen on Sunday. The Jets were held back by their coaching staff on Sunday .
Glenn made a number of poor decisions throughout the contest. From challenging a first-down throw in the first quarter in what ended up being a meaningless snap, to denying a field goal and getting stuffed on fourth down, to putting edge rushers in coverage over A.J. Brown, the Jets' head coach made calls that seemingly held the team back throughout the contest.
His offensive coordinator wasn't much better . Frank Reich's scheme looks completely outdated, and it's most prevalent with the team's short-yardage plays. On back-to-back third- and fourth-and-ones deep inside Patriots territory, the Jets opted to run four plays in the teeth of the defense.
It didn't matter that the Patriots aligned to take those runs away. It didn't even matter that Smith was having a good game throwing the ball. Reich wanted to run the ball up the middle. And that killed the offensive momentum in the first half.
Both Reich and Glenn cost the team with their in-game management and play calls. If this continues, some uncomfortable conversations will need to be had across the board for this entire staff.
Here are Smith's numbers so far this season:
All good, right? Sure, but with the talent at his disposal, New York can live with some of the interceptions if it means pushing the ball down the field. At this point, it seems like the Jets have deliberately told him not to put the ball in harm's way and throw more interceptions.
There's reason for that, of course. Coming into the year, Smith led all quarterbacks in interceptions thrown in the last two years combined. Still, his lack of aggression has also impacted the team so far this season.
New York's offense ranks 26th in yards and 27th in points. They have put up under 20 points in each of the last three games. The Jets need to let Smith out of his shell. It's just that simple. Let the quarterback with a big arm make some plays down the field to unlock this group's potential.
The dinking and dunking aren't working because the offense keeps shooting itself in the foot when it matters most.
Smith needs to let it rip.
When is enough, enough for Garrett Wilson? The Jets passed the ball around to several players on offense. Their star receiver, though, only had six targets.
After the game, a visibly frustrated Wilson tried his best to keep the peace in front of reporters.
Let's be clear, though. Wilson isn't signing up to lose another nine or 10 games this season and not be targeted. It should be no mistake that the offense's three best games have come when Wilson was a central focus.
If this continues, some uncomfortable conversations are going to be had with the team's star receiver. It's unclear how much longer he's going to be willing to have games like this.
The Patriots' offensive line was completely banged up going into the contest. Starting right tackle Morgan Moses left the game early as well. One would think the Jets' defensive line should have been able to get consistent pressure on Maye, right?
New England chipped New York's edge rushers because they knew they could contain the team's interior line. The Patriots were proven right. Will McDonald IV and David Bailey were taken out of the game with the chips, and the trio of Jowon Briggs, Harrison Phillips, and T'Vondre Sweat were all non-factors.
It doesn't matter who was on the field. The entire group was a dud, and it's a problem the team signed up for by bringing in run-stopping players instead of guys who could get after the passer.

title: It's Clear How Braelon Allen Should Fit Into the Jets' Offense Once Breece Hall Returns
full_text:
Since star running back Breece Hall went down with a quadriceps injury in Week 3’s loss to the Lions, the Jets have turned to third-year halfback Braelon Allen to shoulder the workload on the ground .
The former Wisconsin Badger has made the most of his opportunity, impressing fans and the coaching staff with his physical running style. In this three-game stretch, including Sunday's loss to the Patriots , Allen has registered 253 rushing yards (averaging 4.6 yards per carry), recorded 10 carries for 10-plus-yard gains, and forced 17 missed tackles.
Despite New York posting a 1-2 record in this span, Allen has been one of the few productive contributors and has put the team in a position to win games.
Even though Allen’s workload will be trimmed down once Hall returns to the lineup, the Jets must find a way to keep him in the game plan.
Over the last two weeks, Allen showcased his bell cow capability.
A prime example is his Week 5 performance against the Browns, where he posted career highs in carries (24) and rushing yards (116). Allen scored the go-ahead touchdown late in the fourth quarter to help New York beat Cleveland 17-12.
It looked like Allen was heading for another dominant performance on the ground against the Patriots, finishing the first half with 65 rushing yards. However, the Jets abandoned Allen in the second half, with him receiving just five touches, while Isaiah Davis ineffectively rushed for 16 yards on seven carries.
With New York down two scores for the majority of the second half, the team leaned on quarterback Geno Smith to move the offense downfield through the air. Ultimately, this proved to be a bad decision, as Allen was the unit's only productive player.
New England didn’t have much of an answer for the 6-foot-1, 250-pound back, as he recorded four rushes of 10-plus yards. Allen even showcased his value as a pass catcher, recording two receptions for 26 yards.
On one of those catches, Allen bulldozed Patriots star safety Kevin Byard III for a 16-yard gain (h/t NFL).
Braelon Allen, grown man strength. NYJvsNE on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bONdE7sDVr
Plays like this show why Allen deserves a consistent role in the offense, even after Hall returns.
When Hall comes back, he’ll reclaim the lead role again, while Allen’s workload will be reduced. However, if there’s one thing offensive coordinator Frank Reich should have learned over the past few weeks , it’s that New York won’t win games if he gives Allen limited reps.
Moving forward, Reich must establish the run and return to the formula they used against the Titans in Week 1. Against Tennessee, the Jets ran the ball on 39 of their 63 plays, with Hall recording 22 carries and Allen adding 10. New York even ran the ball 15 times during a 19-play drive, showcasing its ability to control the game on the ground.
The Jets can also use Allen in the backfield while using Hall—who's averaging an impressive 34 receiving yards per game—more as a pass-catching option.
Although the Jets averaged just 3.9 yards per carry, their willingness to run the football helped open up opportunities for play-action. However, this commitment faded over the following two weeks. Gang Green ran the ball just 27 times on 72 offensive plays against the Packers and 19 times on 61 plays against the Lions.
Meanwhile, Allen received only nine carries combined in those two games, giving him fewer opportunities to help the offense with his physicality.
The Jets don’t necessarily need to return to a run-heavy approach on every drive, but they must find a better offensive balance. Giving Allen eight to 10 carries a game would keep him involved in the game plan, help wear down opposing defenses, and give Hall a breather without taking his role as the lead back.

title: Biggest Reason Why Jets Loss to Patriots Couldn't Be More Obvious
full_text:
The Jets fell to 2-4 after losing 26-19 to the rival Patriots in Week 6. Gang Green is two games below .500, despite being more competitive than in past seasons. The team looks to have taken a step from last season, but one thing has reared its ugly head throughout the Jets' season and led to the loss to the Patriots.
The Jets were trailing 10-3 when they got the ball with 1:46 left in the first half on Sunday afternoon. This pivotal drive gave them a chance to score and go into the half tied or down by only one score. The drive went incompletion, incompletion, and a six-yard pass to Omar Cooper Jr. The Jets gained only six yards and only took 23 seconds off the clock.
Geno Smith and the offense had a chance to dictate how the half ended. Instead, the Jets punted back to the Patriots, who responded with a seven-play touchdown drive that flipped the game on its head.
Drives like this have been an unfortunate pattern for the Jets this season .
In five out of six games this year, New York has received the ball with four minutes or less on the clock. In those five drives, the Jets have yet to score, and two of the failed drives led to points for the opponent.
Their inability to score late in halves has held them back all season , and Week 6 was no exception.
The Jets' offense falls short at the end of the half, but it's not the only time. They also haven't capitalized on turnovers. New York's defense has forced eight turnovers this season, but has only found the end zone once after them. Gang Green has had chances to take over games thanks to their defense, but the offense has continued to fall short.
Whether up or down, turnovers can shift momentum. Scoring touchdowns off those turnovers can change the game. The Jets forced the Patriots to turn the ball over twice in Week 6, once down by seven, once down by 10. Both of the ensuing drives ended with a field goal, not a touchdown, even though New York drove inside the New England 25.
Touchdowns wouldn't necessarily have won the game for the Jets, but they would've forced the Patriots to change how they operated to maintain or regain their lead. The Jets' inability to finish drives has plagued them all season. New York ranks dead last in red-zone touchdowns this season, leaving them chasing teams that score seven when they get into Jets' territory.
The Jets have clearly improved since last year, yet they keep losing games.
In a league where 50.6% of games are decided by one score (h/t Vertize Sports ), these situational issues are even more glaring. The Jets have talked about winning football and a changed culture. Until they fix how they play situational football, more losses like the one to the Patriots will follow head coach Aaron Glenn and his team.

title: Omar Cooper Jr. Is the Difference-Maker the Jets' Offense Desperately Needed
full_text:
A defining theme of the 21st century: the Jets lose to the Patriots. This happened again Sunday, with Gang Green falling 26-19 to their bitter rival.
Even though the team fought hard, missed opportunities on third- and fourth-down–combining for 3-of-12– and poor coaching decisions ultimately led to New York dropping to a frustrating 2-4 record.
Despite the disappointing loss, there were some positives, including rookie receiver Omar Cooper Jr. After missing the last four games on injured reserve due to a high-ankle sprain, the former Indiana Hoosier reminded fans why the Jets traded back into the first round to select him.
Cooper led the team in receptions (6) and receiving yards (103), while also scoring New York’s lone touchdown in the third quarter (h/t NFL). With his performance against the Patriots, he became the fourth Jets rookie to record a 100-yard receiving game in franchise history, joining Kenyon Sadiq, Al Toon and Garrett Wilson on the list.
The rookie Omar Cooper Jr. makes the 48-yard touchdown catch! NYJvsNE on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/y88N5gruHa
To keep its playoff hopes alive, it's safe to say the Jets must continue to utilize Cooper as much as possible moving forward.
The Jets' underwhelming start can be attributed to the offense struggling mightily this season. Under offensive coordinator Frank Reich, the unit ranked 27th in points scored (18.6) and total yards per game (284) entering Week 6.
While Reich’s playcalling has drawn criticism, we can’t place all the blame on him. Injuries to the receiving corps have derailed the unit, with several key playmakers missing time. This has held the offense back, as it ranked 23rd in passing yards per game (190). Additionally, New York hasn’t gotten consistent production from its receivers outside of Wilson.
Entering Week 6, Wilson led the team in receptions (31), receiving yards (374), and touchdowns (3). Behind him are Kenyon Sadiq and Isaiah Williams, who combined for 25 receptions for 297 yards and two touchdowns.
Those numbers go to show that the offense relies heavily on Wilson to create separation and move the ball downfield. But with Cooper back, Gang Green hopes he takes pressure off Wilson and helps the offense move the ball downfield with his speed and playmaking ability.
The rookie playmaker did exactly that against New England, hauling in a 48-yard touchdown and leading the team in yards after the catch with 25 , per Pro Football Focus.
Cooper's ability to generate yards after the catch could also make Geno Smith's life easier. Because the receivers struggle to get open and Smith doesn’t want to throw the ball into harm’s way, he’s held onto the ball too long at times. At times, Smith has held onto the ball too long, partly because the receivers have struggled to create separation.
Rather than depending on Wilson every play, the 14-year veteran can turn to Cooper, who ran a 4.42-second 40-yard dash at the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine. With him back in the fold, Cooper gives Smith an intermediate option to get the ball out quickly and a deep-threat target.
It also gives opposing defenses another playmaker to account for. The 22-year-old helped open the passing game against the Patriots, as Smith threw for 252 passing yards—the second-most this season.
Of course, Cooper alone won’t solve the Jets’ offensive problems. However, if the rookie can build on his strong return, he can become a consistent contributor alongside Wilson and make New York’s passing game more dangerous.
Cooper's first opportunity to build on his big day will come in Week 7 against the Dolphins, who are allowing the sixth-most yards per completion (7.8) while being tied for the seventh-most passing TDs allowed (11) this season.

title: It's Time to Start Worrying About Garrett Wilson's Future with Jets
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, M.A. — It was obvious from the moment the Jets walked off the field on Sunday afternoon.
Gathered in hushed tones, a frustrated Garrett Wilson wasn't happy. The star receiver in New York's offense had just four receptions for 44 yards on just six targets in the team's 26-19 loss to the rival Patriots .
If you ask the Patriots, neutralizing Wilson was always part of the plan. Taking away an opponent's best player has been something the organization is known for.
"Another key was to eliminate (Wilson) from the game, and I think we did that for the most part," Patriots safety Kevin Byard said. "He didn't really affect the game as much as he probably wanted to."
The Patriots' game plan may have been effective, but the Jets and Wilson didn't help themselves either. After a game with minimal impact, Wilson's frustration was apparent, highlighting an ugly thought the Jets will have to deal with.
If the lack of wins and their offensive game plan don't change, is Gang Green facing a point of no return with their star receiver?
Even before the game, the Jets knew the Patriots would try to place their All-Pro cornerback Christian Gonzalez on Wilson for as long as they could. While Gonzalez didn't travel with Wilson for the whole game, he did blanket the star receiver enough that the Jets only targeted him twice in the first three quarters of action.
Afterwards, Wilson wondered if he could have done anything different to help get the ball.
It was easy to see how frustrated Wilson was after the game, though. He didn't have Gonzalez on him for every snap, and he wasn't a key schematic part of the Jets' offense .
As much as the Jets talk about Wilson being a focal point, they do not scheme him open as one.
"We have all the confidence in the world, whoever guards Garrett, that he can win," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "I think, as the game progressed, we started to get him the ball a lot more."
Glenn is correct. After receiving just two targets in the first three quarters, New York targeted Wilson four times in the fourth. The absurdity of that statement, though, is self-explanatory. It shouldn't take that long to make your star player a key part of the game plan.
It's also not rocket science to see that the Jets wanting to spread the ball around to other receivers makes little sense when those receivers aren't doing enough to win games.
The fact of the matter is that Wilson did not find himself covered by Gonzalez throughout the entire game. Even when he was, there were ways to get Wilson the ball without being stuck in coverage. Moving Wilson out in motion, or keeping him in the slot, would have been helpful.
Instead, they seemingly took their best player out of the game by not giving him many chances.
It is not enough for the Jets' coaching staff and quarterback Geno Smith to argue against targeting Wilson because of the other weapons on the team. After Sunday's loss, Smith pointed to how the Patriots were playing as the reason why Wilson didn't get the ball.
"I think our game plan was working the way it should," Smith said. "Again, if we just finish those drives, I think we're talking a lot different."
This is the wrong answer for any starting quarterback with a top receiver, though.
For example, the Seahawks have many strong offensive targets. They don't have any trouble getting the ball to Jaxon Smith-Njigba. The same is true for Puka Nacua with the Rams, or the Texans with Nico Collins, or all 31 other teams in the league.
Here is the list of targets the Jets have given Wilson by each week:
Is it a coincidence that the Jets' best offensive games have come this season when Wilson was targeted more than 10 times? Is it further coincidence that the worst outings from New York's offense come when its star receiver doesn't get the ball?
Through six games, Wilson is in the top 10 across the NFL in targets, but those numbers don't tell the whole story. The Jets aren't scheming their top player open in their offense, making everything harder for the group than it has to be.
It's also why the team's 2-4 mark is weighing on the receiver more than ever.
Eventually, the arguments that the Jets need to spread the ball around will get thin. Eventually, the consistent losing will reach a tipping point for Wilson.
Through six games, the lack of a consistent plan to get him the ball is only exasperating that very thought. If something doesn't change soon in the win column, as well as his targets, Wilson may finally get to a point of asking something of the team they have tried to avoid for years:
A future without each other.

title: 3 Best 2027 Free Agent Quarterbacks the Eagles Could Consider With Jalen Hurts's Cloudy Outlook
full_text:
It's been a tumultuous season for the Eagles . Two nail-biting wins to begin the campaign have been followed by four devastating losses in a row. It marks the first time the Eagles have lost four consecutive games since head coach Nick Sirianni was hired in 2021.
The disappointment on the field is compounded by injuries, none more impactful than the one suffered by quarterback Jalen Hurts. The three-time Pro Bowler was placed on the injured reserve due to a blood clot sustained in the Eagles' Week 4 loss to the Rams.
The latest update from Hurts's agent, Nicole Lynn, revealed that blood clots have been found in Hurts's lungs. No one can play football while taking anticoagulants, so Hurts will be sidelined for at least a few months as he takes blood thinners. His season is over.
Quarterbacks Tanner McKee, Joe Milton and Cole Payton make up the Eagles' current QB room. It's far from an inspiring group, considering McKee and Milton aren't even under contract beyond 2026.
General manager Howie Roseman will have to address the QB position one way or another during the upcoming offseason. Signing a free-agent signal-caller would be one way to provide depth without surrendering important draft capital.
The Vikings have been one of the league's biggest surprises in 2026, logging a 5-0 record for the second time in the past three years. Quarterback Kyler Murray has started four of those five victories. He was inactive in Week 2 due to a concussion.
The former No. 1 overall pick has completed 68.3% of his passes for 662 yards and two touchdowns (two interceptions). Murray has also showcased his dual-threat capabilities with 93 yards on 20 carries. His 3,286 rushing yards since 2019 are the fourth-most among NFL quarterbacks.
Murray's rushing talent and off-script playmaking skills are comparable to Hurts's, which could make him a viable No. 2 option in 2027. In the scenario that Philadelphia decides to move on from Hurts, it could do a lot worse than a 29-year-old mobile quarterback with 91 career games under his belt.
The Raiders' offseason signing of Kirk Cousins wasn't considered a needle-mover at the time. The veteran has been one of the top passers in the NFL through six weeks, though. Cousins has tallied the most passing touchdowns (14) and the fifth-most passing yards (1,582) in the league.
Cousins has bounced around across 12 NFL seasons, playing for the Commanders, Vikings, Falcons, and Raiders. Accuracy and precision have allowed him to not only stick around but also compete at a high level. Cousins has led his squad to the playoffs three times, most recently in 2022 with Minnesota.
Fernando Mendoza is waiting in the wings in Las Vegas, so the signs point to Cousins entering free agency and landing elsewhere. The Eagles could ink him to a short-term deal as an experienced backup ready to step in at a moment's notice, or as a bridge QB capable of mentoring a young pro.
Tanner McKee will have every chance to prove to Philadelphia's front office that he deserves to be the starting quarterback of the future. The former Stanford standout put together a mixed performance against Carolina, completing 26 of his 45 pass attempts for 215 yards and one touchdown.
An impressive 19-yard touchdown pass to wide receiver DeVonta Smith flashed McKee's upside. He is a traditional pocket passer capable of anticipating routes and delivering well-timed throws. There needs to be improvement in terms of adjusting under pressure and creating plays outside the pocket.
McKee's chemistry with his teammates and familiarity with Philadelphia's coaching staff give him an edge over other free-agent options. That remains the case whether the Eagles stick with offensive coordinator Sean Mannion's system or shift elsewhere in 2027. Now is McKee's chance to take control.

title: Why Tanner McKee Might Be 'Right' Quarterback to Get Eagles Through the Season
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — Tanner McKee might not be the “right” quarterback to lead the Eagles to a sixth straight playoff appearance, but he is the only one who makes sense to be given the opportunity to try .
There isn’t anyone they can bring in, here in late October, who will learn Sean Mannion’s wordy offense in time to be the “right” quarterback. Maybe there’s an outside chance that rookie Cole Payton could get some playing time if McKee falters or gets hurt, but it’s McKee who gives them their best hope of making a run in a bad NFC East.
If he gets hurt, there likely won’t be a sixth straight postseason berth. Even if he stays healthy, that streak may end, and the season will conclude on Jan. 3 in San Francisco.
McKee is in his fourth season, and though he is in his first year in Mannion's scheme, he has been around most of his teammates, and they like how he commands the huddle.
Are there things to be learned? Absolutely, and McKee will have more time to learn them after having just two and a half practices to get starter reps in preparation for the Panthers.
There is no question he needs to play better if the Eagles—mired in a four-game losing streak and sitting at 2-4 but only one and a half games behind the Giants—want to go anywhere.
McKee made just his third career start last Sunday in a 25-14 loss to the Panthers and, implausibly, was asked to throw the ball 48 times. He attempted 45 passes and was sacked three times while completing 26 of his 45 throws (57 percent) for 215 yards and a 19-yard touchdown strike to DeVonta Smith.
Moving forward, McKee realizes the status quo isn't good enough.
“My team needs me to be better,” said McKee after the loss. “I need to be better. I am so much better, and I'm looking forward to learning everything and becoming the player that I know I am and that I can prove that I am. A lot of things, obviously, that were frustrating, that fall on me.”
McKee's previous two regular-season starts were in meaningless Week 18 games. These games are important. He has waited nearly four years to play in one, and that opportunity is here.
It’s never easy for a backup quarterback to step onto the field, no matter the situation. For McKee, it is even more challenging because the Jalen Hurts saga hangs heavily over the team. The handling of the quarterback’s blood clot will be a week-long topic at minimum.
Dealing with distraction...
It is a distraction that McKee and the rest of his teammates must find a way to ignore. And, speaking of those teammates, the challenge facing McKee is even greater still because of the insane number of injuries the team has had to endure and because the offensive line is patchwork, following a retirement, a trade, and a knee injury to center Drew Kendall.
Maybe the line gets Kendall and Landon Dickerson back at left guard for Monday night’s home game against the Cowboys. Maybe Saquon Barkley ends his injury absence after two games and is ready to return after battling a hamstring injury.
“It's another opportunity to grow, to get better,” said McKee. “I think that's something that's very positive about this team, and we're all we have. That's all we need. I think people underestimate how tight-knit we really are.”

title: Eagles Must Be More Transparent With the Jalen Hurts Situation Moving Forward
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — The Jalen Hurts blood clot drama isn’t going away anytime soon . The quarterback is doing well and is expected to make a full recovery, and that’s great news, but there need to be more answers than the ones head coach Nick Sirianni didn’t provide on Monday.
To be fair, the head coach shouldn’t be the one answering the whys and hows of a saga that has become a national news story, with a lengthy segment airing on Monday night’s "ABC World News Tonight."
The lingering questions should be answered by those above Sirianni's pay grade , which in this case are general manager Howie Roseman and maybe even owner Jeffrey Lurie. It is Roseman, however, who oversees virtually everything in the organization, and that includes all things medical, strength and training, and sports science.
Roseman should have been front and center on Monday, along with, perhaps, a member of the medical team or training staff. It’s not too late to make the GM available to help answer some of the lingering questions about why Hurts was allowed to play in the game against the Jaguars and why he was allowed to take an eight-hour transatlantic flight back just hours after the game.
It would clear things up, and in these matters, transparency helps, if only to eliminate any whiff of mistrust that could be harbored by the fan base and, more importantly, by the players inside the locker room.
There are privacy issues to navigate, and Hurts is a very private person, so the answers may not be forthcoming,  and maybe that is a directive from him and his representatives. There’s a chance that Roseman wants to engage on the issue but simply can’t for those reasons.
Still, it’s not a very good look to just run Sirianni out there to face the fire. All the coach did when pressed repeatedly during his day-after-game Zoom call was say that he isn’t a medical professional, that he leans on the medical experts and has full trust and full faith in them.
Sirianni's job is to coach football, and right now, with the Eagles mired in a four-game losing streak, that is where his attention needs to be, not answering questions about decisions he had little to no hand in making.
It should be noted that on Tuesday afternoon, the NFL wrapped up an investigation of the injury reporting on Hurts' calf and the clearance process for the QB ahead of their game in London. The league noted that the Eagles' medical personnel were in constant communication with the NFL and the Cleveland Clinic in London leading up to the game. The NFL's Chief Medical Officer was fully looped into the treatment plan after a superficial blood clot was initially discovered in Hurts' calf.
The Eagles have worked closely with Hurts’ agent Nicole Lynn, whose name was attached to the statement released on Monday, but team officials likely helped craft the message.
The statement did not go far enough. More is needed.
When Andy Reid was the head coach, he would make head trainer Rick Burkholder available whenever necessary, for injuries big, small, and confusing, like the Mike Patterson health scare on Aug. 3, 2011.
It was during a training camp practice that day when the defensive tackle collapsed and had a three-minute seizure. Burkholder and his staff were the first on the scene, and it wasn’t long before he was answering questions from the media.
Patterson had surgery a few months later to remove a tangle of blood vessels near his brain that caused the episode, and he made a full recovery to continue playing.
The Eagles have moved away from making a member of their training staff available since Reid left. Roseman believes the team benefits from letting only one person be the voice of the organization during the season.  And that's OK—except for when something like Hurts happens.
This was scary stuff, no less scary than the day Patterson collapsed. In crises like these, transparency helps to alleviate some of that fear.
It’s not fair to Sirianni or the Eagles in the locker room to let unanswered questions fester, especially with 11 more games to play. Distractions like this won’t make anyone forget about Hurts or whether the Hurts episode was handled properly.

title: Just-Released Veteran RB Could Be Immediate Band-Aid for Eagles' Backfield
full_text:
The early 2026 NFL season hasn't exactly been kind to the Eagles' offensive unit. Heading into a Week 7 clash with the Cowboys, here's just a taste of the medical-related issu es that Philadelphia's offense is going through:
And that's without even mentioning the backfield's problems. A hamstring injury forced Saquon Barkley to miss another game, while Carson Steele exited last week's game against the Panthers early with a shoulder injury. Fellow RBs Tank Bigsby and Will Shipley each found their way onto the IR this month, too, underscoring how Philadelphia could benefit from an extra set of legs.
Fortunately, a potential band-aid for their backfield woes just became available.
On Tuesday morning, NFL insider Ian Rapoport reported that the Giants have released veteran RB Najee Harris , making him a free agent. The former Pro Bowl rusher signed a one-year contract with the Eagles' NFC East rival after tearing his Achilles tendon last season, but a slow start to the year had the Giants ready to turn the page before October ended .
In five games (one start) with New York, Harris converted 31 carries into 99 rushing yards, all while also recording a five-yard catch and one fumble. Those numbers won't blow anyone away, especially coming from a four-time 1,000-yard rusher. At the same time, it doesn't mean Harris isn't worth the Eagles' time and attention.
The 28-year-old RB hasn't popped off lately, but his performance against the Titans in Week 2 showed the type of help he can provide. He averaged 5.8 yards on nine carries for 52 rushing yards, which was his best effort since Week 17 of the 2024 season (74 rushing yards vs. the Chiefs). He might not be capable of that every week, but it's still better than Dameon Pierce's best performance this season (35).
Harris hasn't played for the Eagles before, but he also wouldn't exactly be a new face to some in the locker room. After all, the two-time CFP National Championship-winning RB knows Dickerson, Hurts, and DeVonta Smith from their incredibly successful time at Alabama, and a potential reunion could motivate Harris to prove that he has plenty left in the tank.
Dickerson mostly played center during his two years with the Crimson Tide, which coincide with Harris's most productive seasons in the program. It's also worth noting that Harris recorded his second-most touchdowns (five) and yards per carry (6.6) when rushing to the left side of the center spot compared to any other direction , per Pro Football Focus , further illustrating how a reunion with Dickerson could benefit the ex-Giant.
All of this isn't to say he deserves a 53-man roster spot (he'd need to prove himself first), but Harris could be a solid fill-in for the next little stretch. After all, he could be a game-day practice-squad promotion three times for the Eagles, which is exactly how many games they have left until their Week 10 bye. That's enough runway to let other names heal before general manager Howie Roseman decides what he wants to do at the trade deadline .
And if things don't work out, a split would be painless.
In the meantime, the Eagles better act fast before another RB-needy team beats them to Harris.

title: Medicine Is Not Prophecy: Eagles Have Done Their Best With Jalen Hurts Saga
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — On Monday, the Eagles and quarterback Jalen Hurts’ agent, Nicole Lynn, released a joint statement that ended any remaining uncertainty about the rest of the QB1’s 2026 season .
What began as a superficial vein thrombosis in Hurts’s left calf has been updated to a deep vein thrombosis with bilateral pulmonary emboli—blood clots in both lungs.
Hurts is clinically stable, has no significant functional limitations, and is expected to make a full recovery with no long-term effects. His treatment is anticoagulation with blood thinners, which precludes contact activities.
A typical time frame for that treatment is three months, which will more than likely end Hurts’ season .
The timeline that produced this diagnosis is now public and, in places, unsettling for the general public. What we know is that Hurts believed he was cleated in the calf during the Oct. 4 loss to the Rams. He reported it to the Eagles’ training staff on Oct. 8, practiced fully the next day, and flew to London for a Week 5 matchup against the Jaguars.
An ultrasound there revealed a superficial clot. Specialists and the team’s medical staff concluded that activity and mobility were important and that he could safely play against the Jaguars in London. He did so on limited rest, first reported as 36 hours with no sleep, before being corrected by Lynn to Hurts, at least getting some rest at the stadium (h/t Tom Pelissero).
Just spoke to Jalen Hurts’ agent, Nicole Lynn, who clarified that while Hurts was up until early Sunday morning getting evaluated at a hospital, he was able to sleep upon rejoining the team and the Eagles set aside a room for him at the stadium. Videos from the stadium show Hurts… https://t.co/G35Tn1poa4
It's fair to say mistakes were made and to argue that the Eagles should have erred on the side of caution. That said, the circumstances included a tough-minded competitor pushing to play for an organization trying to halt a rare losing streak.
A follow-up scan later showed movement in Hurts' clot, and he was ruled out of last Sunday’s loss to the Panthers and placed on injured reserve before further evaluation produced Monday’s more serious diagnosis .
Eagles coach Nick Sirianni has deferred repeatedly to the medical experts.
“I’m not a medical expert,” he said. “I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them.”
The organization has emphasized transparency, so perhaps general manager Howie Roseman should have stepped in to explain the layered decision-making protocols rather than letting Sirianni die on the vine as the spokesman for a decision that is too important for public lip service. ⁠
It's natural, especially in a city as passionate as Philadelphia with a team not used to losing—dropping four consecutive games—for questions to surface.
Why was Hurts cleared to play in London? Why was he allowed to fly back immediately? What was the precise overnight hospital timeline in the U.K.?
Pulmonary emboli can be life-threatening without proper treatment; athletes and long-haul travelers have known risk factors. Fans and observers are right to care about player safety.
Yet the baseline assumption that should guide any serious reading of the medical record here is simpler and more grounded: at each step, the people involved—Hurts, the Eagles’ medical staff, independent specialists in London, and later additional experts—were making the best decisions they could with the information available to them in the moment.
Superficial thrombophlebitis is not the same as deep vein thrombosis. Initial imaging and clinical judgment can look different from what subsequent monitoring reveals. Clots evolve. Medicine is iterative; it is not a single snapshot that guarantees a perfect outcome.
Sometimes information is incomplete. Sometimes a small clot moves. Sometimes combining a provoked injury with travel and the physical demands of the sport produces a progression no one anticipated on the first ultrasound.
There is no public evidence of recklessness or ignored red flags; however, there is evidence of evolving clinical findings and adjustments to the medical plan.
In the immediate future, the Eagles turn to Tanner McKee and the rest of the rost er while Hurts focuses on treatment and recovery.
Longer term, the episode should be a stark reminder of the limits of even careful, expert-driven decision-making under uncertainty. Professional sports in passionate sports markets like Philadelphia will always generate second-guessing when a star’s season ends.
The more durable takeaways are quieter than the grift from those making declarative medical statements without the expertise to do so. The people closest to this situation operated with the data in front of them, adjusted as new information arrived and are now managing a serious but treatable condition, with an expected full recovery for Hurts.
In the medical field, that’s Occam’s Razor: the simplest explanation is usually the correct one.

title: 3 2027 QB Draft Prospects Suddenly on the Eagles' Radar With Jalen Hurts Done for the Year
full_text:
It's been over six years since Eagles general manager Howie Roseman told reporters, "We want to be a quarterback factory." It was in reference to drafting quarterback Jalen Hurts in the second round of the 2020 NFL Draft, despite having starter Carson Wentz inked to a long-term deal.
Roseman drafted Hurts to be a high-upside backup and long-term starting option. It's a move that worked in his favor, considering Hurts led the Eagles to a Super Bowl title. Roseman has an opportunity to make a similar move, with Hurts having two years left on his contract.
Hurts was placed on the injured reserve prior to Philadelphia's Week 6 loss due to a blood clot he sustained in his calf against the Rams in Week 4. The latest injury update revealed that the clot has also become present in his lungs, and he will need to take blood thinners for a few months .
It's an update that rules Hurts out for the rest of the 2026 season. Backup quarterback Tanner McKee will command the offense moving forward, but he's slated to hit restricted free agency in March, as is Joe Milton.
The Eagles currently have eight picks in the 2027 NFL Draft that Roseman could use to add a new face to the QB room, including these three options.
Miami has climbed to the top of the AP rankings for the first time since 2002 with a 6-0 record. Quarterback Darian Mensah's consistency and poise have been on full display. The junior leads all of college football with a staggering 80.8% completion rate and boasts an 18:1 touchdown-to-interception ratio.
Calmness in the pocket and an ability to hit receivers in stride pop out in Mensah's game. The 6'3" quarterback possesses great anticipation skills and the shiftiness to scramble for a first down when protection crumbles. He'll need to clean up his turnovers to be successful at the NFL level.
Mensah is expected to be a high first-round pick, though projections can change before June arrives. The Eagles are one of 14 NFL teams with fewer than three wins through Week 6. Landing a top-10 pick would provide a clear chance to draft Mensah. Anything lower, and a trade up may be necessary.
This would be the home run swing option for Howie, and one that makes his plan for the future clear.
Trinidad Chambliss remains a polarizing prospect .
On one hand, he has excelled since taking over the starting gig at Ole Miss, completing 66.6% of his passes for 5,613 yards and 36 touchdowns (seven interceptions) in 21 games. Chambliss has added 654 yards and 14 touchdowns on the ground.
On the other hand, he is one of the oldest quarterback prospects at 24 years old. Most of his collegiate career was spent at the Division II level. There's no denying the upside Chambliss possesses, though. His improvisational style and deep-ball placement make him thrilling to watch.
Chambliss's draft projections vary from a first-round pick to a Day 2 selection. He exhibited impressive composure when he sat behind Ole Miss starter Austin Simmons, waiting for an opportunity. Roseman could snag Chambliss, especially if he falls in the draft, to develop behind Hurts.
Roseman has drafted a late-round quarterback in three of the past four years. That includes Tanner McKee (sixth round in 2023), Kyle McCord (sixth round in 2025), and Cole Payton (fifth round in 2026). LaNorris Sellers's dual-threat capabilities would make him an intriguing addition to that list.
The South Carolina quarterback has shown off an elite arm in college, regularly launching the football 50-plus yards down the field. His 6'3", 240-lbs frame allows him to shake free rushers and bulldoze defenders for a few extra yards. Quarterback sneaks would be no problem for Sellers.
Holding onto the ball for too long has gotten Sellers into trouble. Less hesitancy in the pocket will be needed to thrive in the NFL. Untapped potential is what a late-round quarterback is all about.
The Eagles' front office has had a front-row view of what an athletic QB unafraid of contact can become.

title: Jalen Hurts's Absence Changes More Than 2026 Outlook for Joe Milton
full_text:
The Eagles' 2026 season took a major shift on Monday when the latest news about quarterback Jalen Hurts's blood clot issue hit the internet . Nicole Lynn—Hurts's agent—announced that Philadelphia's starting signal-caller's clot moved from his legs to his lungs, forcing Hurts to pause all football activities.
"We anticipate that (Jalen) will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners," Lynn said in the statement. "In the meantime, he will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will have no long-term effects."
Although Lynn is confident in her client's full recovery, Eagles fans won't see Hurts on the field again this season. NFL insiders like Ian Rapoport and Adam Schefter reported that the 28-year-old QB's season is over , underscoring how letting Hurts play against the Jaguars in London last week was a huge mistake.
#Eagles QB Jalen Hurts, who is out for the season after several blood clots were revealed in his lungs, has been undergoing tests for days. Before the London game, Hurts was in the hospital until 4 am and did not sleep because sleep was a risk. He played without having slept. pic.twitter.com/avMUeBBOua
Losing Hurts for the season is a massive blow to a Philadelphia team still trying to hit its stride. De facto starting quarterback Tanner McKee delivered a good-but-not-great performance against the Panthers in Week 6, further adding to the gloom around the Eagles' QB room.
If that continues and Philly decides to punt the season, head coach Nick Sirianni may be open to looking at the recently signed Joe Milton.
The Eagles signed Milton to their 53-man roster off the Cowboys' practice squad last week, seemingly to provide depth until Hurts returned. But now that Philly will likely be without its gridiron general, it's safe to say that Milton is staring at a huge opportunity that could shape not only the rest of the 2026 season but also his role in 2027.
Both quarterbacks are on expiring contracts and set to hit restricted free agency in March. If McKee can't string together more impressive performances, the door could be open for Milton to show the Eagles why he deserves to make his first career start and should be re-signed and included in next summer's QB2 competition.
The Eagles rolled with McKee in Week 6 because he was their most game-ready option. Milton clearly hadn't been around long enough to learn the playbook, and rookie Cole Payton still needs to develop more. Unfortunately, McKee did little to squash any concerns against the Panthers, completing 26-of-45 passes (57.8%) for 215 passing yards (8.3 yards per completion) and a 19-yard touchdown pass to DeVonta Smith (h/t NFL).
Tanner McKee throws DeVonta Smith a perfect ball for the touchdown CARvsPHI on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/6xngV0MgMW
Not the worst performance, but also not one that screams that McKee can lead the Eagles to the playoffs. They might not even view him as a viable option for the QB room next season, especially if Hurts can't get back on the field as quickly as the team wants.
Milton is young (26 years old), has a big arm, and is experienced enough to give the Eagles another QB option in the present and future. The former 2024 sixth-rounder played six games in relief during his time with the Patriots and Cowboys, going 37-of-53 (69.8%) in the pocket for 424 passing yards, two touchdowns, two interceptions, and a 90.4 passer rating.
Milton would also add some mobility to the Eagles' offense, which McKee lacks. The Michigan/Tennessee product recorded 50 rushing yards (10.0 per attempt) and a first down on five carries in Dallas last season, whereas McKee sits at 14 rushing yards on three carries (4.7 per attempt) and two first downs.
That isn't to say that Milton could impact the Eagles' offense on the ground like Hurts does (very few QBs can), but it would at least unlock more options for Sirianni & Co. that McKee can't bring to the table.
If they want to see if he's a viable QB2 for 2027 and beyond, throwing Milton into the fire after the Week 10 bye could make sense for the Eagles. The aforementioned NFC East gauntlet represents the remaining games before Philadelphia's break, which is enough time to assess McKee and for Milton to learn the ins and outs of the offense.
Add that the bye week provides extra acclimation time, so it makes sense that Milton could make his first career NFL start at home against the Steelers in Week 11. A lineup of winnable games against the Cowboys, Cardinals, and Colts follows, which should be enough of a sample size to deduce what kind of quarterback Milton can be before the final stretch of the regular season begins.
Again, McKee is the Eagles' starting quarterback moving forward, barring a massive disaster. That said, Milton's outlook is impacted just as much by Hurts's absence, and it will be interesting to see whether he captures the brass ring and proves he belongs in Philadelphia's early plans for the 2027 season.

title: What Jalen Hurts's Agent Said About Eagles Quarterback's Long-Term Health
full_text:
Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts was placed on injured reserve for one reason—he is on blood thinners to help with the blood clot in his calf, and you can’t play football while taking anticoagulants.
On Monday, a statement released by his agent, Nicole Lynn, said that Hurts's prognosis is “very good and we expect a full recovery.”
pic.twitter.com/aInIuUYiQJ
Hurts could return as early as Nov. 22, when the Eagles return from their bye week to host the Steelers. That would be the best-case scenario because he will have missed the required four games after being placed on IR on Oct. 17.
The situation, however, is fluid, and a return to play will likely take much longer. NFL insider Ian Rapoport reported that Hurts's season could be over .
Nevertheless, Lynn's statement revealed new information about how and when the clot was discovered.
Hurts was diagnosed by specialists in London with superficial vein thrombosis. Upon returning from England, more tests and monitoring were done. The current condition is deep vein thrombosis as well as bilateral pulmonary emboli. The initial diagnosis was a superficial blood clot, meaning it was close to the skin, but it moved.
An internet search indicates that bilateral pulmonary emboli mean that blood clots are present in the pulmonary arteries of both the left and right lungs. It goes on to say that a standard pulmonary embolism occurs when a blood clot, most commonly originating as a deep vein thrombosis in the leg or pelvis, breaks free, travels through the heart, and blocks an artery in the lung.
Symptoms could include blocked blood flow, sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain, rapid heart rate or palpitations, and dizziness, fainting, or coughing blood.
Ian Rapoport of ESPN / NFL Network reported that, before the London game, Hurts was in the hospital until 4 a.m. and did not sleep because sleep was considered a risk, so he played against the Jaguars—and put the team in position to win until a special teams gaffe—without having slept.
#Eagles QB Jalen Hurts, who is out for the season after several blood clots were revealed in his lungs, has been undergoing tests for days. Before the London game, Hurts was in the hospital until 4 am and did not sleep because sleep was a risk. He played without having slept. pic.twitter.com/avMUeBBOua
That raises another issue that Lynn’s statement did not address. If the diagnosis was so dire in the hours leading up to the game that it was a risk to sleep, why was he then allowed to fly back after the game?
As serious as this situation is, Lynn expressed optimism and calmness. She wrote that Hurts will be able to return to football-related activities once he is off the blood thinners. Until then, he “will remain active around the team and continue to condition.” She added that, “More importantly, we anticipate he will have no long-term effects.”
That’s the good news on the health front.
Hurts's return, whenever it happens, could also be good news, despite a four-game losing streak for the first time since 2020, when Doug Pederson was the head coach. Even at 2-4, there is a chance the Eagles could still be in the race for a third straight NFC East Division title because the division is terrible.
If the Commanders lose to the 49ers on Monday Night Football, it will be the first time a division has had its teams go winless on back-to-back weekends.
The next three games, however, will be important if the Eagles want to make Hurts’s return meaningful, as they face the Cowboys, Commanders and Giants.
