title: The Biggest Decision Robert Saleh Got Right Against Colts And What it Means Moving Forward
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans picked up their first win of the 2026 NFL season on the road, defeating the Indianapolis Colts 26-20 on Sunday.
Despite trailing by double digits at halftime , the Titans continued to fight and made timely plays in all three phases to finally break a seven-game losing streak dating back to Week 17 of the 2025 season.
One unit that deserves a ton of credit for Tennessee's victory over the weekend is the defense, especially the secondary. Though the group has had its struggles this year, they completely shut down the Colts' passing attack in the second half and also picked off two passes, one from safety Amani Hooker and the other from cornerback Cor'Dale Flott.
The secondary showed promise in Week 6, and one major coaching decision by head coach Robert Saleh may have been the difference-maker.
When the Titans announced the inactives for the Week 6 contest, starting cornerback Alontae Taylor was one of the names mentioned . Taylor was one of Tennessee's marquee free-agent additions, and just five weeks into the year, he was a healthy scratch.
Instead of playing Taylor, Tennessee gave the start to Joshua Williams, who made his season debut against the Colts after missing the first five games with a pectoral injury . Williams had 12 games of starting experience under his belt entering Sunday's game, and the Titans were hoping for solid play out of him to help the secondary.
Williams turned in an adequate day of work against Indianapolis in Tennessee's victory. The former Kansas City Chief played every defensive snap (83) and held his own in coverage, allowing two completions on five targets, 16 receiving yards, and a 48.8 passer rating, though Williams did commit a penalty.
Regardless, Williams proved to be an upgrade over Taylor in the back end for the Titans, validating Saleh's decision to hold the prized free-agent signing out. Saleh hasn't confirmed that Taylor was benched, calling it a coaches' decision, but based on his play, it's safe to say Taylor was benched for performance.
We'll see whether Taylor returns to the lineup in Week 7 as the Titans host the Cleveland Browns. Based on how Week 6 transpired, it wouldn't be a surprise if Williams receives his second straight start and Taylor sits on the sideline.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Titans Suddenly Cutting Veteran DT is Latest Sign of Team's Dysfunction
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans made waves throughout the NFL when three front-office executives were suddenly fired. Senior VP and chief revenue officer Adam Nuse, VP of creative Charles Jensen, and senior VP of brand marketing Erin Swartz were all let go in the midst of changes to the "business side" of the organization, per the team's official statement.
Tennessee's front office turnover has become a normal happening under President and CEO Burke Nihill. Somehow, blame continues to shift for everything going wrong for the football team in Nashville. New names come in and yield little improvement, and the cycle repeats.
Now, the team's general dysfunction has extended down to the roster. The Titans have officially released veteran DL Jordan Elliot due to an "incident" at the team facility.
Statement from the @Titans on DL Jordan Elliott. pic.twitter.com/blH9LdpFrt
Elliott missed Week 6 due to "personal reasons." Saleh specifically addressed Elliott's designation last Friday, saying: "He’s dealing with some personal stuff." Now, it appears the Titans have shone a public light on his recent absence, outright cutting the lineman for undisclosed reasons.
Between CB Alontae Taylor being deemed a healthy scratch vs. the Colts and Elliott being cut due to an incident behind the scenes, Tennessee's win from this past week is marred by questions about individuals such as these. The operation doesn't appear clean from the outside looking in.
Turron Davenport reported that the Taylor and Elliott situations are completely separate deals. That saves a little face, but still, that's two unexplained hiccups on the defensive side of the ball just within the last week.
Elliott hasn't been a crucial piece of the puzzle by any means for Tennessee. His activity in the run game with 1.5 STFs this season is about the only serious impact he's managed in Saleh's defense. Still, the vet represented a plug-in asset that the Titans made use of consistently.
Now, he's been removed, and the Titans "will have no further comment on the matter."
Fans can expect DT Nazir Stackhouse to get extended rotational looks in Elliott's absence. Stackhouse found his way into the gaps this past Sunday and had a noticeable impact in the run game. Tennessee may have a solution to losing Elliott, but the franchise frustratingly remains without an answer for why he was cut in the first place.
Perhaps the energy around news like that would be different if the Titans weren't 7-33 in their last 40 football games. That's not the world we're living in, however, which means the spotlight on the people making these decisions is hotter than ever.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Titans Rookie Power Rankings: Carnell Tate Runs Away With Top Spot After Week 6
full_text:
Things are slowly starting to come together for this Tennessee Titans team. You can say that it's already too late, or that one win doesn't mean much after five losses, but I'm just happy to see Robert Saleh get one under his belt.
There's a new air of confidence around this franchise, even if it's mild. With an AFC South victory over the Indianapolis Colts on the resume now, the Titans are pushing for a mid-season resurgence.
That possibility hinges, to some extent, on the team's play-making rookies in crucial roles. Here are our rookie power rankings after Week 6.
RG Fernando Carmona will be left off the list until he returns to the lineup. Let's jump in.
Carnell Tate has become comfortable at the top of our rookie rankings. He's proven his worth as a worthy fourth overall pick up to this point, and while Anthony Hill Jr. may be the more consistent rookie, Tate's offensive explosions are too hard to ignore.
Against the Colts in Week 6, Tate came down with six of his seven targets for 70 yards receiving. The pass-catcher also hauled in his first NFL touchdown in the fourth quarter, which helped spark what eventually became a Titans comeback win.
Tate already looks like WR1 next to Wan'Dale Robinson. Even as Cam Ward struggles to produce, Tate's efficiency hasn't taken any real hit. It's only up for the rookie receiver.
Hill remains top five in the NFL in tackles through six weeks, with 56. The rookie LB has taken no time at all to make an argument as the best player at his position for Tennessee, and he sits just below Tate on this list as a knockout pickup thus far.
Hill played all 78 of the Titans' defensive snaps facing Indy. Fellow LBs Cody Barton and Cedric Gray split their shares at 42 and 37, respectively. The rookie finished with nine total tackles, including one for a loss and one pass defended.
It's not even a question at this point who Tennessee's most impactful LB is, although Hill keeps finding ways to surprise on a weekly basis. Saleh plugged him into the defense from day one, and Hill has yet to slip in his role as a pivotal piece.
Keldric Faulk logged just one QB pressure vs. the Colts in Week 6. The rookie EDGE has slowly come down the runway in Saleh's defense this season, and he's yet to fully take control of the role that Tennessee traded up to draft him for.
Some of Faulk's adjustments have been clouded by the rest of the defensive line's solid performances up to this point. He's got time to develop under Saleh, and has plenty of potential to do so in time. Right now, however, he simply isn't there.
Per PFF, Faulk played just 29 snaps in Week 6. You could say his underwhelming season through six games has to do with opportunity, but that road goes both ways.
Until Faulk breaks out and adds to his current one-sack total, his position here is unlikely to change.
Of course, Nick Singleton was inactive in Week 6. Given his healthy state and on-off appearances in the backfield, I'm still including Singleton on this list.
Like Faulk, the rookie RB just hasn't shown enough flash yet to see the field consistently. Buried behind Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears on the ground, Singleton's role is set to remain limited until something shifts.
Pollard being moved before next month's trade deadline is the most likely scenario in which Singleton could see an uptick in production. However, if Pollard rides out the last year of his contract, we may have to wait until Singleton's second season to see what he's made of in an expanded role.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Grading Every Titans Position Group After Win vs. Colts: 1 Defensive Unit is Miles Ahead
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans finally got in the win column last Sunday, beating the Indianapolis Colts 26-20 in an AFC South showdown between two struggling teams.
The Colts got out to a 13-0 lead that honestly felt insurmountable at the half, but credit to HC Robert Saleh for keeping his guys locked in as they scored 26 points over the final two quarters to pull off the upset.
There was a lot of things to like in this game, along with plenty of reason to be concerned going forward. With that said, let’s take a look at this week’s positional grades.
QB Cam Ward made a handful of plays when the team needed him to, so that’ll keep him from getting an F. But the Titans simply need more from Ward than just 102 passing yards where 50% of his passes thrown short of the sticks, while also ignoring the middle of the field almost completely .
Tennessee desperately needs Ward to start being more aggressive with the ball if they realistically want any chance of turning this season around. Maybe the play calling is ultimately what’s holding him back, or maybe it’s a lack of trust in Ward to push the ball downfield.
Whatever the case may be, the Titans need to see better overall performances out of Ward going forward, or the skepticism and doubt surrounding his long-term future will only get louder with each passing week.
RB Tony Pollard led the way, running the ball 19 times for 76 yards, while RB Tyjae Spears only added one yard on one carry. As far as the former goes, Pollard had a solid outing overall.
It wasn’t anything to write home about, but he was able to help the Titans stay ahead of the chains and pick up first downs when the opportunity presented itself. Unfortunately, Tennessee finished the game with a negative rushing EPA of -0.17, per Pro Football Focus .
Therefore, I think a C is more than fair following a slightly above average (at best) performance from the Titans’ top ball carrier.
Rookie WR Carnell Tate is doing a ton of the heavy lifting on this grade. He made the most of the limited opportunities this passing attack allows, catching six of his eight targets for 70 yards, along with his first career touchdown.
The former Buckeye continues to flash signs of a budding star on the horizon. He finished the game with an overall grade of 87.2 , which was the highest offensive grade for either team.
Aside from the rookie, the rest of the receiver room accounted for just 25 yards combined. Partially due to Ward’s inconsistent play, but also due to self inflicted mistakes (drops, bad routes, not reaching landmarks on time, etc.)
The quarterback play undoubtedly needs to be better, but so do the guys around Tate, because right now, this offense is operating with only one consistent weapon at its disposal.
The tight end room continues to be non-existent, especially in the passing game. Neither of the Titans’ four tight ends caught a single pass yesterday.
Again, there weren’t a lot of passes to go around yesterday, and they did occasionally contribute to a couple of nice runs as well, but this group has to start contributing more than they are. Otherwise, it’s a safe bet that Tennessee will be looking to upgrade this position come springtime.
We gotta give this group some credit. They followed up an absolutely horrendous performance a week ago with an all-around strong outing last Sunday. The group upfront created lanes for Pollard to work with throughout the game.
More importantly, they didn’t allow a single sack over 23 pass blocking snaps. LG Peter Skoronski had one of his better games of the year, earning a grade of 74.2 after allowing a pressure rate of just 4.3%.
LT Dan Moore Jr. caught a lot of heat last week, most of it warranted, but that didn’t seem to faze him on Sunday. Moore pitched a shutout over his 23 pass-blocking snaps, allowing zero sacks, hits, pressures, or hurries.
If the Titans can continue to perform like they have most of this season, then this offense will have a puncher’s chance to right the ship as the season unfolds.
The Titans’ pass rush completely took this game over in the second half. In total, the group combined for a whopping 24 pressures, with DT Jeffery Simmons (eight), DL John Franklin-Myers (five), Jermaine Johnson (three), and Jacob Martin (two), accounting for 18 of them.
Simmons, in particular, was dominant once again, as evident by his team leading overall grade of 88.7. On top of his eight pressures, the All-Pro defensive tackle recorded six tackles, three run stops, two sacks, two tackles for loss, two QB hits, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery.
Simply put: Simmons is playing at a completely different level than the rest of his peers at the moment. As long as that continues, you can expect these grades to continue being rather high.
Rookie LB Anthony Hill Jr. continues to flash serious potential. The Texas product totaled nine tackles, three pressures, one tackle for loss, one pass breakup, one run stop, one
LB Cedric Gray also saw an increased workload, playing a total of 38 snaps while LB Cody Barton was on the field for 44 snaps. The trio of Hill, Barton and Gray are an intriguing group that should only get better with the more reps they get together.
The team decided to make CB Alontae Taylor a healthy scratch , and that bold decision certainly paid off.
The trio of CB Cor’Dale Flott (zero yards allowed), Joshua Williams (16 yards allowed), and Marcus Harris (25 yards allowed), combined for just 41 passing yards allowed between the three of them. Flott graded out as the Titans’ second-best defender, earning a grade of 84.7 after his solid performance that saw him reel in an interception.
Let’s start by giving S Tony Adams some credit. He stepped in for the absent Kevin Winston Jr. and played admirably, totaling 12 tackles, one QB hit, one tackle for loss, and one pass breakup.
However, S Amani Hooker was the star of this group. The former Hawkeye had a phenomenal outing on Sunday, recording 13 tackles, one pass deflection, and one beautiful interception in the red zone that directly took points off the Colts’ scoreboard.
Hooker nearly had a second interception late in the game that practically mirrored his pick from earlier in the game, but he wasn’t able to get both feet down the second time around.
The Titans’ veteran safety continues to make his presence felt along the backend, and if the pass rush continues to wreak havoc like they did against Indy, then there could be a lot more splash plays in Hooker’s near future.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that. He also writes scripts for EA Sports' Madden games, where fans may have heard his work.

title: So Crazy it Just Might Work: How Titans Would Benefit From Trading CB Alontae Taylor
full_text:
If you’d have asked me heading into this season who was on the trade block for the Tennessee Titans , a few obvious names come to mind. In fact, those names are still in play.
Veterans like RB Tony Pollard and LB Cody Barton remain in the conversation, even given the former's current hold on Tennessee's backfield production. Seeing either of those names move would check an expected box for a Titans team that just secured their first win of the season.
However, with the November 10 deadline approaching, one surprise name may be in trade contention. There’s a case to be made for trading CB Alontae Taylor.
Crazy, I know, but it makes sense for Tennessee in the present moment.
For the folks about to point out that Taylor was signed to a $58 million, three-year deal this offseason: That was my first thought as well. It’d essentially be moving off of an experienced piece and admitting fault in the investment.
But would it be better to hold on to a player that just isn’t taking to the system in the hopes that he eventually pans out?
The ongoing Calvin Ridley experiment in Nashville says no.
Saleh on whether Alontae Taylor is a one-week inactive, and if he's now week to week: We'll discuss it as a staff and make a decision that is best moving forward @Titans
If Robert Saleh’s decision to sit Taylor in Week 6 vs. the Indianapolis Colts is any indication of Taylor’s standing with the team, it may be better for the Titans to squeeze any potential-based trade value out of him right now.
Coach Saleh has talked about the complication of his zone-structure defensive system numerous times. He’s even touched on the learning curve that comes with that; see Cedric Gray’s sudden drop in snaps for a prime example.
It hasn’t been confirmed that Taylor’s issue is with the system. However, he’s struggled to make any significant difference in the Titans’ secondary through five games.
What’s worse, Saleh sitting him yesterday resulted in what was perhaps the unit’s best performance of the year. Two interceptions in the first game without Taylor suggests a loud issue with his involvement.
The Titans wouldn’t get a king’s ransom for Taylor. You’d likely be looking at a mid-to-late draft pick or another waning defensive playmaker. But if the defense is better off without Taylor already, what does Tennessee have to lose there?
It’s not even a one-game sample size that I’m judging this on. PFF has Taylor ranked 100th among just 102 eligible CBs in the NFL. It isn’t a coincidence that the team looked better without him on the field.
Maybe there’s a team out there that believes in Taylor’s progression. Maybe that team has more time to allow him to come to grips with a change. If such a team exists, the Titans couldn’t be blamed for embracing the quick-draw nature of that decision and making a call.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Titans Stock Report: 2 Players Rising and Falling After Win vs. Colts
full_text:
We've finally made it to a Tennessee Titans stock report that drops following a win. The vibes are a lot higher after Robert Saleh's team toppled the Indianapolis Colts on the road in Week 6.
However, a victory doesn't negate the struggles. Believe it or not, there's still a lot to dig into for a 1-5 team. A pair of individuals are rising, while another pair feature as fallers. We've got one picked out for each category on either side of the ball.
Entering Week 7, here are two players on the rise, and the fall, for the Titans.
Carnell Tate has become a regular riser, and for good reason. Tate is comfortably the most productive rookie WR the Titans have had through six games since 1999, per Mike Herndon, and just scored his first career touchdown against the Colts.
In addition to his toe-tapping score, Tate caught six passes on seven targets. It was a perfect performance from the first-year playmaker that helped shine a little light on an otherwise dour showing from the offense.
Tate is a big reason Tennessee utlimately pulled away from Indy, and deserves a nod as a riser on the Week 6 list. Don't be surprised if he's featured here again next week.
In spite of the team winning, Cam Ward continues to fall short of the mark at the QB position. He completed only 11 passes on 22 tries in Week 6, barely eclipsing the 100-yard mark and throwing a pick to match his touchdown in the process.
In fact, as the team improves around him, Ward increasingly looks like a weak link. He has the weapons on offense to succeed (see Tate, among others), as well as a line strong enough to give him the time he needs.
Ward had a better second half against the Colts; he avoided any disastrous mistakes and found Tate once in the end zone. But the Titans don't win this game without a season-best showing from the defense in basically every facet.
That's not enough from your first-overall pick. Ward remains on the downturn on this list.
Hooker's sideline interception in the first half was only scratching the surface of what became a defining peformance for the veteran S in Week 6.
On top of his pick, Hooker would finish with a team-high 13 tackles. His interception brought him to two total on the season, which means he's accounted for half of Tennessee's takeaways through the air.
Arguably nobody in this defense has benefitted from Saleh's takeover as much as Hooker. His breakout against Indianapolis earns him a spot as a riser this week, and PFF currently has Hooker ranked at 10th among 98 players at his position.
Hooker's steady presence downfield has been a huge win for Saleh's defense up to now, and in Week 6, he had perhaps his best game of the 2026 campaign yet.
The catch with Taylor is, of course, that he didn't play yesterday. However, it's the nature of his absence, as well as how the secondary did without him, that earns Taylor a spot at the bottom of this list.
It was Saleh's call to keep Taylor off the field in Week 6. The veteran, recently-signed CB was otherwise healthy and ready to go. In his wake, Hooker and the rest of Saleh's secondary heavily limited Daniel Jones' efficiency through the air. He was held to a passer rating of just 60.5, completing 22 passes on 42 attempts and, again, turning the ball over twice.
Saleh remaining shadowy on Taylor's availability going forward bodes poorly for the Tennessee native's hold on the starting CB spot. It's unclear exactly what's going on behind the scenes.
No matter what the reason is for his sitting, however, the Titans simply looked better without Taylor on the field. That means his stock is falling, and falling fast, heading into Week 7.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Titans Mill: The 2 Biggest Questions Tennessee Has to Answer After Week 6 Victory
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans have won a football game. It's shocking how much one victory can do for a team and their fanbase's general morale, although when you factor in an 0-5 start, I suppose the shock fades away a little.
Still, with Robert Saleh having found his way into the victory column, things are looking up for Tennessee. Yesterday's triumph over the Indianapolis Colts also pulled the Titans to 1-1 in the AFC South. Tennessee didn't win a single divisional game all last season.
There are improvements to write home about here. However, even in the wake of a win, today's Titans Mill poses two questions that Saleh and Tennessee still have to answer from this point forward.
The Titans may have put up 26 points in the second half vs. the Colts, but Brian Daboll's offense is still fundamentally broken.
12 of those points came from Joey Slye field goals. Seven more were due to a blocked punt that DE Femi Oladejo returned for a touchdown. That left precisely one passing score from Cam Ward to Carnell Tate in the fourth quarter, on Ward's way to an abysmal 11/22, 102-yard showing through the air.
Saleh's defense "locking in," if you will, only makes Ward and the offense's struggles look that much more dire. If Tennessee wants to build on their momentum from this point forward, they'll have to quickly decide whether or not this offense can succeed without making a serious change.
Is that change under center? At play-caller? Somewhere else between the lines? It's hard to tell, but the system as it's currently operating isn't up to par, even after a win.
Next, the Titans' defense went from allowing 26 points to the Houston Texans in a no-turnover blowout at home to holding the Colts to six less than that. Oh, and Tennessee picked Daniel Jones off twice, recovered a fumble, and again, blocked a kick.
Between the special teams unit making up for lost time and Saleh's defense clicking into dominant place, a question has to be begged about the odd absence of CB Alontae Taylor.
Taylor was ruled a healthy scratch due to a coach's decision prior to kickoff. The $58 million CB was brought in this offseason to anchor the Titans' secondary. Right after Saleh pulled him out of the lineup, that unit came down with two interceptions.
Could Taylor have really been so bad as to disrupt the entire defense? It probably isn't that dire, but PFF has him graded at 101 of 104 eligible players at his position. He has no interceptions this season.
After the Titans' victory, Saleh said Tennessee would discuss Taylor's status as a team and make a decision moving forward. It could've been a fluke, sure, but the Titans can't be shy about making this sacrifice consistently if the secondary looks that much better without Taylor.
Spending big on a player doesn't mean you're forced to play him over better options.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: The Titans May Have Won, But Cam Ward Still Has to Improve... and He Knows It
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans picked up their first win in emphatic fashion, as they overcame a 13-point halftime deficit to beat the Indianapolis Colts 26-20.
This was the Titans’ first win over the Colts since 2022. More importantly, it finally gives Tennessee something positive to build off of. Things certainly looked bleak in the first half. The Titans seemed well on their way to a sixth straight loss after being out-gained by 168 yards over the first two quarters.
In total, Tennessee produced just 64 yards of offense and three first downs.
QB Cam Ward accounted for 37 of those yards with an ugly interception on top of it. It was the kind of half that made you wonder how much longer this was truly sustainable. Fortunately, Ward played better in the second half, albeit nothing truly noteworthy outside of a couple of nice throws to rookie WR Carnell Tate.
Going into the third quarter, the Titans had an active streak of 13 consecutive scoreless drives dating back to last week. That streak came to a screeching halt after halftime as the Titans dropped 26 points over the final two quarters.
While the major nod has to go to the defense and special teams for their second-half performances, credit has to be given to the Titans’ young signal caller for making the winning plays when they were there to be made.
After Sunday’s win, Ward talked about the importance of complementary football on a day where all three units fed off each other to complete the second-half comeback.
“I think going into the second half, we didn’t play how we wanted to offensively. We still got a lot of things to clean up offensively. But the mindset didn’t change in the locker room," said Ward.
"It was a two-possession game coming out (of the half). Defense gave us a great turnover, and we were able to capitalize on that with a field goal. We really need seven, though. But at the end of the day, I think all three phases complemented each other at the right time.”
The second-year quarterback also talked about his budding connection with Tennessee’s rookie pass catcher and how important he is to this offense.
“He’s real big (for the team). He’s a great contested catcher like you seen today. He’s good at scramble drill. But the biggest thing about him is he doesn’t show no emotion. Each and every drive, no matter what happens, he comes back, he wants the football, and he’s trying to make plays for the team.”
Tate was undoubtedly the focal point of the offense. He accounted for 68 percent of Ward’s yardage on the day, catching six balls for 70 yards, along with the first touchdown of his career:
Tate gets his first NFL TD! 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/sQ7HfdARtC
However, outside of Tate, no other pass-catcher topped 22 receiving yards, resulting in Ward totaling just 102 passing yards for the game.
That’s something that has to change for this offense to truly take off. There will be times when Tate is taken away, and somebody else will have to step up. Unfortunately, nobody has proven that they’re capable of doing that for this team just yet.
But in reality, for any of that to happen, they’ll need more efficient play out of their young quarterback going forward, which is something Ward acknowledged after the game.
“I gotta improve each and every day. There’s still a lot of stuff that we have to clean up offensively. There’s a lot of plays that we want back for sure. But at the end of the day, we’ll take an ugly win over a loss each and every week."
The Titans are taking the correct approach to a win like this. Enjoy it, but make no mistake about it, there’s still a lot of work to be done before this team reaches its full potential.
“We know [we have to be better]...'', Ward said. “we’ll enjoy this for the next couple of hours, and as we get into the building tomorrow, it’s time to reset and try to get a win next week.” The Titans face the Browns next Sunday as they try to win consecutive games for the first time since November 2022.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that. He also writes scripts for EA Sports' Madden games, where fans may have heard his work.

title: Postgame Quotes That Matter from Head Coach Robert Saleh After Titans' Gritty Win Over Colts
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans have won a football game in 2026. Despite trailing 13-0 at halftime and showing no life for the first 30 minutes, the Titans put together an excellent second half and picked up a 26-20 win over the Indianapolis Colts on the road.
Everything came together for Tennessee in the final two quarters. The defense held the Colts' offense to one second-half touchdown and also forced two turnovers, the special teams blocked a punt in the fourth quarter and returned it for the go-ahead touchdown, and the offense did just enough to seal the deal.
Head coach Robert Saleh spoke to the media after his first win as Titans head coach, and here are the most notable quotes.
After starting his tenure in Tennessee 0-5 , Saleh finally captured a win as head coach of the Titans, and he admitted that it's a relief to win games in the NFL . Saleh added that Tennessee needs to get back to work as the team looks to build on the momentum gained from the comeback victory on the road.
"Winning in this league is relief," Saleh said. "We'll enjoy it for about 24 hours, but we gotta get back to work."
Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk has caught a lot of heat to start the year because of her organization's dysfunction being at an all-time high. Sunday's win over the Colts came at the perfect time for Strunk, and Saleh made sure to give her a shoutout while at the podium.
"I'm happy for Miss Amy – I apologize to her that it took a little longer than we all wanted. The players, these kids put in so much work, and this league is hard. We'd been close on a few occasions, and to knock this one out for them, I am much more excited for them than for myself," Saleh said.
Saleh acknowledged that his group, especially the defense, came out and played with a different fire in the second half. The Titans head coach credited superstar defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons for his message to the team at halftime and called Simmons the best defensive tackle in football .
"I want to give a special shoutout to Jeff Simmons, who I thought was outstanding in the locker room" Saleh said. "It made it more noticeable for me when watching and observing the team.. He's the best defensive tackle in football."
Despite facing double teams for most of the day, Simmons still tallied six tackles, two sacks, and two tackles for loss against the Colts. It's hard to argue that the franchise has seen a more dominant defensive player in the last two decades than Simmons.
The Titans will look to kick off a winning streak next week as they return home to face the Cleveland Browns. Though Tennessee still has a lot of work to do , it's nice to get their first win as October nears its end.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: 3 Major Takeaways From Titans' Wild Comeback Victory vs. Colts: Robert Saleh Finds Identity in Defense
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans have finally found their way into the victory column. After trailing the Indianapolis Colts 13-0 at the half, Tennessee stormed back in the final two quarters to claim a 26-20 victory on the road. We'll take the hit for out first-half pessimism.
Tennessee may be 1-5, but the Titans are 1-1 in the AFC South. Robert Saleh needed a win in the worst imaginable way, and he secured just that with his back against the wall in Week 6.
Here are our three biggest takeaways from the Titans' first win of 2026, starting with Saleh's most notable success of the day.
With six sacks, one fumble recovery, and two interceptions, Robert Saleh’s defense more than made up for their lackluster showing against the Houston Texans last week.
Was benching CB Alontae Taylor all it took to unlock the secondary? Let’s hope not, if not only for the sake of the nearly $60 million that Tennessee invested in him this offseason. Whatever Saleh did, it has to be replicated going forward.
We’ll mention the blocked punt in the fourth quarter, too, even given that special teams get the particular nod there.
This is the biggest takeaway from today by far. It wasn’t a perfect showing, but a winning one nonetheless. Saleh’s team may have found their identity in his defense.
Cam Ward has thrown for 200 yards just once this season with Tennessee. After today, his season touchdown-interception split has come to an even four and four.
Even as his weapons improve and the defense does their part, Ward’s numbers beg for an answer. Today, the second-year QB completed only 11 passes on 22 attempts for 102 yards. His puzzling interception late in the second quarter defined yet another disappointing showing under center.
Tennessee may have won this game (and Ward deserves credit for leading a fair second half), but the Titans still very much have a problem under center, even if the rest of this roster is beginning to make up ground as a full product.
What’s worse, it’s hard not to think that Ward and the offense are running out of time to grow. We'll take a win for now, but Ward didn't do enough therein to wash his own worries away.
After hauling in just one catch on five targets vs. the Texans last week, rookie WR Carnell Tate more than returned to form against the Colts. The first-year playmaker is officially on the board with a touchdown.
Ward found Tate on an out in the end zone early in the fourth quarter, which helped Tennessee pull the score even at 13-13 on their way to a comeback. Tate would finish with six catches for 70 yards on the day.
What was initially arguable as an untimely has proven to be perhaps the sneakiest pick of the whole bunch. Tate looks like a star in the making within an offense that hasn’t come close to meeting their potential.
It’s only up from here for the rookie. Regardless of the team’s struggles in his opening season, the Titans appear to have a real cornerstone in Tate.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: When Could Terry McLaurin Return? What NFL History Says About Patellar Tendon Tears
full_text:
The Washington Commanders learned Tuesday that veteran receiver Terry McLaurin suffered a torn patellar tendon in his left knee during Monday night's 23–17 loss to San Francisco . McLaurin, 31, had to be carted off the field after suffering a non-contact injury in which he fell to the field and clutched his left knee. Dan Quinn spoke about it at his press conference Tuesday: "He'll get surgery, and he's going to miss the rest of the season. So I had a chance to speak with him last night on the plane and again after testing today," Quinn said. "Man, I'm gutted for him as a captain and one of our real leaders. So we're all here to support him. That was certainly tough news."
Looking ahead, NFL history shows us a median return timeline of around 11.4 months, according to a 2025 study in the Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine that examined patellar tendon and quadriceps tendon injuries among NFL players. The study identified 45 NFL players with patellar tendon tears; 26 of them returned to play at least one game (57.8% return rate). The middle 50% of return times ranged from approximately 9.7 to 12.6 months. Two solid, but different examples of players who returned from injury are former New York Giants WR Victor Cruz and former Saints/Seahawks TE Jimmy Graham. Both had the injury; both had different timelines to return. Cruz tore his patellar tendon on October 12, 2014 , against Philly, but also had a completely separate calf injury during his return that led to him missing the entire 2015 season. In September of 2016, he finally returned after 700 days and caught a touchdown in his return. Graham tore his on November 29, 2015, had surgery, and returned for the 2016 season. He did miss a lot of training camp and all of preseason, but by November 2016, Graham was producing at a high level again , including an eight-catch, 103-yard, two-touchdown performance against Buffalo. If your brain is already doing forward math, the study's median time to return to play was 11.4 months for those who returned, which would put McLaurin sometime around early October 2027. It is important to note: no timeline has been set for Terry McLaurin, and returning to practice, being cleared for contact, and playing in an NFL game are all different checkpoints. With McLaurin, an emotional, fiery team leader and captain, gone for the season, the team will now need more from Stefon Diggs and the other receivers on the roster . Quinn talked a bit about the depth at his presser Tuesday: "I felt him in so many unique ways this season, from training camp to in-season. For him to even start the game like he did, I thought was significant. So we do have a deep crew at that position, and we'll lean in on a number of the guys to find some of the unique roles that Terry does." McLaurin's contested catch ability is something the team will miss. Quinn acknowledged that, "Terry's superpower is really on the contested catches, and that's one of the things that makes him excellent. But it's a big hit, and we'll lean on a number of guys."
For those wondering, the Commanders do have a potential out in McLaurin's contract after this season, according to Spotrac , but as the graphic above shows, it would come with a considerable amount of dead cap ($25.5 million). There's been no indication Washington is considering that option, and the bigger question right now is what McLaurin's recovery will look like heading into 2027. title: Commanders Keep Fighting, but Dan Quinn Keeps Falling Short | Hughes’ View
full_text:
Watching the Washington Commanders in the first half of Monday Night Football was like a scary rollercoaster ride without the fun hills. I literally had to do a double take at halftime when I saw the box score and realized the 49ers had 17 first downs, the same number of plays Washington ran, as the offense failed to sustain drives and the defense struggled to end them. Those problems compounded each other. Honestly, to be down only 20-3 at the half was surprising after that display. The biggest first-half number was the total yardage: San Francisco gained 303 yards, while Washington gained only 90 and managed just two first downs. What happened in the second half was a combination of things that led to the Commanders somehow fighting back and making a game of it against the undefeated Niners. Niners fans will be quick to say it was all because Mike Evans went down with a stiff Achilles, and maybe it was because the guy is still a nightmare to cover for the entire NFL. No matter, Washington came back from 23-3 to make it a game in the fourth quarter.
49ers splits with Mike Evans tonight WOW 👀 Mike Evans ON field: +0.57 EPA/play, 9.0 yds/play Mike Evans OFF field: -0.14 EPA/play, 4.4 yds/play Passes only: ON field: +0.58 EPA/att, 50% success, 11.6 YPA OFF field: -0.54 EPA/att, 29% success, 6.8 YPA
Oddly enough, Quinn said after the game that the week of practice coming into the game was their best overall this year: "I loved the team’s week of practice this week, and I grade every practice, look at some KPIs that I want to see in each of them. So for a team, it was our best overall week leading to it," Quinn said. "So to have the performance in the first half was certainly disappointing, you know, like I told, um, it gives you a chance to play well. It doesn’t—doesn’t mean you’re going to, and you have to go execute in the spot." That doesn't sound like what the world laid eyes on Monday night. Those who watched also saw the team commit another "possible" gaffe: on fourth down near the endzone, Jayden Daniels threw the ball away without trying to score. Now, it's easy to say, well, there was also a penalty that could have been accepted, which is true, but if they tried and scored, that would have forced the 49ers to accept the penalty, and Washington could have kicked the field goal. Quinn said afterward that he knew it was fourth down; the video footage and the ability to read lips make most of us not believe him.
“Field goal.   Oh, that was 4th down?” certainly looks like lip readers believe Dan Quinn was completely unaware that it was 4th down and wanted to kick a field goal 💀💀💀 pic.twitter.com/yJYuAUmVZX
Regardless of why it happened, Washington outgained San Francisco 224–72 after halftime, and the coaches do deserve at least some credit for the improvement. Of course, the team would be better served by a consistent path forward where they play smart situational football and take the layups when they're available. I know analytics are a major part of the game these days; I get it that he's got someone in his ear telling him the percentages. Until he gets things completely running right, he needs to take the points in those types of games. As it stands, if he had in the first half, they would have been playing to get three points at the end instead of six. Second-stop coaches in year three do not still make those mistakes and stay employed. READ MORE: Commanders Report Card: Two Troubling Grades Expose Why Washington Fell Short vs. 49ers
Another fly in the ointment is that the team gets far too many penalties that seem to hit them at the worst times. Many of those are pre-snap issues, a problem that seems to start with the huddle breaking late in some games. The biggest dagger this week was Chris Paul’s facemask penalty that erased Jeremy McNichols’ 31-yard touchdown that would have been the go-ahead score. I know some will want to mention the intentional grounding penalty at the end, but if you watch that play again, no receivers have turned around at the moment the pressure came in on Daniels. It was better for him to take the intentional grounding and the 10-second runoff than to take the sack without a timeout.
On 2nd-and-10 with 21 seconds left, the #Commanders ran some variation of four verticals. Obviously the interior pressure is what blew the play up, but I just don't get this play call from OC David Blough. It gave Daniels nowhere to go. They still had time for a shorter throw. https://t.co/qVYYAJiZ9I pic.twitter.com/symsvYLTcj
The bigger question is why David Blough is sending Daniels out with no check-downs or even receivers who peek back in to see if he's in trouble. Without some sort of safety net , the play was open to failure the moment it started. Add that the 49ers sent only three rushers after Daniels, who had six blockers protecting him, and you can see problems here beyond personnel. The players clearly respond to Quinn, but they need more consistency and control over situational football across four quarters each week. It doesn't help that he has not one, but two rookie coordinators , which adds to the normal growing pains. The problem, of course, is that with only one win, Quinn is facing win-now status with no room for error. Even as a nice guy, Quinn doesn't need sympathy here, as he painted himself into this corner by hiring those two first-year coaches heading into year three. title: Commanders Report Card: Two Troubling Grades Expose Why Washington Fell Short vs. 49ers
full_text:
The Washington Commanders' last three weeks of winless football have provided far more pockets of hope than the results would imply, just enough to continually suck the fan base back into this frustrating product.
When the squad looked its most haggard, having relied on the rookie arm of Athan Kaliakmanis just earlier this month, in came Jayden Daniels to save the season the very next week. He was cleared for Week 5 against the New York Giants, and while he did tally a pair of rushing touchdowns in a loud return to action, his miscommunication that doomed Washington to a humiliating tie instantly overshadowed any good he contributed.
Again, this time on a primetime Monday Night Football slate, his group fell short of a last-second win . At least now, it was against a proper contender in the San Francisco 49ers, who improved to 6-0, and the ending wasn't quite as uniquely hare-brained. It did, however, include some of the squad's wildest swings in consistency; had the uncoordinated offense and leaking defense managed to seize any momentum before the second half, this latest collapse folded within a comeback attempt wouldn't have been quite so dramatically necessary.
Count this as another week in which Daniels' loudest mental lapses overshadowed his winning contributions. Had it not been for another joint brain cramp on fourth down suffered alongside similarly confused head coach Dan Quinn , he could have made something of one red zone trip in what eventually went down as a one-score finish.
Jayden Daniels throws it away on 4th down at SF 13-yard line Commanders were also flagged for illegal shift on the play pic.twitter.com/X8xTgnLY0b
If anything, his intentional grounding in that roaring final minute hurt their odds of winning far more than any first-half gaffe, but he still produced an overall positive outing. 300 yards and two touchdowns on 29-of-40 passing convinced fans who stuck through that sleepy first half that winning was never out of the question, with the gifted Daniels uniting the offensive front.
While decision-making remains a concern, especially off the heels of what promises to go down as an infamous final-moment blunder last week, he's still far from this situation's fall guy.
This is as hard a position group to grade as any. Had Chris Paul not been called for a facemask hold in the final minutes of the Commanders' rally, Jeremy McNichols' mad dash to the finish line would have stood as the go-ahead score.
Jeremy McNichols had a TD here that was wiped away from Chris Paul’s facemask penalty Heartbreaking pic.twitter.com/bvk5eSwiYt
Without that chunk play, McNichols, Rachaad White, and Austin Ekeler totaled 43 yards. Jacory Croskey-Merritt was missed after being placed on injured reserve yesterday, though it's hard to feel like this is a remotely contending running back room, even when healthy.
I'm granting a bit of grace here, given how brutal of a loss this particular group was faced with early in the outing.
Terry McLaurin left the game early on the medical cart after sustaining what looked to be a knee injury. His leg gave out mid-route, and early reactions to the longtime Commander's exit didn't sound optimistic.
The #Commanders have already ruled out WR Terry McLaurin with a knee injury. This is what happened: pic.twitter.com/bSnfNhxsWj https://t.co/Uny13N2zH3
That certainly stung the receiver room's depth, though they rallied well without him. Stefon Diggs caught a touchdown on one of his six receptions, Treylon Burks continued his breakout as a reliable deep-ball weapon, and Antonio Williams remained viable in the clutch, leaving Daniels with very few drops to reckon with. And it's a good thing the threesome performed admirably when they did; assuming the 31-year-old McLaurin misses extended time, this is the A-team wideout corps that fans should start coming to expect.
Count it: two straight weeks of 60+ yards for Chig Okonkwo. He and the Commanders' coaching staff seem to have found their stride in finding the best role for the jumbo receiver, as he has to be mentioned as helping to support Daniels' passing attack following a 69-yard outing.
Outside of Okonkwo, there's little to say regarding memorable tight end play. John Bates got his government-mandated reception early in the game as a reward for his blocking, while Ben Sinnott and Colson Yankoff combined for zero targets.
This isn't even an indictment of their pure blocking prowess. Several of these protectors, specifically Sam Cosmi, Chris Paul, and Josh Conerly Jr., actually held their ground over the course of the season and much of this specific 49ers matchup, but the never-ending slew of errors has to fall on the position group that can't keep their hands out of the cookie jar.
Penalties couldn't stop the Commanders from getting upfield, with five infractions falling on the offensive line. But with the game on the line, halfway up the field and outnumbering San Francisco's rushers six to three, Washington made time for one punctuating blocking error, allowing all three sack threats to collectively take Daniels down before he could fire any game-winning shot.
49ERS SECURE THE DUB WITH A GAME-WINNING SACK ‼️ pic.twitter.com/g8ysCLNgPr
We didn't learn anything new from this result, at least pertaining to the offensive line. As underappreciated as their roles are in football's social media highlight culture, Daniels can't survive and run a functioning scheme while the spot-starters and overtasked stabilizers sustain this level of clumsiness.
This group looked much more spirited after halftime, once the 49ers finally slowed down, but the pace they set at the game's electric start made the Commanders' front defensive line look as futile as it has been all year. They had absolutely no answers for Christian McCaffrey in the first half, whose 64 yards do little to illustrate the smoothness with which he located holes between the bodies, and Brock Purdy looked plenty comfortable quickly firing over the top when he was armed with his favorite targets.
Fans can still walk away with another Sonny Styles highlight as a disruptive in-coverage stopper, as he notched a second straight game with 13 tackles. Odafe Oweh and Shy Tuttle each got their sacks. If anything, though, fans will remember this particular defensive effort as uneven, with their varying effort and attention to detail against the 49ers' short-passing attack largely explaining the deep hole the Commanders fell into.
The defensive backs and safeties have been held to a high standard since Amik Robertson and Rasul Douglas started shining as starting-caliber deterrents, and Trey Amos' long-awaited return raised the stakes on their collective challenge to hold 49ers star Mike Evans down in the backfield.
Evans looked spry at first, grabbing a few balls over the middle in the lengthy matchup nightmare Washington fans feared, though he wouldn't remain in the game for long. His Achilles tendon soreness flared up, sparing the defense the task of guarding Purdy's top gun.
The deep-ball magnet pulled a few defenders out of the flat, but the secondary pieces, usually excellent at blowing up settling checkdowns, looked helpless against Purdy's dinking and dunking. Again, the intermediate section around the first-down markers seemed regularly unmanned, with few initial adjustments to boot.
Add this group to the list of positional rooms that need some consistency when the Commanders return from their bye.
This group wandered way too close to a flunking grade when Luke McCaffrey required video replay to prove that he didn't muff a fourth-quarter punt, a successful review that spared the return man from what could have been a fate-sealing call, that is, before the Commanders inflicted a few more wounds upon themselves with the offense actually on the field over the next few minutes.
Hold up... this ball never touched Luke McCaffrey. This is surely reversed on review. Surely... #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/XNWa1ASqqu
They felt…

title: Commanders Lose Terry McLaurin to Knee Injury, Carted Off Against 49ers
full_text:
The Washington Commanders lost receiver Terry McLaurin to what appeared to be a serious knee injury. The team ruled him out for the remainder of the game but hasn't provided a diagnosis or timetable for his return. McLaurin went down near the sideline late in the first quarter against the San Francisco 49ers while being covered by Deommodore Lenoir, grabbing his left knee as Washington's medical staff came onto the field. His leg was placed in a splint before he was carted off, with players from both teams coming over to check on him. McLaurin recently returned from the hamstring injury that kept him out against Indianapolis, playing last week against the Giants before heading to San Francisco. With Stefon Diggs also returning Monday after missing last week's game, Washington finally had both receivers back on the field with Jayden Daniels, who missed two games himself with an elbow injury. That didn't last through the first quarter, as McLaurin left after catching one 27-yard pass. UPDATE: Terry McLaurin suffered a torn patellar tendon in his left knee.
#TerryMcLaurin @Commanders By video, worry for left patella tendon rupture Leg just gives out. Horrible. 🙏 Would mean surgery and season. Carted off with airsplint. pic.twitter.com/haMuICJFxu
Washington still has options in the passing game, with Diggs, Antonio Williams, Dyami Brown, and Treylon Burks available at receiver, along with Chig Okonkwo at tight end. The Commanders have spent much of the first six weeks working around injuries, though, and losing McLaurin means Daniels will have to adjust again after finally getting some of his weapons back. As for how long McLaurin could be out, Washington hasn't given any indication beyond Monday night's game. Dan Quinn may have more information afterward, but the team will likely need to evaluate the injury further before knowing what it's dealing with. The Commanders have their bye in Week 7, giving McLaurin some additional time before their next game, but there's no way to know yet whether that will be enough. title: Commanders’ Late Rally Can’t Undo a Disastrous Start Against 49ers | Game Pulse
full_text:
FINAL: 49ers 23, Commanders 17 The Washington Commanders fell behind 23-3 before giving themselves chances to win late, but their comeback went unfinished Monday night in San Francisco. Washington heads into its bye at 1-4-1. Below are the final Game Pulse observations, organized by quarter, followed by the archived game feed. You can also see the full game feed at the bottom of this page, including play-by-play updates and social posts during the game.
- Washington was able to tighten the score at the end after the defense tightened up and forced the three-and-outs, but the first half was hard to watch. - At some point, somebody has to ask in the media if Dan Quinn thought bringing in new coordinators on both sides of the ball in year 3 was a wise decision. Clearly, it says Quinn thought his job security was very high. I still don't think Josh Harris and company will fire him in-season, but they'll fire him after if each week brings a new gaffe. - The rewatch will help me answer this more, but right after watching the game, I'd say this team is still fighting for Quinn heading into the bye despite losing their fourth game of the season. They missed Jacory Croskey-Merritt and need to game plan better around what they do have in Jeremy McNichols, whom they clearly trust. - I counted at least three major flags that were not thrown on the 49ers; that's not to say there weren't any on the Commanders, but for Washington, it's hard to beat the team and what seems to be the refs who miss hits where star defenders lead with the brim of their helmet. - Dan Quinn left more points on the field again, choosing to forgo points for chances that fail...all of this is adding up to Quinn's seat being hotter than the Iron Throne after it was smelted. - Where is the discipline? Penalty after penalty (seven for 66 yards) truly speaks volumes when they lose to an undefeated team by six points.
- Halftime gave Washington a chance to reset, but holding, a false start, and a sack made the opening possession look painfully familiar. - Holding San Francisco to a field goal was something to build on, but Washington needs more touchdowns before this turns into playing out the clock. - With McLaurin hurt , Washington needs to keep working through Okonkwo and Burks instead of waiting for Daniels to rescue every possession. The Niners are extremely aggressive on defense; Washington had ot work on making third downs shorter.
- Situational football is not the strong point for this team. When Jayden Daniels rolled out on fourth down and threw it away, after the ref later said the 49ers had declined the penalty, you could see Dan Quinn say, "It was fourth down?" To be clear, Daniels had just thrown it away on fourth down without actually targeting a player after they went for it, and the coach acted like he didn't know it was fourth down. YIKES. You ask Daniels to protect himself, so I get why he didn't try to play Superman, but is Quinn the only one who didn't know it was fourth down? I have real questions about this. - Washington has been getting killed by penalties. Most of them have put the offense in third and unmanageable situations. - The 49ers had 17 first downs in the first half; Washington only ran 16 plays.
- Washington had a ball go through Stefon Diggs' hands early on; if caught, that drive would have likely ended in seven points. Refs missed an unnecessary roughness after the drop, but hey, that's expected league-wide at this point. - The Niners have looked good; Washington finally stopped them on the drive as the first quarter ended, so let's hope they can build on that success. - Terry McLaurin being carted off is about as bad as it gets in terms of losing players.
- Washington has allowed 95 second-half points through five games, and now faces a San Francisco offense averaging nearly 31 points per game. Whatever the Commanders get done early, I’ll be watching how Daronte Jones’ defense handles the adjustments after halftime. - With Croskey-Merritt on injured reserve, it'll be interesting to see which direction the backfield goes in. McNichols joins Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler, giving Washington options, but how the staff divides those opportunities could tell us plenty about its plan to keep the offense moving. - Bosa’s absence helps, but Washington still has to make life easier on Daniels. The Commanders converted just four of 12 third downs against the Giants, and David Blough pointed to too many third-and-long situations. Getting something out of first and second down needs to show up tonight.
The Washington Commanders are in Santa Clara for Monday Night Football against the unbeaten San Francisco 49ers , looking to move past a game they had plenty of chances to win. Washington enters at 1-3-1 after last week’s 27-27 tie with the New York Giants, while San Francisco has won its first five games. Jayden Daniels makes his second start since returning from his elbow injury, but Washington needs more than another strong performance from its quarterback. The Commanders let a 14-point fourth-quarter lead slip away against New York, and those same mistakes could make for a long night against Brock Purdy and Kyle Shanahan’s offense. Washington placed Jacory Croskey-Merritt on injured reserve Monday and activated Jeremy McNichols, Trey Amos and Jordan Magee. Stefon Diggs is active , while San Francisco has ruled out Nick Bosa and Deebo Samuel Sr.

title: Commanders Place Jacory Croskey-Merritt on IR, Activate Three Ahead of 49ers Game
full_text:
After missing practice all week , the Washington Commanders have placed RB Jacory Croskey-Merritt (groin) and OLB Javontae Jean-Baptiste (pectoral) on injured reserve, meaning they will miss at least four games now. With the team's bye falling in Week 7, the two won't be eligible to return until Week 11 against the Cincinnati Bengals. With Croskey-Merritt on the shelf , Washington is getting Jeremy McNichols back, whom the team activated today, a move that shows he's ready to return from the quad injury that kept him on IR until the team opened up his 21-day practice window earlier this month . McNichols practiced fully this week and was officially listed as questionable on the team's final injury report. While his role isn't clear yet, McNichols will be available Monday night. Two defensive players were also activated: CB Trey Amos (ankle) and LB Jordan Magee (hamstring) are now eligible to play in Santa Clara as well. While the plan for Amos is still unclear, he'll need time to get familiar with playing in Daronte Jones' system, which he spent the entire offseason learning but didn't get much field time with in camp. With Jean-Baptiste headed to IR and Charles Omenihu already ruled out, Washington could use the additional defensive help. To finish off the roster moves , the team released LB Austin Keys, who was promoted from the practice squad before last weekend's Giants game. The team also elevated OLB T.J. Maguranyanga from the practice squad to the active roster for game day only.

title: Washington Can Jump From Last to Second in the NFC East Tonight — Commanders Daily
full_text:
Yesterday, the New York Giants (3-2-1), Philadelphia Eagles (2-4), and Dallas Cowboys (2-4) all lost . While the Giants still lead the NFC East, Washington (1-3-1) is the only team left in the division to play in Week 6 and could move from last to second with an upset victory tonight in Santa Clara . Under NFL rules , a tie counts as half a win and half a loss, so 2-3-1 gives Washington a better winning percentage than 2-4, giving the Commanders an opportunity to pull back to within one game of New York heading into their Week 7 bye. Of course, the other three teams play during Washington’s bye, so second place tonight would not be guaranteed to last through next week. On the flip side, if Washington loses tonight, it would drop to 1-4-1, and the NFC East would become the first division since the 1970 AFL–NFL merger to go winless in consecutive weeks in which every team played. The Commanders and Giants even played each other last week. Beating a 5-0 team on the road is never easy, but it's not impossible. Washington hasn't won on the 49ers' home field since 2004. Washington's 2020 win over the Niners was played in Glendale, Arizona. The rest of the NFC East gave Washington an opening Sunday. Beating San Francisco is the part the Commanders have to handle themselves.

title: Commanders vs. 49ers Weather Forecast for Monday Night Football
full_text:
The Washington Commanders head to Santa Clara, California, this week to face the San Francisco 49ers on Monday Night Football , and the weather forecast looks fairly manageable as Washington tries to pick up its second win of the season. Rain chances are low throughout the game, although wind gusts could still affect throws downfield and longer field-goal attempts. Kickoff at Levi’s Stadium is scheduled for 8:15 p.m. ET on Monday, Oct. 19, which is 5:15 p.m. for fans attending the game.
The National Weather Service’s hourly forecast for the stadium area keeps rain chances at 3% through the game. Temperatures fall as the evening goes on, with west-northwest winds easing later. NWS forecast updated Sunday, Oct. 19, at 4:26 p.m. ET / 1:26 p.m. PT. Monday’s hourly forecast:
Gusts are forecast to reach 21 mph from 5–7 p.m. Pacific.
For Jayden Daniels and Brock Purdy , those gusts are worth paying attention to when throwing downfield. Both quarterbacks will get a chance to see how the ball is carrying during warmups, but they’ll still have to account for changes in the wind once the game begins. The conditions at field level will matter more than the forecast number alone. The kicking game could require a little more judgment as well, particularly when Dan Quinn is deciding whether to try a longer field goal. Distance is already part of that decision, and a gust blowing into the kicker’s face could make an attempt less appealing than it looked before the drive started. Washington’s kicking unit should get a better feel for that in both directions before kickoff.
Anyone going to Monday night’s game should bring a sweatshirt or light jacket, especially if the plan is to arrive early and stay through the final whistle. Temperatures are expected to fall into the upper 50s by 8 p.m. Pacific, and sitting in the stands with a breeze could make that extra layer useful. The stadium’s event guide lists parking lots opening at 1:45 p.m. Pacific and general stadium gates opening at 3:15 p.m. Fans tailgating will have several hours outside before kickoff, so it makes sense to dress for the temperature when leaving the stadium as well as when arriving.
